chunks.heading: 4.1 Turbulent Weather
chunks.text: Definition Turbulence is the result of atmospheric and environmental effects, which can result in, light/moderate or severe turbulence. A rapid change in altitude usually causes large airspeed fluctuations resulting in undetected clear air turbulence. Flight Crew Responsibilities Flight Crew shall inform the Purser the type of forecast turbulence and the estimated duration Flight crew should switch on the Fasten Seat Belt sign during turbulence Purser/CCMs Responsibilities During turbulence, CCMs shall ensure passengers adhere to the fastening seatbelt regulation. When carrying out duties during turbulence, CCMs are advised to be cautious and avoid placing self in danger. In case of injury to crew, passengers or damage to property the PIC should be informed and a detailed Incident/ Accident report shall be forwarded to the cabin safety section. If carrying out a service/part of a service which may contribute to a safety hazard, the Purser may can-

chunks.heading: 4.1 Turbulent Weather
chunks.text: cel the service or part of the service. Service during Turbulence When the seat belt sign is turned on due to turbulence and If meal service is underway during this time, the purser shall communicate with the PIC to determine if it’s safe to continue with the service. In the event it requires for the crew to be seated immediately during a meal service, CCMs shall lock the carts and be seated. Hot beverages shall not be served while the seat belt sign is switched on to prevent potential spills and burns. Passenger Announcement The following PA announcement shall be initiated by CCMs: “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, AS THE CAPTAIN HAS SWITCHED ON THE SEAT BELT SIGN, PLEASE REMAIN SEATED AND FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS. PLEASE REFRAIN FROM USING THE TOILETS DURING THIS PERIOD. THANK YOU”.

chunks.heading: 4.1.1 Light Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
Signs
• Liquids in open containers may shake but might not splash
• Carts could be wheeled with slight difficulty
• Passengers might feel a strain against the seat belt Purser/CCM Responsibilities
1. Initiate the turbulent weather announcement. Ref 4.1
2. Maintain cabin lights intensity at “Dim 1”
3. Secure carts/containers in the galleys
4. Latch/lock all loose equipment in galley

chunks.heading: 4.1.1 Light Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
5. Secure the cabin
6. Check lavatories for passengers
7. Remove infants from bassinets and secure with a kangaroo belt
8. Cabin Supervisors shall report secured cabin/galleys to the Purser
9. Remain secured as required/advised Post Light Turbulent Weather The PIC shall inform CCMs when turbulence is cleared by switching off the “Fasten” seat belt sign.

chunks.heading: 4.1.2 Moderate Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
Signs
• Items could fall or be lifted off the floor
• Liquids might splash out of open containers
• Unsecured items could be tossed about
• Difficulty in being steady
• Manoeuvring the carts would be difficult
• Definite strain against the seatbelt PIC Announcement “CABIN CREW, BE SEATED”. Purser/CCM Responsibilities
1. Initiate the turbulent weather announcement. Ref 4.1
2. Maintain cabin lights at full intensity
3. On the way to the crew seat, check that all passengers are seated with their seat belts securely fastened
4. Secure carts/containers in galleys
5. Latch/lock all loose equipment in the galleys
6. Secure the cabin
7. Remove infants from bassinets and secure with a kangaroo belt
8. Check lavatories for passengers
9. Cabin Supervisors shall report secured cabin/galleys to the Purser
10. Curtains/class dividers should be opened and secured
11. Remain secured until advised by the PIC

chunks.heading: 4.1.2 Moderate Turbulent Weather
chunks.text: Post Moderate Turbulent Weather The PIC informs CCMs when the aircraft is clear of turbulence by switching off the “fasten seat belt sign”. Purser should initiate an announcement for CCMs to proceed with their duties.

chunks.heading: “CREW YOU MAY PROCEED WITH YOUR DUTIES”
chunks.text: As a precautionary measure, CCMs shall check on crew and passengers in lavatories/galleys/cabin and administer first aid/assistance as required. Any injuries shall be reported to the PIC.

chunks.heading: 4.1.3 Severe Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
Signs
• Items could fall or be lifted off the floor
• Liquids would splash out of open containers
• Unsecured items would be tossed about
• Walking might be impossible
• Definite strain against the seatbelt PIC announcement “CABIN CREW, BE SEATED”. Purser/CCM Responsibilities
1. Initiate the turbulent weather announcement. Ref 4.1
2. Do not attempt to check passenger compliance
3. If there are trolleys in the cabin, set the brakes on in their current location Put jugs/pots of hot beverages on the floor
4. Sit down immediately, in the nearest available seat (this includes passenger seats) and fasten seat belt/harness
5. Remain secured until advised by the PIC Post Severe Turbulence The PIC informs CCMs when the aircraft is clear of turbulence by switching off the fasten seat belt sign. Purser should initiate an announcement for CCMs to proceed with their duties “CREW YOU MAY PROCEED WITH YOUR DUTIES”.

chunks.heading: 4.1.3 Severe Turbulent Weather
chunks.text: CCMs should check on crew and passengers in lavatories/galleys/cabin and administer first aid/assis- tance as required. Any injuries should be reported to the PIC. The Purser shall ensure detailed Incident/Accident and or Illness reports are filed as required.

chunks.heading: WARNING : CABIN CREW SHALL NOT COMPROMISE PERSONAL SAFETY WITH SERVICE RELAT-
chunks.text: ED DUTIES DURING SEVERE TURBULENCE. THE PERSONAL SAFETY OF THE CABIN CREW IS THE PRIORITY.

chunks.heading: 4.1.4 Unanticipated Severe Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
Clear air turbulence at high altitudes is potentially hazardous to the safety of the aircraft as its presence cannot be detected prior to encountering. PIC announcement “CABIN CREW, BE SEATED”. Purser/CCM Responsibilities
1. Initiate the turbulent weather announcement. Ref 4.1

chunks.heading: 4.1.4 Unanticipated Severe Turbulent Weather
chunks.text:
2. Do not attempt to check passenger compliance
3. If there are trolleys in the cabin, set the brakes on in their current location Put jugs/pots of hot beverages on the floor
4. Sit down immediately, in the nearest available seat (this includes passenger seats) and fasten seat belt/harness
5. Remain secured until advised by the PIC Post Unanticipated Severe Turbulence The PIC informs CCMs when clear of turbulence by switching off the fasten seat belt sign. Purser should initiate an announcement for CCMs to proceed with their duties. “CREW YOU MAY PROCEED WITH YOUR DUTIES”. CCMs should check on crew and passengers in lavatories/galleys/cabin and administer first aid/assis- tance as required. Any injuries shall be reported to the PIC. The Purser shall ensure detailed Incident/Accident and or Illness reports are filed as required.

chunks.heading: 4.1.5 Anticipated Turbulence Weather Procedures
chunks.text: Anticipated turbulent weather shall be conveyed during the PIC/Purser preflight briefing, allowing cabin crew to complete cabin/gally securing procedures and secure themselves. Purser/CCM Responsibilities Ref 4.1.1 Post Anticipated Turbulent Weather Ref 4.1.1

chunks.heading: 4.2 Cabin Pressurization/Oxygen System
chunks.text:
The aircraft cabin is pressurized between 6000’ to 8000’ feet altitude. However, failure of the pressuri- zation system would result in loss of cabin pressure and supplementary oxygen is necessary for survival. The aircraft is equipped with two independent fixed oxygen systems.
1. Cabin/Galley/Lavatories/CCM stations – Chemical Oxygen
2. Flight deck – Gaseous Oxygen The supplementary oxygen in the cabin is produced through chemical reaction. When activated the generator casing can reach a temperature of 285° C (545 ° F). The area exposed to the passengers doesn’t exceed 66° C (150 ° F). The flow of oxygen to the mask is indicated by the inflation of the green portion of the reservoir bag.

chunks.heading: 4.2.1 Cabin/Galley/Lavatories - Fixed Oxygen System
chunks.text: Oxygen generators are installed in the oxygen stowage compartment above each row of seats. Each unit

chunks.heading: 4.2.1 Cabin/Galley/Lavatories - Fixed Oxygen System
chunks.text: contains a Sodium Chlorate oxygen generator with two or more continuous flow masks with breathing bags and a state indicator. Locations Masks are located in the cabin/galley/lavatories/CCM stations. The system when activated will supply continuous flow of oxygen for approximately 22 minutes. Spare Masks Spare oxygen masks are installed at each bassinet position, each lavatory, at every set of seats in the Cabin and at CCM stations.

chunks.heading: 4.2.2 Oxygen Masks Deployment
chunks.text: The oxygen stowage compartment doors could be electronically opened from the flight deck or manual- ly at each unit by using the manual release tool (MRT)Located under each crew seat. In the event of a loss of cabin pressure, oxygen masks will automatically deploy at 14000 (±500) feet cabin altitude. The power supply to the compartment door release mechanism automatically switches off after 30 seconds (to avoid risk of fire). Oxygen masks are engineered to deploy automatically in the event of cabin depressurization. This acti- vation is controlled by an independent cabin pressure switch that continuously monitors cabin altitude. It is essential to understand that this switch functions independently from the Cabin Pressure Control- lers (CPCs) located in the flight deck, which are responsible for triggering the CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT alert. When ALL oxygen masks deploy, Cabin Crew must immediately inform the Flight Crew. This is a

chunks.heading: 4.2.2 Oxygen Masks Deployment
chunks.text: vital cue for the Flight Crew to identify a possible depressurization event and initiate emergency procedures, including an emergency descent. However, this should be considered when ALL oxygen masks deploy and not in the case of partial deployment of the oxygen masks. Partial deployment of oxygen masks in the cabin is due to mechanical failures and not depressurization. In such instances, Cabin Crew shall follow standard fault reporting procedures and notify the Flight Crew accordingly. Note: The number of masks in each unit is indicated on the door stopper.

chunks.heading: 4.2.3 Activation of the Oxygen Flow
chunks.text: One drop down mask has to be pulled to activate the oxygen flow. Pulling the mask releases the safety pin attached to the generator by a cord initiating a chemical reaction. Passenger Announcement Purser may initiate a PA announcement, explaining the possibility of the burning odour. “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, YOU MIGHT EXPERIENCE A BURNING ODOUR DUE TO THE OXYGEN GENERATORS FUNCTIONING. PLEASE DO NOT HESITATE TO DRAW ANY FURTHER CONCERNS TO THE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION OF THE CABIN CREW”.

chunks.heading: 4.2.3 Activation of the Oxygen Flow
chunks.text: Note: Once activated, the oxygen generation cannot be stopped.

chunks.heading: 4.2.4 Inadvertent Deployment of Oxygen Masks
chunks.text:
Although the situation is not dangerous, the inadvertent deployment of oxygen mask could be an un- pleasant and a frightening experience. The following procedure should be adhered to: Purser/CCM Responsibilities Mask Deployed - O2 Generator Activated
1. Inform Flight Crew
2. Leave the oxygen compartment door opened and do not attempt to close it as the supply of oxygen and the activation of the power switch mechanism is a potential combination for a fire hazard
3. Try to relocate passengers and the masks should be removed by cutting it close to the generator.
4. In the event alternate seats are not available, CCMs shall brief passengers of the location/s a spare oxygen mask available in the vicinity by checking the door stoppers on the oxygen com- partments. The PIC shall be kept informed.
5. Purser shall make a log entry in the cabin defects log book. Mask Deployed - O2 Generator Not Activated

chunks.heading: 4.2.4 Inadvertent Deployment of Oxygen Masks
chunks.text:
1. Inform Flight Crew
2. Leave the oxygen compartment door opened
3. Advice passengers not to pull or stow the masks
4. Relocate passengers if possible
5. Do not remove the masks or cut the tubing
6. Purser shall make a log entry in the cabin defects log book. Note: Generator state indicator band is yellow prior to activation and will turn black after use due to the heat.

chunks.heading: 4.2.5 Flight Deck Oxygen System
chunks.text:
The flight deck oxygen system supplies gaseous oxygen. It has an optional adjustable facility of oxygen flow with ambient air or 100% oxygen on a continuous flow. Oxygen masks are stowed in a readily accessible console adjacent to each seat. The mask has a clear lens visor/microphone and a flow type adjuster. Donning the Flight Deck Oxygen Mask Could be worn using one hand:
1. Squeeze the red clips toward each other and pull the mask out of its box.
2. The harness inflates, oxygen flow starts, and the mask microphone is active.
3. Don the mask covering the nose and mouth and release the red grips.
4. The harness deflates hugging the head.

chunks.heading: 4.2.5 Flight Deck Oxygen System
chunks.text: 100% / Normal Selector When the flight crew selects the “N” position (normal position), the system supplies the mask with a mixture of ambient air and pure oxygen. When the flight crew selects the “100%” position, the oxygen system supplies the mask with 100% pure oxygen.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Decompression
chunks.text: Definition Commercial aircraft operates economically at high altitudes. An additional advantage of cruising at high altitude is avoidance of bad weather and turbulence. As altitude increases, the density of air and the pressure decreases. To breathe comfortably, the pressurization system of the aircraft creates a denser atmosphere within the cabin. There is always a possibility of loss of cabin pressure in any pressurized aircraft through a rupture in the aircraft’s structure. The rate of decompression depends on the cabin volume/size of the opening/altitude/Pressure difference and is categorized as slow or rapid decom- pression. When decompression occurs, pressurized air escapes from the cabin. The remaining air will be cold/thin and moisture will condense in the form of a fine mist. When carrying out duties during decompression, CCMs are advised to be cautious and avoid placing themselves in danger.

chunks.heading: 4.3.2 Slow Decompression
chunks.text: A pressure leak due to a cracked/leaking window or door/malfunctioning of the pressurization system can cause a slow decompression.

chunks.heading: 4.3.3 Rapid Decompression
chunks.text: Loss/damage to a window/door or a rupture in the fuselage could cause rapid decompression and require an immediate emergency descent. Sudden loss of cabin pressure would trigger the cabin drop down oxygen system to operate automatically when the cabin pressure reaches 14,000 feet approxi- mately.

chunks.heading: 4.3.4 Precautions
chunks.text:
Even though Flight Crew is trained to detect/deal with any signs of decompression at its earliest stage, CCMs should be vigilant during flight for any signs of dizziness or difficulty in breathing etc. and report to the PIC immediately. If the drop down oxygen masks deploy during flight, the following would take place.
1. Cabin lights would be on full intensity
2. The ordinance signs would illuminate
3. Automatic announcement (when cabin altitude reaches approximately 14000 feet) Ref 4.3.5 (a)
4. The PIC announcement Ref 4.3.5 (b)
5. The aircraft commences descending If the above does not occur, it may be due to an accidental mask deployment and the PIC would initiate an announcement. However, if such an announcement is not initiated or any of the above points does not occur or the aircraft continues to ascend or cruise, the situation is considered as Code Red and the Purser shall immediately enter the flight deck by using the emergency mode. Ref 5.7.3.3

chunks.heading: 4.3.5 Announcements during a Decompression
chunks.text:
a. If the aircraft cabin pressure altitude reaches 14000 feet an automatic announcement shall be heard on all aircraft. “ATTENTION, ATTENTION, THIS IS AN EMERGENCY, THIS IS AN EMERGENCY. THE CABIN AIR PRESSURE SYSTEM HAS FAILED. RETURN TO YOUR SEAT AT ONCE. FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS. STOP SMOKING. PULL THE MASK IN FRONT OF YOU. COVER YOUR NOSE & MOUTH. BREATHE NORMALLY. PULL THE ELASTIC BAND OVER YOUR HEAD TO HOLD THE MASK IN PLACE. PUT ON YOUR MASK FIRST, AND THEN HELP ANY CHILDREN OR ELDERLY PEOPLE NEXT TO YOU”.
b. The PIC shall initiate the following announcement only once the aircraft is safely established on the emergency descent. “ATTENTION CABIN CREW WE ARE ON AN UNSCHEDULED DESCENT”.

chunks.heading: “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, THIS IS YOUR CAPTAIN
chunks.text: THE USE OF OXYGEN IS NO LONGER REQUIRED. CABIN CREW PROCEED WITH YOUR DUTIES”.

chunks.heading: 4.3.7 Procedures during Slow Decompression
chunks.text:
Signs A formation of mist and prominent sound from the leak would be heard. The cabin would get cold and uncomfortable.
1. PIC shall brief the Purser on the situation/course of action and commence decent
2. Purser shall brief CCMs on the situation/course of action
3. The PIC may depending on the situation initiate a PA announcement Purser shall initiate a PA announcement: “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, REMAIN SEATED AND FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS IMMEDIATELY”.

chunks.heading: 4.3.7.1 Emergency Descents
chunks.text: PIC shall carry out a PA announcement informing that the aircraft is performing an emergency descent. Ref 4.3.5 (a) The drop down oxygen may be activated manually by the PIC. In the event the oxygen masks are de- ployed, CCMs shall be guided by the following Ref 4.3.9.2

chunks.heading: 4.3.8.1 The PIC Announcement
chunks.text: Oxygen mask not deployed Ref 4.3.6.1 Oxygen mask deployed Ref 4.3.6.2

chunks.heading: 4.3.8.2 Purser/CCM Responsibilities
chunks.text:
Oxygen mask not deployed
1. Ensure no smoking
2. Check - immediate CCMs/lavatories/flight deck etc.
3. Check - passengers with an alert/ Infants Ref 2.24.3/4/5
4. Administer first aid/Oxygen if required Ref 9.3
5. Report injuries to the PIC Oxygen Mask Deployed Ref 4.3.10.1

chunks.heading: 4.3.9 Procedures during Rapid Decompression
chunks.text:
Objective and Subjective Signs
1. A loud noise at the opening/air rushing out
2. A rapid drop in temperature/fog in the cabin
3. Debris and loose objects flying around the cabin
4. Ordinance signs will be illuminated
5. Cabin lights will be on to full intensity
6. Difficulty in breathing as air is sucked out of the lungs
7. Sinuses and ears momentarily feel full /cold sensation/difficulty in speaking There would be no time for the PIC to brief the Purser regarding the intentions. CCM shall be vigilant and respond.

chunks.heading: 4.3.9.1 Emergency Descent
chunks.text: PIC may initiate an emergency descent under the following conditions but not limited to; Rapid or Slow decompression/Smoke or Fire/Bomb Threat Crew may experience a steep descent with vibration due to the rapid descent, Oridinance signs togeth- er with the exit signs will illuminate. PIC shall initiate an announcement informing, that the aircraft is performing an emergency descent. Ref 4.3.5 (a) Crew Shall immediately secure themselves and await further instructions from the flight deck, if in the cabin by wedging between seats. Communication would be impossible. CCM shall not place themselves in danger.

chunks.heading: 4.3.9.1 Emergency Descent
chunks.text: Revision No 01 Revision Date 01 April 2024

chunks.heading: 4.3.9.2 Oxygen Mask Deployed
chunks.text:
Activation of the Flow of Oxygen The PSU doors would open/ oxygen masks will drop and hang from the lanyards.
1. To activate the flow, pull on one of the masks (cord)
2. Inflation of the green section on the breather bag indicates the flow of oxygen
3. Place the mask over the nose and mouth, elastic strap should be placed around the head and tightened to fit the mask, breathe normally CAUTION: ADULTS SHOULD DON THE DROP DOWN MASK BEFORE ASSISTING DEPENDANTS. CCMs if in the cabin shall don an extra drop-down mask and remain secured until further directives are given by the PIC. CCMs shall Speak through drop down mask or use gestures to demonstrate the don- ning of masks.

chunks.heading: 4.3.10 Post Rapid Decompression Duties
chunks.text: PIC should initiate the applicable PA announcement Ref 4.3.6

chunks.heading: 4.3.10.1 Purser/CCM Responsibilities
chunks.text:
CCMs shall be on oxygen (portable) prior to commencing post decompression duties. If restrained in the cabin the spare drop down oxygen masks may be used to reach the designated bottles of oxygen. Purser to carry out the announcement regarding the oxygen generators’ Ref 4.2.3
1. Ensure no smoking
2. Be on oxygen from the designated bottles
3. Check - immediate CCMs/lavatories/flight deck etc.
4. Move passengers from the area the fuselage was damaged
5. Check - passengers with alerts and infants Ref 2.24
6. Administer first aid/Oxygen if required Ref 9.3
7. Inform PIC of any passengers or crew injuries and cabin status.
8. Stow all drop down masks in the overhead bins before landing. Note: Post decompression, Oxygen from all bottles may be used until the gauge reaches zero. Crew shall not use personal bottle of oxygen to administer oxygen to a passenger post decompression and if a passenger requires oxygen it shall administered using the drop down oxygen mask.

chunks.heading: 4.3.11 Hypoxia and Its Effects
chunks.text: The deficiency of oxygen to the brain is called hypoxia. The greatest danger during a decompression is Hypoxia. To prevent becoming significantly impaired or incapacitated, CCMs must continuously observe passengers and Crew for signs and symptoms of hypoxia. It is important for the CCMs to realize that even in mild hypoxia, though not fatal, can have fatal results as hypoxia can significantly reduce the ability to perform and consequently lead to fatal errors. Hypoxia causes a subtle decrease in individual performance, followed by incapacitation; the symptoms may not be identified until it is too late. The most common type of aviation hypoxia is “hypoxic hypoxia”, that occurs due to low partial pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood. If oxygen is not administered immediately in hypoxia cases, it is possible that occupants become incapacitated and lose consciousness in a very short time.

chunks.heading: 4.3.11 Hypoxia and Its Effects
chunks.text: The table below indicates the effects of hypoxia on a person at different altitudes.

chunks.heading: SEA-LEVEL NORMAL
chunks.text: 10,000 feet Head ache/fatigue on long expo sure 14,000 feet Sleepiness/headache/dizziness/impaired vision/personality changes/ loss of muscu- lar co-ordination/Cyanosis (bluing of fingernails). 18,000 feet All of the above in a more serious condition. 22,000 feet Convulsions/collapse and coma in approximately 3 minutes.

chunks.heading: 4.3.12 Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC)
chunks.text:
The TUC refers to the time available to individuals to perform their tasks after they have been deprived of oxygen, but are still aware of their environment and capable of controlling their actions. It is impor- tant for the cabin crew to realize that the time of useful consciousness is different for each individual, and depends on the:
1. Altitude
2. Duration at Altitude
3. Temperature
4. Physical Exertion
5. Emotional State
6. Amount of activity. The cabin crew must remember that in cases of continued physical activity, the time of useful con- sciousness is significantly reduced. Time of Useful Consciousness

chunks.heading: ALTITUDE (FEET) MODERATE ACTIVITY SITTING QUIETLY
chunks.text: 22,000 05 Minutes 10 Minutes 25,000 02 Minutes 03 Minutes 28,000 01 Minutes 01 Minutes 30 Seconds 30,000 45 Seconds 01 Minutes 15 Seconds 35.000 30 Seconds 45 Seconds 40,000 18 Seconds 30 Seconds It is important to emphasize that this table is only a guideline, and provides average values that can increase or decrease, depending on the skills needed to accomplish a task, on the individual’s health, and on the amount of activity. For example, the time of useful consciousness for cabin crew involved in moderate activity is significantly less compared to a passenger that is sitting quietly

chunks.heading: 4.4 Fire
chunks.text: General Description A fire is the most dangerous hazard during flight and could be frightening. As it creates panic, in such situations CCMs should maintain a calm and positive attitude. In any type of fire, the PIC shall be informed immediately and other CCMs communicated to extinguish the fire as soon as possible. The flight deck door shall remain closed and monitored for security reasons during the entire fire drill. Removing one of the elements from the fire triangle should extinguish a fire. Assessing the situation and deciding the correct course of action is of prime importance when dealing with fire. The type of fire will determine the method of fighting it. Cabin fires could also be extinguished with materials readily at hand, such as blankets/cold towels or non-alcoholic beverages. Based on the severity of the fire, the fire fighting method may require the use of a fire extinguisher and a PBE. Pre-

chunks.heading: 4.4 Fire
chunks.text: caution should be taken to protect oneself when opening closed doors and creating an opening to fight a fire. Once the fire is extinguished, the Purser shall coordinate with the station staff to retain and dispatch possible evidence to base for a root cause analysis. Purser shall carry out an entry in the cabin defects log book for follow up action.

chunks.heading: 4.4.1 Elements of Fire
chunks.text: Fire Triangle

chunks.heading: 4.4.2 Classes of Fire
chunks.text: Class A Fires - Combustibles fire, such as cloth/paper and wood. Such fires could be extinguished by using a fire extinguisher or the area should be cooled with water or any non-flammable liquid.

chunks.heading: CAUTION: DO NOT USE FLAMMABLE LIQUIDS
chunks.text: Class B Fires - Flammable liquids fire, such as /hydraulic fluids or chemicals (Petrol/Oil) These fires are best extinguished by smothering or by using an extinguisher. CAUTION: DO NOT USE LIQUIDS AS IT INCREASES AND SPREADS, RATHER THAN EXTINGUISH - ING THE FIRE.

chunks.heading: CAUTION: DO NOT USE FLAMMABLE LIQUIDS
chunks.text: Class C Fires - Electrical fire, electrical equipment and wiring. Switch off and disconnect the power sup- ply as a priority and use an extinguisher CAUTION: DO NOT USE LIQUIDS AS IT CONDUCTS ELECTRICITY. Class D Fires – Metals fire such as lithium batteries, use an extinguisher to extinguish the fire and douse in water to prevent reignition. CAUTION: DO NOT USE WET ICE CUBES TO COOL, AS THIS MAY FORM A CRUST OVER THE FIRE

chunks.heading: 4.4.3 Prevention of fire
chunks.text: Always be alert for potential fire hazards. Galley electrical faults are a potential source of danger. If a circuit breaker (CB) has popped out, do not to reset it. Such defects should be reported to the PIC and entered in the cabin defects log book.

chunks.heading: 4.4.3.1 Prevention of Cabin Fire
chunks.text:
1. Be vigilant
2. Lookout for passengers smoking while embarking or disembarking
3. Do not place paper, plastic or any foreign material to cover lights that cannot be switched off

chunks.heading: 4.4.3.2 Prevention of Galley Fire
chunks.text:
1. Be vigilant
2. Do not store items in bun warmers/hot cups or ovens
3. Check ovens prior to switching it on/switch off ovens after use
4. Do not switch on ovens without inserts
5. Ensure hot cups contain liquid prior to switching them on
6. In the event water supply to a heater element is shut off, ensure the power to the devices are switched off immediately Note: The galley shall not be left unattended when any electrical equipment is in use

chunks.heading: 4.4.3.3 Prevention of Lavatory Fire
chunks.text:
1. Be vigilant
2. Check for serviceability of the fire extinguisher
3. Check for obstructions of the smoke detector
4. Ensure waste bin is not filled up/flaps are spring loaded/ doors are lockable
5. Water shut off valve shall be in the OPEN position
6. Carry out regular checks during flight

chunks.heading: 4.4.4 Fire Fighting Procedures and Techniques
chunks.text: There are a limited number of extinguishers on board the aircraft and usage should be maximized. An extinguisher can be used on all types of fire. Back up extinguishers should be available when fighting a fire and ensure the correct technique is adopted. As a precaution, always monitor the area after fighting a fire

chunks.heading: 4.4.4 Fire Fighting Procedures and Techniques
chunks.text:
1. Remove the fuel to starve the fire
2. Remove the Oxygen to smother the fire
3. Remove the heat to cool the fire

chunks.heading: 4.4.4.1 Identifying a Fire
chunks.text:
1. The fire fighter should assess the fire before reacting
2. In a hidden fire, be cautious when opening the panel/door
3. Use the back of the palm against the panel/door to detect the heat Once the location/source and the type of fire is determined, the most effective method should be adopted. When fighting a fire, the extinguisher should be held firmly/directed at the near edge of the base of the flames and progress forward or upward. The discharge nozzle should be moved rapidly with a side-to-side sweeping motion.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5 Fire Drill
chunks.text: The fire-fighting drill involves a fire fighter/a communicator and a coordinator.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.1 Fire-fighting equipment
chunks.text: Fire-Fighting equipment shall consist of the following but not limited to, Fire extinguisher/Heat resistance gloves/ PBE/ Crash axe. In the event an extinguisher is used to fight a fire, it is mandatory wear the protective equipment.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.2 Fire Fighter
chunks.text:
The CCM, who discovers or is informed of the fire, shall be the fire fighter The duties shall be:
1. Identify the type and source of the fire
2. Switch off all electrics as appropriate
3. Communicate to CCM who will become the Communicator
4. Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment
5. Wear the smoke hood/Heat resistant gloves (as appropriate)
6. Fight the fire

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.3 Communicator
chunks.text:
The CCM the fire fighter communicated with shall be the communicator and should locate self at the most appropriate interphone with a clear view of the fire/smoke to keep the PIC updated. Communication Guidelines
1. Should be focused not panic and speak clearly
2. Identify self and location and be precise regarding the details
3. Inform the location of the smoke or fire
4. Listen to the questions asked by the PIC and answer one question at a time
5. If not sure of the question, clarify
6. Inform the reaction of the passengers
7. Inform the type/source of the fire if it has been established

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.3 Communicator
chunks.text:
8. Provide specific details/any other vital information such as but not limited to:
9. Disconnected power sources/number of extinguishers used/colour of the smoke/source/etc. CAUTION: DO NOT IDENTIFY ANY LAVATORY TO THE FLIGHT CREW BY ITS ASSIGNED NUMBER. IDENTIFY THE LAVATORY BY ITS SPECIFIC LOCATION.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.4 Coordinator/s
chunks.text:
The third CCM involved in the Fire-Fighting procedure is the coordinator. The responsibility of the coor- dinator is as follows:
1. Make available back-up Fire-Fighting equipment
2. Move passengers away from smoke/ toxic fumes with the permission of the PIC
3. Remove portable oxygen from the area
4. Remove passenger baggage from the area to avoid contributory factors
5. Distribute wet towels to passengers to cover their nose and mouth
6. Advice passengers to stay low and cover nose and mouth
7. Delegate a CCM to man the flight deck door.
8. Standby to take over from the fire fighter.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.5 Post-Fire Procedures
chunks.text: After fighting a fire monitor the area for re-ignition. Retain the evidence of the fire for investigation purposes.

chunks.heading: WARNING: TOXIC GASES EMITTED BY BURNING SEATS/CARPET AND OTHER PARTS OF THE
chunks.text: CABIN COULD INCAPACITATE CREW AND PASSENGERS.

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.6 Types of Flash Fire
chunks.text: Flash fire Fire that can grow rapidly by heating combustible materials on the path, as burning materials become a new source of ignition. Combustible material in an enclosed area could produce sufficient heat for flammable vapour to spread the fire rapidly. Flash back fire A fire in a confined area which could spread rapidly towards an opening due to the inflow of oxygen. Flash over Fire Combustible gases accumulated at ceiling level which will ignite with a mild explosion

chunks.heading: 4.4.5.7 Cabin Smoke
chunks.text:
Smoke entering the cabin from the aircraft ventilation system.
1. Inform PIC

chunks.heading: 2. Don PBE
chunks.text: 3. Distribute wet towels and inform passengers to stay low

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.1 Fire on a Person
chunks.text:
1. Smother the flames using a coat or blanket
2. Do not fan the flames/Do not use an extinguisher

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.2 Oven Fires
chunks.text:
1. Keep the Oven door closed (By keeping the oven door closed, the fire will usually extinguish itself)
2. Switch off oven electrics/Pull circuit breakers out
3. Communicate to PIC & other CCMs
4. Obtain fire-fighting equipment and monitor the situation
5. If fire is present, open oven door slightly and discharge fire extinguisher (4 to 5 bursts), Don PBE if required
6. Do not open the oven door until smoke has subsided
7. Monitor oven for re-ignition and repeat process if necessary
8. Check the surrounding area for signs of heat or fire
9. Do not use the affected oven for the duration of the flight

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.3 Waste Bin Fires
chunks.text:
1. Open the waste bin flap and discharge extinguisher
2. Ensure that the discharge force does not scatter the contents outside the bin.
3. Saturate with non-flammable liquid

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.4 Seat upholstery (cushion) Fire
chunks.text:
1. Smother with a blanket
2. Use water or any non-flammable liquids
3. Check for source of the fire as it may be connected to electric wires

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.5 Seat Motor and IFE Fires
chunks.text:
1. Cut off the electrical power from CMT and Inform PIC
2. Use an extinguisher if required
3. If the source of the fire could not be determined consider it as a class C fire

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.6 Curtain Fire
chunks.text:
1. Use extinguisher
2. Start at the bottom of the curtain and work up wards

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.7 Carpet Fire
chunks.text: Smother with blanket/use extinguisher/use water or any non-flammable liquid.

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.8 Electrical Panel/Light Fixtures Smoke
chunks.text:
1. Switch off power/ Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment
2. Stand-by with an extinguisher
3. Monitor the area
4. Do not switch on the power for the rest of the flight

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.9 Cabin Baggage Fire
chunks.text:
1. Precaution should be taken for items that could explode (compressed gas canisters, Lithium batteries)
2. Smother with a blanket or use an extinguisher

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.10 Cargo Compartment Fire
chunks.text: The aircraft system is equipped with a cargo compartment smoke/fire warning system. In the event of smoke/ fire, the extinguishing system is activated from the flight deck.

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.11 Electrical Fire
chunks.text:
1. Switch off power
2. Pull circuit breakers out
3. Communicate with other CCMs
4. Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment and fight the fire

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.12 Lavatory Fire
chunks.text:
1. Communicate with other CCMs
2. Assess the conditions
3. Carry out a tactile search WARNING : DO NOT OPEN THE DOOR BEFORE CHECKING THE HEAT, MOVE THE BACK OF THE

chunks.heading: FIRE
chunks.text:
If the door is Cool To the Touch
1. Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment
2. Stay low/open the lavatory door. Stand behind the door using the door as a shield (Be cautious of a “flash back” fire)
3. Enter the Lavatory with caution
4. Locate the source of the fire
5. Discharge the Extinguisher to the base of the fire
6. Check surrounding areas including panels for fire and heat
7. Cool embers with water if it’s a class A fire If the door is Hot To the Touch
1. Keep the door closed.
2. Communicate with other CCMs
3. Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment
4. Don the smoke hood/ heat resistant gloves
5. Stay low and open the door slightly / Stand behind the door using the door as a shield, insert the nozzle/fully discharge extinguisher
6. Immediately Close the door and monitor
7. Discharge a second extinguisher if required, ensure fire is completely extinguished
8. Enter lavatory with caution keep low below smoke levels for optimum visibility. Always don a

chunks.heading: FIRE
chunks.text:
PBE to avoid breathing toxic fumes.
9. Cool embers with water if it’s a class A fire
10. Monitor area for re-ignition
11. Placard as an inoperative lavatory for the rest of the flight
12. Cabin crew to monitor for re-ignition for the duration of the flight

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.13 Overhead Bin Fires
chunks.text:
Smoke/fire in overhead bins may be caused by the contents in hand luggage (e.g. electronic devices, spare lithium batteries) or electrical malfunction in the Passenger Service Unit (PSU).
1. Move the passengers away from the area
2. Obtain Fire-Fighting equipment
3. Carry out a tactile search to locate the fire. (Using the back of the hand, feel the overhead bin to determine the temperature and presence of fire)

chunks.heading: CAUTION : OPENING THE OVERHEAD BIN MORE THAN NECESSARY CAN CAUSE CONTAMINA-
chunks.text:
TION OF THE CABIN WITH SMOKE AND CAN RESULT IN SMOKE INHALATION. If the Overhead Bin Cool To the Touch
1. Wear heat resistant gloves
2. Smother with a blanket
3. Move cabin baggage away, as the contents could be a contributory factor If the Overhead Bin Hot To the Touch
1. Precautions should be taken when opening the overhead bin as items on fire could fall out
2. Don smoke hood/ Heat resistant gloves
3. Open the relevant overhead bin just enough to pass the nozzle of the fire extinguisher and dis- charge (Get on top of seat if necessary)
4. Protect against contents that may scatter due to the pressure of the extinguisher
5. Cabin crew to monitor for re-ignition for the duration of the flight

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.14 Hidden Fire/Inaccessible Fire
chunks.text:
A fire behind a panelling can cause fumes or smoke to appear in a totally different part of the cabin. Locating the source of fire is important. This can be achieved by carrying out a tactile search for the hot spots behind the aircraft panels with the back of the hand.
1. Carry out a tactile search.
2. Locate the area hot to the touch (Hot spot)
3. Communicate to other CCMs
4. Obtain directives from the PIC to open a or create an opening above the hot spot to pass extin- guisher nozzle
5. When opening panels with an axe precautions should be taken not to damage aircraft equip- ment and wiring
6. Discharge extinguisher.
7. Monitor area for re-ignition

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.15 Engine Torching
chunks.text: At the beginning of a flight an engine may exhaust fire and smoke upon start-up, due to residual fuel settling in the burner of the engine. When engine torching is observed CCMs should calm passengers and inform the PIC

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.15.1 Engine Fire
chunks.text:
1. Inform Flight Crew or Engineer
2. Be alert for a possible evacuation

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.16 Auxiliary Power Unit Fire (APU)
chunks.text:
1. Inform Flight Crew or Engineer
2. Be alert for a possible evacuation

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.17 Fuel Spills/Fires
chunks.text:
1. Inform Flight Crew or Engineer
2. APU should be shut down and refuelling stopped
3. Switch off all electrical equipment immediately
4. Be alert for a possible evacuation
5. Standby with Fire-Fighting equipment until the airport emergency services arrive

chunks.heading: 4.4.6.18 Flight Deck Fires
chunks.text:
1. Halon/BCF extinguisher shall be used, on any fire occurring in the flight deck
2. While using the fire extinguisher inside the flight deck, CCMs should wear a smoke hood, heat resistant gloves for their safety.
3. Extinguisher shall not be used on any crew member Note: It’s mandatory that Flight crew members have to don, their oxygen masks prior to CCMs dis- charging the extinguisher.

chunks.heading: 4.5.4 Fuel Jettison (Dumping)
chunks.text: Fuel jettisoning is carried out for quick reduction of aircraft weight. Flight Crew would liaise with the Purser and may carry out an announcement to the passengers. Jettisoning fuel may be visible from the cabin in the form of two vapour trails from the wings. CCMs should calm and reassure passengers.

chunks.heading: 4.6.1 Types of Evacuation
chunks.text: Most emergencies occur during take-off and landing. CCMs shall prepare themselves for an emergency with no prior warning. Passenger /Cabin/galley preparations shall be carried out prior to every take-off and landing and CCMs shall observe STS when secured for a take-off and landing in anticipation for an emergency. Evacuating an aircraft shall be determined by the situation depending at that moment and at present what it might lead to. Assessment and sound judgement shall be a key factor to arrive at a final deci- sion. There is a significant difference of a rapid de-planing as a preventive measure and an evacuation after a disaster.

chunks.heading: 4.6.1.1 Prepared
chunks.text: The PIC has time to advice CCMs of the nature of the emergency and his intentions and the CCMs may have sufficient time to prepare the passengers/cabin and galleys prior to impact appropriately (phase 1/2/3). Ref 4.10/11

chunks.heading: 4.6.1.2 Unprepared
chunks.text: The PIC has minimum or no time available to advice CCMs of the nature of the emergency and his in- tention. WARNING: IN AN EMERGENCY CCMS SHALL NOT PLACE THEMSELVES IN DANGER, BUT CALCU - LATED RISKS MAY BE TAKEN TO ACHIEVE THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF SAVING LIFE CCMs should be alert to react to any situation in the shortest possible time. Evacuating passengers from the aircraft shall be completed within 90 seconds with half the exits in operation. The ability of CCMs to prevent an emergency developing into a disastrous situation depends upon their judgment and efficiency. As with any unplanned impact, one of the first actions cabin crew need to take is to shout out, the commands to adopt the brace position. This will reduce the amount of injury to the passengers and give them a better chance of being able to evacuate the aircraft and survive. There maybe be more than one impact and everyone will need to remain in the brace position until the aircraft finally comes to a

chunks.heading: 4.6.1.2 Unprepared
chunks.text: complete stop

chunks.heading: 4.6.2 Silent Thirty Second Review (STS)
chunks.text:
When CCMs are secured for take-off and landing, each CCM shall silently review the five actions which relate to an emergency situation as follows:
• Brace for impact
• Door operation
• Evacuation commands
• Evacuation route
• Passenger control

chunks.heading: 4.6.3 Land Evacuation at an Aerodrome
chunks.text: An evacuation at an aerodrome is supported by emergency rescue teams such as fire rescue/medical aid/emergency response teams etc.

chunks.heading: 4.6.3.1 Away From an Aerodrome
chunks.text: An evacuation away from an aerodrome would result in unforeseen situations on impact and after an evacuation. CCMs would be faced with many challenges in medical and survival demands.

chunks.heading: 4.6.4 Water Evacuation
chunks.text: Serious injuries or fatalities during evacuations in water are due to deceleration forces and failure to board rafts. Floatation is the most important requirement for survival in water. The aircraft may float unless it is badly damaged, however, CCMs should evacuate all passengers in the shortest possible time, as it may be difficult to assess how long the aircraft will remain afloat.

chunks.heading: 4.6.4.1 Tidal Flats
chunks.text: Also known as mudflats as coastal wetlands that turning in areas when the (sea water meets the land) where sediment has been deposited by tides or rivers. Areas when sediment from rivers run off or inflows from tides, deposit mud or sand. Levels of walls built to prevent water reaching terrain on an air field. Tidal Flats is an external factor affecting an evacuation.

chunks.heading: 4.6.5 Initiating an Evacuation
chunks.text:
An emergency evacuation command can be initiated from either the flight deck or the FAP/AAP or PA. The visual indicators are installed in the flight deck/FAP and AAPs. The audio (pulsating) horn is heard throughout the cabin. CCM shall begin evacuation immediately upon F/D Command. To initiate an evac- uation, primarily the aircraft has to come to a complete stop. Ensure engines are not running before opening door directly forward or aft of an engine. Be prepared for more than one impact .Conditions for CCMs to initiate an evacuation without waiting for commands from Flight Deck are, but not limited to the the below life threatening situations:
1. Smoke
2. Fire
3. Structural damage
4. Abnormal condition of the aircraft
5. Threat to life

chunks.heading: 4.6.5 Initiating an Evacuation
chunks.text: Note - CCMs shall initiate an evacuation during a ditching after the aircraft has stopped, CCM shall immediately initiate evacuation after evaluating the outside conditions for water level or other haz- ards.

chunks.heading: 4.6.5.1 Initiation from the Flight Deck
chunks.text: PA announcement and or by pressing the EVAC command Indications in the Cabin CHIME Pulsating horn throughout the cabin. AIP EVAC Alert with a flashing red-attention getter FAP/AAPs EVAC reset switch flashes red. ACP No Indications When the PIC initiates an evacuation, he will be guided by the following order of priority: Once the aircraft comes to a complete stop, command: “ATTENTION CABIN CREW AT STATIONS”. Carry out the check list. (Approximately 20 seconds), Ensure the engines are shut down.,Command: “EVACUATE, EVACUATE EVACUATE”. The Flight Crew is not required to inform the side or doors to be used for evacuation, Once the aircraft comes to a complete stop and if no command from the Flight Crew is initiated, CCMs shall take the responsibility to initiate an evacuation under conditions stipulated, Ref 4.6.5

chunks.heading: 4.6.5.2 Initiated From the Cabin (FAP) or AAP (If Availabe)
chunks.text: Initiate the PA announcement to evacuate and Press EVAC command on FAP

chunks.heading: ALH
chunks.text: Indications in the Flight Deck A 3-seconds buzzer and the EVAC alert light will illuminate in the flight deck. Indications in the Cabin The EVAC CMD switch on the FAP will brighten. The indications are similar as when initiated from the flight deck. Ref 4.6.5.1

chunks.heading: 4.6.5.3 Initiated From Any CCM Station
chunks.text: Depending on cases which are life threatening, CCMs should use their best judgment to initiate an evac- uation, but shall try to establish communication with the Flight Crew prior to initiating an evacuation. Ref 4.6.5 CCMs could initiate an evacuation from any station through the PA system once the aircraft has come to a complete stop, the commands would be.

chunks.heading: 4.6.5.4 Silencing the EVAC Command
chunks.text: Press ‘EVAC RESET’ prior to commencing an evacuation. It silences the EVAC alert horn on the FAP/AAPs area wise.

chunks.heading: 4.6.5.5 Accidental Activation of an EVAC Command
chunks.text: Press EVAC command switch at the originating station. A PA announcement shall be initiated immedi- ately.

chunks.heading: 4.7 Gate/Apron Emergencies
chunks.text: An emergency which could occur when the aircraft is parked with or without steps/aero-bridges being connected. To de-plane (depending on the situation) it is recommended to use the aero-bridge and/ or stairs to minimize injuries. However in the event of an evacuation there is no restriction in deploying slides to evacuate. CCMs shall ensure the slides are armed prior to opening the door and the ground area is clear of ob- struction. In the event a passenger transport vehicle is used to de-plane passengers, care should be taken to ensure correct positioning steps /aero-bridges prior to commanding passengers to evacuate.

chunks.heading: 4.7.1 Conditions to Evacuate/ De-plane
chunks.text: Depending on the seriousness of the situation, there could be a call for an evacuation. CCMs may initi- ate an evacuation due to but not limited to, life threatening conditions. The proximity of fire or wreckage could make a slide unusable. Extreme wind conditions could cause the slide to move or slides may deploy at an unexpected angle. CCMs should assess the situation prior to ordering passengers to evacuate. The passengers may be de-planed as a preventive measure if the situation is not serious. Ref 4.6.5

chunks.heading: 4.7.2 Nose Gear Collapse
chunks.text: AFT Slides(L4/R4) should not be used for evacuation as the angle could be too steep and the slide may not reach the ground.

chunks.heading: 4.7.3 Main/Total Gear Collapse
chunks.text: All slides may be used for an evacuation. Note - Main Gear Collapse L3, R3 ,L4, R4 and Total Gear Collapse all doors, the command shall be “Run down the slide”. This is due to the reduced angle of the slides. Directing Passengers The Passenger should be directed to move away from the aircraft after de-planing/evacuation. It is recommended to move the passengers up-wind to avoid the danger of embers which could be blown towards the passengers.

chunks.heading: 4.8 Evacuation Commands
chunks.text: General CCMs shall be in uniform to be easily identifiable and for commanding passengers during an emergency. A high degree of authority and calmness should be maintained during an emergency. Passengers with negative emotions should be dealt firmly. Passengers should be prevented from assum- ing leadership, as their directives may confuse and result in loss of life. Commands to the passengers should be positive/relevant/timely and delivered in a firm authoritative manner. CCMs shall take a protective position at the exit by holding on to an assist handle and avoid obstructing the free flow of passengers. Passengers should be prevented from sitting down on the door-sill. However, if they do sit down, do not bend down to assist them but use the foot or knee to guide them. If exits are congested passengers should be redirected to usable exits

chunks.heading: 4.8.1 Emergency Landing
chunks.text: Commands

chunks.heading: “YOU TWO STAY AT THE BOTTOM AND HELP “
chunks.text: (Pre-selected ABPs) “MOVE FASTER,

chunks.heading: JUMP AND SLIDE”
chunks.text: Preparation Commands “REMOVE HIGH HEELED SHOES,

chunks.heading: “OPEN SEAT BELTS/EXITS OVER HERE
chunks.text: YOU COME THIS WAY,

chunks.heading: YOU STAY AT THE BOTTOM AND HELP “
chunks.text: (Randomly selected of ABPs) “MOVE FASTER,

chunks.heading: JUMP AND SLIDE”
chunks.text: Commands at L2 / R2 Exits All of the above and as there is a ramp extended when the slide is deployed

chunks.heading: 4.8.2 Inflated and Deflated Slide
chunks.text: If the inflated slide deflates, instruct four ABPs once evacuated from the aircraft to hold the no fail han- dles and direct one passenger at a time to evacuate. Commands to ABPs

chunks.heading: 4.8.3 Blocked Exit
chunks.text: Passengers should be directed to usable exits to expedite the evacuation. CCM shall remain at the door and redirect passengers to usable exits. Inform in brief the reason the exit is blocked. Assess usability of other exits prior to re-directing passengers. Commands “EXIT BLOCKED/FIRE OUTSIDE ,

chunks.heading: GO BACK/GO FORWARD/CROSS OVER THE AISLE/CROSS THROUGH THE SEATS”
chunks.text: etc

chunks.heading: 4.8.4 Ditching
chunks.text: Commands

chunks.heading: “OPEN SEAT BELTS/EXITS OVER HERE
chunks.text: COME THIS WAY,

chunks.heading: INFLATE LIFE VESTS”
chunks.text: (At the door-sill)

chunks.heading: “YOU TWO BOARD RAFT AND ASSIST OTHERS”
chunks.text: (Pre-selected ABPs) “MOVE FASTER,

chunks.heading: STEP INTO THE RAFT/CRAWL TO THE FAR END”
chunks.text: Preparation Commands “LIFE VEST UNDER YOUR SEAT, TAKE IT OUT, PUT IT ON, REMOVE HIGH HEELED SHOES ,

chunks.heading: “OPEN SEAT BELTS/EXITS OVER HERE
chunks.text: COME THIS WAY,

chunks.heading: INFLATE LIFE VESTS “
chunks.text: (At the door-sill)

chunks.heading: “BOARD RAFT AND ASSIST OTHERS”
chunks.text: (Randomly selected ABPs) “MOVE FASTER,

chunks.heading: STEP INTO THE RAFT/CRAWL TO THE FAR END”
chunks.text: Raft Commands “REMAIN SEATED IN THE RAFT,

chunks.heading: CRAWL TO THE FAR END”
chunks.text: Raft Commands “REMAIN SEATED IN THE RAFT,

chunks.heading: 4.9.1 Impending Emergency/Pilot Incapacitation
chunks.text: Alert Signal from Flight Deck to Cabin During a prepared emergency or pilot incapacitation the Flight Crew shall initiate the following an- nouncement; “PURSER TO THE FLIGHT DECK IMMEDIATELY”. Note - in the event of an Abnormal or Emergency situation PIC shall brief the Purser on NITS

chunks.heading: 4.9.2 NITS Briefing
chunks.text: On hearing the alert signal, the Purser shall proceed to the flight deck immediately for instructions and a briefing from the PIC. The purser shall acknowledge the Commander’s briefing by repeating the instructions given and clarify anything unclear. Synchronize the watches.

chunks.heading: DEFINITION EXAMPLES
chunks.text: NATURE Actual situation/threat Technical malfunction

chunks.heading: INTENTIONS
chunks.text: Intentions of the PIC Emergency landing or ditching or diversion

chunks.heading: TIME
chunks.text: Time available before touchdown Preparation/objectives and how to achieve it/order of priorities SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS Specific instruction of the threat Exits to be used, Specific instruction of the threat/ the plan for a safe evacuation

chunks.heading: 4.9.2.1 Following NITS Briefing
chunks.text:
The Purser must take note of the time in order to manage the time available for the relay briefing. A certain amount of time is allocated to each task on each phase. The Purser will need to closely monitor the time in order to accomplish as many tasks as time permits
1. On receiving the NITS briefing, the Purser shall relay brief CCMs by initiating an all station call or conducting a face to face briefing in the forward galley
2. Cabin Crew shall in turn acknowledge clear understanding of all points correctly.

chunks.heading: 4.9.2.2 Cabin Crew Procedures Following The PIC’s Call
chunks.text:
Cabin crew upon hearing the command “Purser to the flight deck immediately”
1. A senior CCM to make an announcement instructing passengers to return to their seats and to fasten the seat belts
2. Suspend service, stow and secure trolley/carts.
3. Secure galley and loose equipment.
4. All CCMs to take their stations and await an all station call.

chunks.heading: 4.9.3 Emergency Communication
chunks.text: Each emergency situation is unique and no procedure can include all possible types of emergency situations. Neither is it possible to dictate the exact procedure to follow in such situations. Emergencies could occur with no indications or warning in the flight deck, such as, Auxiliary power unit fire/refuel- ling truck fire/cabin fire/smoke in the cabin/noise and vibrations from the aircraft etc. Providing and receiving instructions should be clear and concise without ambiguity. CCMs receiving instructions should verify and ensure the directives are clearly understood. As appropriate, depending on the situation, CCMs should try to establish communication with the Flight Crew prior to initiating an

chunks.heading: 4.9.3 Emergency Communication
chunks.text: evacuation. However, in cases which are life threatening, CCMs shall use their own initiative to order an evacuation. Ref 4.6.5

chunks.heading: 4.9.3.1 Cabin to Flight Deck
chunks.text: Press PRIO CAPT on the hand set and await communication and response.

chunks.heading: 4.9.3.2 Purser to CCMs
chunks.text: On receiving the NITS briefing, the Purser should (relay) brief CCMs by initiating an all station call or by conducting a face to face briefing.

chunks.heading: 4.9.3.3 Effective Communication Skills
chunks.text: Crew shall use accepted and commonly used aviation phrases when the need arises to communicate mandatory information.

chunks.heading: 4.10 Preparation for an Emergency Landing
chunks.text:
Phases of Preparation Depending on the time available, phase 1, 2 and 3 should be carried out prior to impact. If time is re- stricted, completion of phase 1 is mandatory.
1. The Purser shall receive the NITS briefing. Ref 4.9.2
2. CCMs shall secure cabin/galleys and standby for the briefing.
3. Purser shall carry out the relay briefing.
4. The cabin lights should be maintained at full intensity.
5. PIC shall carry out a PA announcement regarding the emergency.
6. Purser shall initiate emergency preparation phase 1.
7. CCMs to carry out emergency preparation phase 1.
8. CCMs commence emergency preparation Phase 2.
9. Purser may call for volunteers as ABP/Buddies.
10. Door primaries shall brief ABPs.
11. CCMs shall brief Buddies and re-seat them.
12. CCMs commence emergency preparation Phase 3.
13. Secure self for impact.

chunks.heading: 4.10.1 PIC- Emergency Landing Announcement
chunks.text: An appropriate announcement shall be carried out by the PIC,

chunks.heading: “LADIES & GENTLEMEN, THIS IS YOUR CAPTAIN
chunks.text: WE PLAN TO MAKE AN EMERGENCY LANDING IN ... MINUTES. IT MAY BE NECESSARY TO EVACUATE THE AIRCRAFT AFTER LANDING. PLEASE PAY ATTENTION TO THE CABIN CREW MEMBER’S INSTRUC- TIONS & FOLLOW THEM AT ALL TIMES. YOUR CO-OPERATION IS ESSENTIAL.

chunks.heading: 4.10.2 Emergency Preparation - Phase 1
chunks.text:
Demonstration Before the emergency demonstration begins, the cabin crew shall ensure that:
• The class dividers are open
• The lighting is selected to full intensity.
• The entertainment system is switched off The cabin crew shall carry out a manual demonstration in their assigned areas. In order to conduct an effective briefing, the cabin crew must not distract the passenger’s attention.
1. Method to fasten/tighten and open seat belts
2. Bracing positions (The diagram should be pointed out on the safety card).
3. Point out the closest and alternate exits Demonstration Positions A330-200 CS1 shall demonstrate if S1 is not detailed. Demonstration Positions A330-300

chunks.heading: PURSER CCM ACTIONS
chunks.text: “CREW TO YOUR DEMONSTRATION POSITIONS” Demo positions: with seat belts/ safety card. “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, WE SHALL NOW GIVE YOU MORE DETAILED INFORMATION IN PREPARA- TION FOR AN ORDERLY AND SAFE EVACUATION. YOU MUST FOLLOW THE INSTRUCTIONS OF THE CREW AS THEY HAVE BEEN TRAINED TO EVACUATE

chunks.heading: CAREFULLY TO THE INSTRUCTIONS”
chunks.text: Ensure all passengers are seated.

chunks.heading: “YOU ARE REMINDED THAT SMOKING IS PROHIBITED.”
chunks.text: (Pause)

chunks.heading: “TO FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELT, INSERT THE METAL FITTING ON ONE
chunks.text: STRAP INTO THE BUCKLE ON THE OTHER STRAP AND TIGHTEN.

chunks.heading: PORTION OF THE BUCKLE. “
chunks.text: (Pause) Demonstrate the fastening / tightening and opening of the seat belt.

chunks.heading: THE BRACING POSITION AS SHOWN.”
chunks.text: (Pause) Point to the bracing picture on the safety card and show the location of the safety card walk down a few rows.

chunks.heading: THIS MAY DELAY THE EVACUATION.”
chunks.text: (Pause) Point to the floor path marking, Point to the exits in sequence, aft exits/right turn/show the closest/fwd exits.

chunks.heading: “PLEASE READ THE SAFETY INSTRUCTION CARD NOW.”
chunks.text: (Pause) CCM holds up safety leaflets and shows both sides. “STOW HAND BAGS UNDER YOUR SEATS. PLACE YOUR SEAT BACK IN THE UPRIGHT POSITION, STOW YOUR TRAY TABLE AND FOOTREST, LEAVE THE HEAD SETS IN THE SEAT POCKET IN FRONT OF YOU. PLACE YOUR ARMREST DOWN. YOU’RE COOPERATION AND ASSISTANCE IS EXTREMELY IMPORTANT. AS THERE COULD BE MORE THAN ONE IMPACT, DO NOT OPEN YOUR SEAT BELTS UNTIL THE AIR-

chunks.heading: CRAFT COMES TO A COMPLETE STOP.”
chunks.text: “CREW PREPARE CABIN”. “LADIES AND GENTLEMAN, AIRLINE CREW, SHIPS CREW, MILITARY PERSONNEL OR OTHER PERSONNEL, WHO WISH TO ASSIST IN THE EVACUATION, PLEASE IDENTIFY YOUR-SELF TO A MEMBER OF THE CABIN CREW, THANK YOU!”

chunks.heading: 4.10.2.2 Purser Announcement to Clear the Cabin
chunks.text: “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, WE WOULD BE CLEARING THE CABIN IN PREPARATION FOR IMPACT, STOW YOUR SPECTACLES IN THE SEAT POCKET. HIGH-HEELED SHOES TO BE HANDED OVER TO THE CREW, WE RECOMMEND FLAT SHOES IN PREPA- RATION FOR THE EVACUATION. YOUR IMMEDIATE RESPONSE IS ESSENTIAL,

chunks.heading: 4.10.3 Emergency Preparation - Phase 2
chunks.text:
Preparations are carried out to obtain the most effective protection against an impact.
1. Passenger preparation.
2. Cabin preparation.
3. Galley preparation.

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.1 Passenger Preparation
chunks.text: Passenger preparation should commence from the forward of each zone for a faster response and clear- ance. While clearing the cabin, passengers should be requested to stow all cabin baggage/loose luggage/open all window blinds/stow chair tables/chair backs placed upright/ footrest stowed/ seat belts fastened. The cabin clearance should commence on completion of the demonstration using bags (sales/garbage). Spectacles/pens should be removed for impact and stored in the seat pocket. Ensure passengers stow hazardous items (if any) and loosen their ties and unbutton the collars. Females should remove high- heeled shoes in order to be able to brace for impact with feet firmly on the floor and to prevent the slide from being damaged when evacuating. High heel shoes should not be placed in seat pocket as there is a possibility that they may injure the passenger when adopting the bracing position. Passengers

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.1 Passenger Preparation
chunks.text: to be advised to wear a flat pair of shoes.

chunks.heading: F/SS2/F/SS4
chunks.text: L1 to L2 and stow the items in the lavatory at L2. Continue L2 to L3 and stow the items in the lavatory at L3.

chunks.heading: F/SS1/F/SS3
chunks.text: R1 to R2 and stow the items in the lavatory at R2 Continue R2 to R3 and stow the items in the lavatory at R3 F/SS6/G2 L3 to L4 and stow the items in the lavatory at L4 or L3. F/SS5/CS3 R3 to R4 and stow the items in the lavatory at R4 or R3 The toilet bowl shall be closed and lavatories locked after checking the cabin

chunks.heading: F/SS1/F/SS3
chunks.text:
4.10.3.3.Selecting/Briefing ABPs - Prepared Emergency Landing ABPs shall be profiled and selected during boarding by each CCM to be utilized only during an emergen- cy. Three ABPs per exit should be selected to assist CCMs during an evacuation and be briefed based on:
1. Willingness to help
2. Physically fit
3. Preferably traveling alone
4. Speaks and understands the language
5. Not nervous/not intoxicated
6. Be over the age of 18 Door Primaries should introduce self to the selected ABPs and brief them on the assistance required. The briefing should be carried out at the respective door primary exit and allocate seats for them clos- est to the exit where assistance is required. Ensure the ABPs fully understood the instructions by requesting them to repeat the steps/question them to avoid misunderstanding and confusion. One ABP shall be briefed to take over the duties of the door primary in case of crew incapacitation. The other two ABPs shall hold back passengers during door

chunks.heading: F/SS1/F/SS3
chunks.text: operation, slide inflation and slide down to assist passengers at the bottom of the slide. Preference to selection of ABP shall be given to the following passengers Trained airline personnel/Armed forces/ship’s crew etc. First aiders/sports reps etc. Traveling alone/volunteers

chunks.heading: F/SS1/F/SS3
chunks.text:
Given below is a guide to brief ABPs.
1. Wait until the aircraft comes to a complete stop
2. Await for command (Evacuate) and/or when other doors are been opened
3. Check outside for danger (Fire/Smoke/Obstructions)
4. Hold assist handle and lift the door handle fully up and push open the door, Pull the manual inflation handle (Bottom Right)
5. Check for correct slide inflation (Show safety card)
6. Send two ABPs to evacuate as soon as the slide is inflated to assist CCM/passengers
7. Remove incapacitated CCM and send down the slide (Demonstrate the opening of seat belts)
8. Ensure passengers are evacuated, be forceful if required
9. Ensure a smooth flow of passengers
10. If the exit cannot be used, Block Exit & redirect PAX to usable exits.

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.4 Selecting/Briefing ABPs- Unprepared Emergency Landing
chunks.text:
Identify ABPs whilst evacuating and brief them.
1. To slide down and assist at the bottom of the slide
2. Assist in crowd control
3. Help passengers who require special attention

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.5 Selecting/Briefing of Buddies – Prepared Emergency Landing
chunks.text:
Buddies are required to assist passengers with medical and assistance alert. Ref 2.24 Selection should be on the same guide lines of selecting an ABP. Ref 4.10.3.3 Purser to ensure the following guidelines are followed when CCMs brief buddies
1. Introduce the dependent by name.
2. Explain the nature of assistance needed by the dependent.
3. Seat the buddy next to the dependent.
4. Inform the buddy to evacuate last to avoid any injury to the dependent (passengers with medi- cal Alert)

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.6 Re-Seating Of Passengers
chunks.text: Passengers reseating shall be done with the authorization of the PIC. Reseating is required for better protection against impact by moving PAX from overloaded seats to empty seats. When possible, it is recommended to reseat two passengers in each triple row of seats. Note : A seat row which is not fully occupied will withstand a higher impact force than a fully loaded row of seats.

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.7 Restrained Passengers
chunks.text: Passenger restrains (if used) should be removed during passenger preparation appropriately with the

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.7 Restrained Passengers
chunks.text: authorization of the PIC.

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.8 Cabin Preparation
chunks.text:
Loose equipment/objects as mentioned below but not restricted to, should as appropriate be removed /cleared /stowed /secured /latched/restrained/opened.
1. Bassinets
2. Individual video screens/drop-down monitors
3. Headsets
4. Overhead stowage compartments (maintain allowable weight as placarded).
5. Newspapers and magazines
6. Exits/aisles and cross aisles
7. Class divider curtains
8. Window blinds/blinds on doors
9. Un-used loose equipment

chunks.heading: 4.10.3.9 Galley Preparation
chunks.text:
Loose objects/equipment as mentioned below but not restricted to, should be removed /cleared/ stowed/secured/latched/restrained/opened/closed.
1. Carts/trolleys/air larders/Curtains
2. Waste carts/waste bins flap closed Note : Crew shall remove personal items such as pens, name tags and pins

chunks.heading: 4.10.4 Emergency Preparation - Phase 3
chunks.text:
Rechecking Phase 3 is carried out when time permits to ensure clearance/preparation of phase 1 and 2 is satisfacto- rily completed. The re-check includes any other preparations not carried out in phase 1 and 2 Ref 4.10.2/3
1. The seatbelts are fastened and adjusted
2. Tray- tables stowed, seat back in the upright position
3. Window blinds opened
4. IVS stowed and strapped
5. Special passengers have understood their bracing positions
6. All dependants are seated with buddies
7. All Infants and children are seated with adults
8. Safety seating arrangements adhered to
9. CCMs report to the Purser that the assigned duties have been completed
10. Purser to confirm completion of preparation and seek update of situation / time remaining from

chunks.heading: PIC
chunks.text: 11. Cabin lights adjusted accordingly to the outside conditions

chunks.heading: 4.10.5 Commands Prior To Impact
chunks.text: CCM shall be seated at their designated seats restrained and observe STS. Ref 4.6.2

chunks.heading: 4.10.5 Commands Prior To Impact
chunks.text: “CABIN CREW TO BE SEATED FOR LANDING”. Approximately 20 Seconds prior to impact, the brace command shall be initiated by the PIC “BRACE BRACE BRACE”. CCMs shall adopt the brace position and continue to shout the below commands until the aircraft reaches a complete stop. “HEADS DOWN, STAY DOWN”.

chunks.heading: 4.10.6 Command for Evacuation
chunks.text: If an evacuation is required the PIC shall initiate the EVAC command. Ref 4.6.5.1 “EVACUATE, EVACUATE, EVACUATE”. Indications in the cabin : Ref 4.6.5.1 If the P.A is unserviceable, PIC and the Purser shall coordinate on a signal to be used.

chunks.heading: 4.10.6.1 The Cabin Evacuation Process
chunks.text:
The evacuation must begin immediately upon receiving the evacuation signal. Positive, assertive ac- tion from the cabin crew will directly impact the rate and flow of passenger movement to the exits and down the slides. The commands used by the cabin crew are an essential part of the evacuation process. Commands should be:
1. Assertive
2. Short
3. Loud
4. Clear
5. Negative commands shall not be used

chunks.heading: 4.10.7 Emergency Landing CCM Responsibilities
chunks.text: Door Primary

chunks.heading: ENSURE CORRECT SLIDE INFLATION
chunks.text: INSTRUCT 2 ABPs TO EVACUATE AND ASSIST AT THE BOTTOM OF THE SLIDE

chunks.heading: ASSIST ON GROUND
chunks.text: Blocked Exit (Door Opened)

chunks.heading: REDIRECT PASSENGERS TO USEABLE EXITS
chunks.text: Blocked Exit (Door Closed)

chunks.heading: REDIRECT PASSENGERS TO USABLE EXITS
chunks.text: Door Assist

chunks.heading: WHEN ALL ASSISTANCE RENDERED EVACUATE AND ASSIST ON GROUND
chunks.text: Use eye contact/positive commands/effective body language and if required physical force to ensure passengers safety. ABPs assistance may be used to block an exit.

chunks.heading: PIC

chunks.heading: 4.10.7.4 Assessing Outside Conditions
chunks.text:
Before opening an exit, the cabin crew must check that the outside conditions are safe, and that the slide deployment area is clear of:
1. Fire
2. Smoke
3. Obstructions
4. Debris. The cabin crew should open the exit, only if it safe to do so by holding on to the assist handle of the door frame. The cabin crew can use commands such as ‘STAND BACK, STAND BACK’ to hold back pas- sengers, during the exit opening and slide deployment sequence.

chunks.heading: 4.10.8 Crowd Control
chunks.text:
Successful evacuations have been achieved due to CCMs having control over the situation and passen- gers following instructions. Be assertive when commands and instructions are carried out to passengers as reactions of the passengers will wary. Such as,
1. Panic (screaming/crying/hysterical)
2. Negative panic (does not react to the situation)
3. No perception that danger exists
4. Exiting with carry-on baggage
5. Attempt to get ahead of the others

chunks.heading: 4.10.9 Use Of The Assist Space
chunks.text: Each aircraft has a dedicated assist space located on either side of the door. If possible, use the assist space facing most of the passengers. The cabin crew must firmly grasp the frame assist handle and posi- tion themselves correctly in the assist space. This will prevent the cabin crewmember being pushed out and obstructing the evacuating passengers.

chunks.heading: 4.10.13 Evacuation of a stretcher passenger
chunks.text: Check with the accompanying medical practitioner regarding the stretcher passengers’ special needs and lifting techniques during evacuation. In a prepared emergency when a stretcher passenger is on board, ABP’s will be required to lift the passenger off a stretcher and carried to the exit.

chunks.heading: 4.10.13.1 Evacuation Techniques
chunks.text:
1. Sit behind stretcher Passenger
2. Secure him with the arms around the chest area.
3. Secure the wrist from under the arms of the handicapped passenger to prevent friction burns on the hands as he slides down.
4. The patient will be positioned between the ABP’s knees and they will slide down together (To- boggan style) NOTE: The hand of the handicapped passenger should be folded

chunks.heading: 4.11 Preparation for an Emergency Ditching
chunks.text:
Phases of Preparation Depending on time available, Phase 1, 2 and 3 shall be carried out prior to impact. If time is restricted, completion of Phase 1 is mandatory. CCMs shall wear personal life vests for the demonstration.
1. The Purser shall be briefed by the PIC (NITS)
2. CCMs shall secure cabin and galleys and standby for the briefing
3. Purser shall carry out the relay briefing
4. The cabin lights shall be switched on to full intensity
5. PIC shall carry out a PA announcement regarding the impending emergency
6. Purser shall call for emergency preparation phase 1
7. Carry out or activate pre-recorded emergency landing announcement
8. Carry out emergency preparation phase 1
9. Commence emergency preparation Phase 2
10. Distribute infant’s life vest
11. Purser may call for volunteers as ABP/Buddies
12. Door primaries shall brief ABPs
13. CCMs shall brief Buddies and re-seat them.
14. Commence emergency preparation Phase 3

chunks.heading: 4.11.3.3 Selecting/Briefing ABPs – Prepared Ditching
chunks.text:
Ref 4.10.3.3 The briefing depends on the category. Given below is a guide to brief ABPs.
1. Wait until the aircraft comes to a complete stop
2. Await for command (Evacuate) and/or when other doors are been opened
3. Check outside for danger (Water level, Oil fires, Debris)
4. Hold assist handle and lift the door handle fully up and push open the door, Pull the manual inflation handle (Bottom Right)
5. Check for correct slide inflation (Show safety card)
6. Send two ABPs to board raft as soon as the slide raft is inflated to assist CCM/passengers
7. Remove incapacitated CCM and place in the raft (Demonstrate the opening of seat belts)
8. Ensure passengers inflate life vest and board raft
9. If the exit cannot be used redirect passengers to usable exits.
10. Explain detaching and disconnecting the raft from the aircraft

chunks.heading: 4.11.3.4 Selecting/Briefing ABPs - Unprepared Ditching
chunks.text:
Identify ABPs whilst evacuating and brief:
1. Advice two ABPs to board the raft
2. One ABP to control passengers at the far end
3. One ABP to remain at the board end and assist passengers in to the raft
4. Advice the third ABP to remain on-board and help passengers who require assistance (give out infant life vests/assist to inflate etc)

chunks.heading: 4.11.3.5 Selection/Briefing Buddies - Prepared Ditching
chunks.text:
Buddies are required to assist passengers with medical/assistance alert. Ref 2.24.4/5 Buddies shall be selected on the same guide lines of an ABP. Ref 4.10.3.3 In addition to above selection, preference should be passengers who are capable/ willing to assist in water. The Purser shall ensure the following guidelines are followed when CCMs brief buddies.
1. Introduce the dependent by name

chunks.heading: 4.11.7 Crowd Control
chunks.text:
Successful evacuations have been achieved due to CCMs taking control over the situation and passen- gers following instructions. Be assertive when commands and instructions are carried out to passen- gers. Passengers may not be familiar or comfortable with the sight of water and may be reluctant to evacuate. Physical force may be required to evacuate passengers with negative emotions. Constrains in a ditching could be but not limited to:
1. Panic at the sight of water
2. Climatic conditions and extremely cold water
3. Panic (screaming/crying/hysterical)
4. Negative panic (does not react to the situation)
5. No perception that danger exists
6. Evacuating with carry-on baggage
7. Attempt to get ahead of the others
