chunks.heading: 4.11.9 Post Ditching CCM Responsibilities
chunks.text:
If the raft is at an angle from the door-sill
1. Detach the raft from the door sill
2. Pull the raft towards the aircraft
3. Instruct passengers to inflate their life vests
4. Jump in to the water
5. Hold on to the life line and board raft When in the raft Instruct passengers to be seated on the floor with their backs to the buoyancy tubes. Equally distribute the weight to avoid the raft from capsizing. Rescue Search for any passengers and crew near the ditching site, particularly in the direction of the waves as passengers may be unconscious and floating.

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.1 Raft Duties Sequence
chunks.text:
1. Detach and Disconnect the raft from the aircraft
2. Move away from the aircraft - approximately 50 Meters
3. Deploy Sea Anchor
4. Deploy ELT (If applicable)
5. Retrieve survival pack
6. Deploy Sea Dye Marker
7. Tie the Rafts together
8. Erect the Canopy

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.2 Detaching and Disconnecting the Raft from the Door-sill
chunks.text: To detach, lift girt bar cover flap and pull the white release handle. If the pull handle gives way undo the white lacing manually. The raft would release from the door sill end but still remain connected to the aircraft by the Mooring line. To disconnect, cut the Mooring line with the hook knife or Pull the manual release handle on the top buoyancy chamber at the door-sill end, The manual release handle is located in a pouch covered by a Velcro strip on the top buoyancy chamber

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.3 Moving Away From the Aircraft
chunks.text: Once the raft is released, move to a safe distance from the aircraft as it may sink (approximately 50 meters)

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.8 Tie the Rafts together
chunks.text:
Rafts a should be tied together with the Heaving Ring line with slack on the line to prevent capsizing in rough waters.
1. For Safety - will be able to redistribute the loads.
2. Re unite family’s and groups- There will be an opportunity to reunite Families who were separat- ed during the evacuation.
3. Pooling Expertise - The ability to work out a coordinated plan of action based on a wider range of expertise and experience. “Look-outs” duties can be shared.
4. Centralize Treatment - The ability to assemble all the injuries and medical expertise in one area. Make the best use of the available medical supplies.
5. Increase Target for search and rescue -As two or more rafts are easier to locate as it forms a larg- er and more easily identifiable target.
6. Share Resource - The ability to share first aid Kit and survival equipment.

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.9 Erecting the Canopy
chunks.text:
The canopy protects occupants from weather conditions. For installation be guided by the following:
1. Board End - This marking on the canopy should be at the door sill end of the raft
2. This side up – The luminous side should face the sky
3. Even numbers – Should be on the right hand side guided by the door sill end
4. Care should be taken when unrolling the canopy to avoid being blown away
5. Commence unrolling from the direction the wind is blowing toward you. Keep both ends of the canopy low until a few points are attached.

chunks.heading: 4.11.9.10 CCM Responsibilities in the Raft
chunks.text:
1. The door primary should position himself closer to the sea anchor; it would enable him to ma- noeuvre and control the direction of the rafts away from fuel-saturated waters and also guard the raft against damage from sharp debris
2. A headcount should be carried out/administer first aid as required/set an order of priority and delegate responsibility
3. The commander of the raft should nominate and delegate work as movements are restricted. Keep all signalling devices in close proximity of the commander for quick use. Nominate one passenger for an inside watch and one passenger for an outside watch.

chunks.heading: • INSIDE WATCH
chunks.text: 1. Assign an ABP to monitor the condition of the passengers in the raft.

chunks.heading: • OUTSIDE WATCH
chunks.text:
1. Assign an ABP look out for persons in the water and for Search and Rescue operations (SAR).
2. These duties should be rotated every few hours to give people a sense of responsibility. Passen- gers should be reminded that cooperation is necessary to survive.
3. Keep the raft clean and dry to prevent illness and infection. Bail out water and wipe dry with fabric bailing bucket and sponges from Survival Kit.
4. Instruct passengers to be seated on the floor with their backs to the buoyancy tubes. Equally distribute the weight to avoid the raft from capsizing.
5. Reassure Passengers that help will arrive shortly.
6. Check buoyancy tubes for damage and proper inflation. Properly inflated tubes are firm but not drum tight. If punctures are found, repair with kit and instructions provided in the Survival Kit

chunks.heading: 4.12 Bracing
4.12 Bracing
chunks.text: the tips of the toes touch the bulkhead (do no push feet against the bulkhead).

chunks.heading: 4.12.2 Rearward-facing cabin crewmember seats
chunks.text: Cabin crewmembers shall brace according to the following instructions, as shown in Figure below

chunks.heading: 4.12.2 Rearward-facing cabin crewmember seats
4.12.3.1 Passengers Facing Forward
chunks.text: Seat belt should be securely fastened/seat back placed upright and the tray table stowed. Lean forward, place hands and arms on the seat back in front, one on top of the other. Fingers should not be inter- locked. Place the head on the hands resting on the front seat and feet placed firmly flat on the floor slightly forward. Bracing position options for passengers

chunks.heading: 4.12.3.1 Passengers Facing Forward
chunks.text: Bracing positions for passengers are clearly illustrated on the safety card. Cabin Seats - When seated at a location with a seat in front the adult shall lean forward and place the hands and arms against seat back. Bulk head seats- The adult should lean forward arms tucked under the knees. Head facing down or The adult should sit upright and place chin on the chest and hold the seat firmly with both hand to pre- vent forward movement.

chunks.heading: 4.12.3.2 Bracing Position-Pregnant Women
chunks.text: The seat back shall be placed upright/tray table stowed. The seat belt should be securely fastened and placed low below the abdomen so that it applies its force to the pelvis. Lean forward, place the hands on the seat pan for support. Pillows and blankets may be placed on the lap to rest the head. The feet placed flat on the floor slightly forward with knees together.

chunks.heading: 4.12.3.3 Bracing with Lap Held Infants - Options at standards seats
chunks.text:
1. The seat back shall be placed upright/tray table stowed.
2. The seat belt should be securely fastened.
3. The feet placed flat on the floor slightly forward with knees together.
4. Place the infant facing the adult, a larger infant may need to straddle the adult’s hips.
5. Lean forward and use one hand to support the back of the infant and hold the infants head fac- ing out wards with the palm of the hand.
6. Place the other hand of the adult on the seat in front.
7. In the event the front seat cannot be reached by the adult, sit upright, chin on the chest, sup- port the infant as above and use the other hand to hold and support the adults head by placing it on the upper back part of the head.

chunks.heading: 4.12.3.4 Bracing with an infant at the bulk head seats/Business Class Seat
chunks.text:
1. This shall be applicable to an adult with an infant, seated where the bulk head cannot be reached to rest the head or the hands for protection.
2. The adult shall sit with the lumbar fully resting on the seat back.
3. Restrain the infant with the kangaroo belt as per the laid down procedure.
4. Place the infant facing the adult - the infants legs may be placed on to the two side of the adult if possible.
5. Place the infants head to a side allowing the infant to breath comfortably.
6. Place one hand of the adult along the infant’s spine and hold on to the head of the infant for protection.
7. Place the other hand of the adult on the back of the adult’s head.
8. Place the adult’s legs firm together on the floor.
9. Place the adults chin on the chest for protection from whiplash.
10. Keep the body of the adult upright for the impact.

chunks.heading: 4.12.3.5 Bracing Position – Children
chunks.text:
1. Children occupying passenger seats should adopt the same brace positions as adults. Due to their small stature, the flail envelope of children is smaller than that of adults, so they are less likely to suffer secondary impact with the interior of the aircraft.
2. The lap strap should be placed low on the child’s torso, just above the legs at the hips. If the lap strap cannot be adjusted so that it is tight on a small child, the child may sit on a pillow or blanket in order to raise the child so that the lap strap will fit securely. The pillow should not be placed behind the child.
3. Children seated in a forward-facing seat should bend forward over the lap strap and rest their head on the seat cushion between their legs, or bend their head forward, over the edge of the cushion, as appropriate for their height. This is done to reduce head flailing.

chunks.heading: 4.12.4 Brace Signals (Prepared/ Unprepared Emergency)
chunks.text: The alert signal would be initiated by the flight crew 20 seconds (Approximately 200 feet) before im- pact. “BRACE, BRACE, BRACE”.

chunks.heading: 4.12.5 Brace Commands to Passengers
chunks.text: CCMs shall adopt the bracing position and follow the command from the PIC and shout, “HEADS DOWN, STAY DOWN”. The commands should be synchronized for a louder and clearer tone to prevent passengers from raising their heads. The CCMs should continue to shout out the bracing commands till the aircraft comes to a complete stop. WARNING: OPENING THE SEAT BELTS PREMATURELY COULD BE FATAL FOR CCMS AND PAS-

chunks.heading: 4.12.5.1 Emergency Commands from the Flight Deck
chunks.text:
Guide Lines for an Evacuation CCMs should assert their authority in order to avoid delays in passenger flow and be prepared to use a certain amount of physical force if required. Aircraft certifications require that all the passengers and crew should evacuate within 90 seconds with only half the exits in operation.
1. 20 Seconds before touch down “BRACE, BRACE BRACE”.
2. After landing “ATTENTION CABIN CREW AT STATIONS”.

chunks.heading: 4.12.5.1 Emergency Commands from the Flight Deck
chunks.text:
3. If evacuation is required “EVACUATE, EVACUATE, EVACUATE ”.
4. If evacuation is not required “CABIN CREW AND PASSENGERS REMAIN SEATED”.

chunks.heading: 4.12.6 Signals/Indications in the Cabin
chunks.text:
1. Pulsating horn throughout the cabin
2. Red attention getter flashing on the AIP ‘EVAC ALERT’– text Note: Evacuation will be carried out only when the aircraft comes to a complete stop and the en- gines are switched off. CCMs should be observant for any eventuality in the event the PIC announc- es the situation is under control. Note : When the A/C comes to a complete stop, in the absence of any response from the Flight Crew, CCMs shall try to establish communication with the Flight Crew (if situation permits), failing which shall initiate an evacuation.

chunks.heading: 4.14 Post Evacuation Survival
chunks.text: There would be many unforeseen situations in an emergency and crew at all times should use their best judgment in order to save lives. Immediate Action after Land Evacuation Evacuate from the aircraft when it comes to a complete stop. If passengers are injured nominate other passengers to assist them. Carry as much water as you can. Move away from the aircraft until danger of fire has ceased. Grouping A group of people always have a better chance of survival than alone. For protection from fire and fumes CCMs should be aware of up/ down wind and move away from the air craft, to avoid any explo- sion. Set out an order of priorities.

chunks.heading: 4.14 Post Evacuation Survival
chunks.text: Assess the mental and physical condition of the passengers.Administer first aid as required Check Emergency Equipment, Including Rations Check the survival packs. Examine the other equipment in the aircraft e.g. fire axe etc. Drain off supplies of fuel and oil for signalling purposes, check available rations and water supplies.Institute Immediate Rationing No matter how much food and water is available, attempt to conserve it as long as possible by rationing.

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text:
Survival on Land In order to survive and be rescued, certain basic principles should be followed. These must be applied in order of priority.
1. Protection, from the weather (heat, cold, wind, rain)
2. Water
3. First aid
4. Food
5. Rescue Protection Immediate steps must be taken by the survivors to protect themselves from the adverse effects of the environment, heat, cold, wind, rain, the chilling effect of wind on wet clothing, and extreme tempera- tures. Water Water is more important for survival than food. Take stock of emergency supplies of water and keep them for an emergency. Water found in holes will probably be muddy, filter it first, and then allow set- tling for a few hours, filter again and purify before drinking. If on the seashore dig a small hole a short distance above the high tide, and stop digging as soon as you find water. Water collected in this way should be fairly free from salt; fresh water floats on the top of salt water, hence don’t dig too deep.

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: Stagnant water is not necessarily infected, but as a precaution filter it and purify. Stagnant water may be found in small pools, amongst rocks, dead tree- stumps, etc. First-Aid Attend promptly to all injuries. Remove all injured personnel into the shade as soon as possible. Follow established first-aid practices. Location Having protected oneself from the wind and weather, the survivors must check and prepare all signal- ling equipment and have it ready for immediate use. Food Check on rations available, remembering that food should not be consumed unless there is sufficient water available for metabolism, and that proteins require more water than carbohydrates. Plant food alone is not likely to keep you alive indefinitely. It will, however, be a welcome addition to other food

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text:
and will keep starvation away for several days. There are a number of potential food plants to be found throughout the jungle. There is no need to worry unduly about the effects of poisonous plants, though a few might be considered highly dangerous, the greater number will most likely cause you to be indis- posed for a matter of days. Should there be at any time, an uncertainty of the plant you wish to eat, the following points may be of guidance, Eat strange plants sparingly, until you can be quite certain as to the reaction
6. Avoid plants which are unpleasant in taste, those which are bitter, or acid
7. Avoid plants, which give a milky or soapy sap
8. Monkey’s eating habits would be a good guide to safe food if found Desert Survival The word “desert” invariably produces in one’s mind a picture of large, dry, barren tracts of land, hot in the daytime and cool at night, where survival is most difficult. The temperature range in the extreme

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: desert regions is considerable. Hot days may be followed by freezing nights; the temperature fluctuates by as much as – 50 to – 70 degrees Fahrenheit. The decision to stay or travel would be vital for survival and rescue. It would be advantageous to be in the vicinity of the crash site if possible as it would be eas- ier to locate from the air than persons traveling. The aircraft provides you with shelter, signalling aids, and other useful emergency equipment and will avoid the difficulties and hazards of desert travel. Shelter The inside of the aircraft is unsuitable as shelter from extreme heat. CCMs need to be mindful of work during the day which would result in increased sweat rate and exertion. Desert - First-Aid Administer immediate first-aid to the slightest scratch as in hot and tropical climates the risk of poison- ing from an open wound is possible. Sources of Water Water is the key to survival in the desert. Your life expectancy under emergency conditions is deter-

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: mined by the amount of water available and the degree to which you can protect your body from direct exposure to the sun and heat, thereby minimizing loss of body fluids through perspiration. The following are some of the possible sources of water in desert regions: Wells and Water Holes They may be quite deep, with the water level below easy reach; it is advisable to carry a length of life line for lowering a can or some suitable container. Small water holes in dry stream beds are often kept covered with a flat rock or sand and require a careful search for their location. Edges of ancient water holes are built up above their surroundings by accumulations of excrement around them. Dry Stream Beds and Gullies By digging at the lowest point of the outside of a bend in the bed of a channel, or the lowest point between dunes, a source of water may be found. If wet sand or mud is found, put it in a cloth and wring

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: out the water.

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: Desert Plants Some desert plants store water in their trunks, branches or roots. Such plants are found mainly along desert fringes in semi-arid terrain and near water holes. Avoid plants with milky sap - they are poi- sonous. The presence of vegetation is not always a sign that water is available. In the Middle East, for example, the palm is the only plant which indicates that water is close at hand. Purification Water obtained by any of the methods previously outlined, or water that may be tainted or suspect, should be purified before drinking by one of the following methods. Desalting Tablets Crush and dissolve one Hal zone tablet in each pint of water. Shake well and allow to stand for an hour before drinking. If this is insufficient to produce a distinct smell of chlorine, add more tablets until the odour is present. Boiling Boil the water for at least three minutes and allow any sediment to settle while cooling.

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: Iodine Add two or three drops of iodine to each quart of water and allow to stand for 30 minutes. Rain During the rainy season, rain traps should be erected to catch as much water as possible. Any piece of tarpaulin or dinghy apron can be suspended between four stakes, allowing the water to drain down and accumulate in the centre. An inflated raft will also serve this purpose. Condensation During the cooler months some deserts are humid enough at night for dew to form. To collect this, scoop a shallow basin in the ground, and line it with canvas or raft material. Pile stones until the basin is filled. During the night the dew will collect on the stones and trickle down on to the lining. Metal parts of the aircraft will also collect dew. Dew should be collected at first light before it evaporates. Food and Water As far as surviving at sea is concerned, it is sufficient to follow three simple rules:

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text:
The quantity of the food and water rations must be varied in direct proportion to each other. If you have plenty of water you can increase the food ration, but as the water ration decreases the food ration must be decreased. Food containing protein, such as any raw fish/bird, or seaweed will require more water than your emergency rations. Do not drink un-purified water; it will only lead to dysentery. Do not drink alcohol - it will cause nausea and increase thirst. It is dangerous to drink alcohol under such conditions and may even bring about convulsions. Do not drink urine - it is poisonous and will decrease your resistance and increase your thirst. Immediate Actions - After Evacuation
1. Clear aircraft

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text:
2. Administer first aid
3. Put On warm clothing
4. Inflate rafts; disconnect slide-rafts and use for shelter.
5. Drain from engine sump to provide source of fuel for heating and cooking before the oil freezes
6. Place signalling equipment handy
7. Relax, read survival booklets (from first aid kits and raft survival packs)
8. Consider further action Shelter During summer the fuselage will provide adequate shelter. It should not be used as a shelter in winter, unless it is insulated. The metal is a good conductor of heat and will quickly dissipate any available heat. Consider using slides as shelter. Any rafts removed from the aircraft should be inflated as soon as possi- ble before cylinders become chilled and less efficient. The raft fabric will also harden quickly due to the extreme cold. Canopy side curtains should be extended to provide protection against wind and cold. Survival Hints

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: Maintain morale by good command and organize duties. Protection from cold would be an immediate and constant problem as such. Check for frostbite. Keep dry and warm. Carpets, upholstery, pillows can be used for extra clothing and foot protection. Wet clothes can be dried by removing and allowing them to freeze outside and beat the frozen moisture out of the article. The best policy for survivors is to stay in the vicinity of the crashed aircraft and await rescue rather than to travel to seek assistance. The aircraft is an easier target to spot from the air than people on the ground. Only if the surface of landing appears unsafe should a move to safer ground be considered. Do not touch metal with bare hands. This will damage skin and cause severe frostbite. Congealed oil/fuel can be used to make fires. During summer, use insect repellent and cover as much bare skin as possible with clothing. Baggage from holds can be used to shape distress signals visible to

chunks.heading: 4.14.1 Basic Survival Factors
chunks.text: search aircraft.Do not cause the body to sweat when working. Perspiration and wets clothing decreases effective insulation and increases the chances of freezing. If necessary, remove outer clothing when working. For water, melt ice rather than snow. If snow is used, melt a little first, and keep adding as it melts. Do not attempt to suck ice or snow.

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: Hypothermia Hypothermia is the condition when the body temperature is below normal and can be recognized by decreasing resistance to cold. Cover the victim with waterproof or insulation material if available. The victim should be placed on a dry improvised bed, ensuring the buttocks, shoulders and feet are well insulated. If possible, change the victim into warm dry clothes or wring out wet clothing. Prevent heat loss and provide heat preferably by a warm person’s body heat. Stimulation with hot drinks will help if the victim is conscious and does not vomit or cough. Wind Chill Wind increases heat loss by dispersing available heat. This heat loss increases with increase of wind speed. Survivors should take advantage of wind barriers e.g. side of crashed aircraft for shelter.

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: Frostbite Frostbite is the freezing of some part of the body and is a constant hazard in sub-zero conditions, par- ticularly in strong winds. It usually affects the extremities and exposed parts of the body which have the least circulation e.g. the face, nose, ears, hands and feet. The symptoms of frost-bite consist of small patches of white or cream coloured skin, stiff and firm to the touch. A prickling sensation may be felt. If the condition is allowed to become serious, tissues and bones may freeze and blood-cells clot. When the affected part is warmed, there will be a swelling and redness of the skin with accompanying pain depending on the degree of frost-bite. Protection is obtained by keeping as warm and dry as possible, moving limbs, and exercising face mus- cles. Affected parts must not be rubbed or massaged, but warmed gently with breath, warm hands, or other warm parts of the body.

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: Place frostbitten hands under clothing against the chest, under the armpits or between the legs at the groin. Hold frostbitten foot against a companion’s stomach or between his thighs. Never forcibly re- move frozen shoes or gloves. Never rub a frostbitten area and never rub with snow. Snow Blindness Snow blindness is a temporary form of blindness caused by the exposure of the unprotected eye to glare or snow. It can occur even on cloudy days. Prevention is done by wearing dark glasses at all times when outside in daylight. A handy substitute is a piece of wood, leather or cloth with narrow eye slits cut in it. Symptoms are redness, pain, watering or sandy feeling in eyes, and headaches. Treatment is to get the victim to a dark place or place a dark, light bandage over the eyes. Carbon Monoxide Poisoning It’s caused by a fire in an unventilated area. No symptoms. Unconsciousness and death may occur without warning.

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: Prevention is by ensuring that the shelter has enough ventilation when a fire is lit. Seasickness The performance of duties requiring some concentration helps to ward off seasickness. Its treatment is to refrain from eating and drinking for some time, to lie still, and to maintain body warmth. Anti-sick- ness tablets are normally provided in the first- aid kits. Immersion Foot Exposure of feet to cold water for some time results in damage to the tissues. The affected part be- comes red and painful and difficult to move. This is followed by swelling, the appearance of blisters and dark patches, and breaks in the skin. Prevention lies in keeping the feet as warm and dry as possible, and in ensuring that the floor of the raft is dry. The toes and feet should be moved frequently to assist blood circulation, and tightly fitting boots should be discarded. Remedial action is to remove footwear;

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: wrap feet in loose dry articles of clothing; raise the feet clear of any water; and keep the body warm. The affected parts should not be rubbed. Salt Water Sores These are caused by prolonged exposure to salt water. Prevention is by keeping the body as dry as pos- sible. The sores should be gently cleaned (but not squeezed), and antiseptic cream should be applied. Large sores should be covered with a dressing.

chunks.heading: 4.14.2 Hazards
chunks.text: Sore Eyes Sore eyes result from excessive exposure to glare from the sky and water, and should be treated by applying antiseptic cream to the eyelids and bandaging lightly. Relief may also be obtained by the use of damp bandages alone. Constipation or Difficulty in Urination These complaints should not give cause for alarm, as they are to be expected with a shortage of food and fresh water.

chunks.heading: 4.14.3 Survival And signalling Equipment
chunks.text: Survival Kit Supplementary Raft Accessory Kit (SRAK) Emergency Locator Transmitter Signalling Mirror/Heliograph Sea Dye Marker Whistle Flares Communication If the aircraft radio equipment is intact, try and contact the outside world. Prepare all Signalling devices for immediate Use. The time for preparation of Signalling equipment is limited when a search and rescue team is sighted. Light up fires and position oil and fuel to create a dense column of smoke at short notice. Adding fuel/ oil to the fire would create a rapid flare-up. Clear area for display of ground signals, or move to a clear area nearby. Spread out slides, keep polished aluminium panels for reflection. Try and improvise Signalling methods which will show above the jungle top e.g. Smoke columns or raft material spread over the trees.

chunks.heading: 4.14.3.1 Ground to Air visual Signal codes
chunks.text: The following are examples on international ground to air distress signals. It should be used in clear terrain for search and rescue operations to identify from a distance. The length of each indicator should be a minimum of 8 feet and the formation could be made of any visible materiel. e.g.; Rocks/Stones/Branches/Fabric. Message Code Require Assistance V Require Medical Assistance X Negative (No) N Affirmative (Yes) Y Proceed in this direction

chunks.heading: 4.14.3.1 Ground to Air visual Signal codes
chunks.text: If the distress signal is identified, the Aircraft would go in to a roll (longitudinal movement of the air- craft). Lack of the above signals indicates that the ground signals have not been met. The following actions performed by an aircraft indicate the aircraft wishes to direct a surface craft to- wards an aircraft or a distress sight. Circling the surface Passing the air craft close at a low altitude. At night flashing the landing lights or switching on/off the navigation lights.

chunks.heading: 4.15 Missed Approach
chunks.text: Missed approach is when a landing has to be aborted on the final approach. There will no communica- tion from the flight deck specifying a missed approach. CCM shall remain seated until advised.

chunks.heading: 4.16 Rejected - Take Off
chunks.text: Description A rejected take-off is when a take-off is discontinued on the runway. The indications are rapid decelera- tion. In such situations CCMs should remain seated until further instructions are carried out by the PIC.

chunks.heading: 4.16.1 Flight Deck Communication
chunks.text: Pending a decision the PIC shall initiate a PA announcement: “ATTENTION CABIN CREW AT STATIONS”.

chunks.heading: 4.16.2 Cabin Crew Member Procedures
chunks.text: After the initial command from the PIC, the CCMs should remain seated and await further instructions. In the event an evacuation is required follow evacuation procedures. If evacuation not required the following announce “CABIN CREW AND PASSENGERS REMAIN SEATED”. CCMs should advice passengers to remain seated and remain alert for signs of fire/smoke or any abnor- mality should be informed to the PIC immediately etc.

chunks.heading: 4.17.1 Incapacitated Flight Crew Member
chunks.text:
In case of an incapacitation of a Flight Crew member, the remaining Crew Member shall alert the CCM. “PURSER TO THE FLIGHT DECK IMMEDIATELY”. The Purser or any CCM in the vicinity shall proceed to the flight deck immediately. The CCM should,
1. Fasten the shoulder harness to the lap strap/ manually lock and tighten
2. Move the hands off the controls
3. Pull the seat completely aft
4. Recline the seat back
5. Follow instructions from the remaining flight crew
6. Provide first aid /Assistance It would take at least two people to move an unconscious person from the flight deck seat Purser/CCM to Get instruction from the remaining flight crew such as:
1. To move the incapacitated flight crew member to the cabin or to keep him in the flight deck.

chunks.heading: 4.17.1 Incapacitated Flight Crew Member
chunks.text:
2. Seek the assistance from a medically qualified passenger if available
3. Check discreetly for any Qualified Pilot, preferably from Srilankan airlines to replace the Incapac- itated Pilot.

chunks.text:
Light turbulence momentarily Causes slight, rapid and rhythmic bumpiness without noticeable changes in the aircraft alti- tude or attitude
• Liquids are shaking but are not splashing out of cups

chunks.heading: 5.1.1 A330
chunks.text:
Description The Airbus A-330 aircraft is a medium to long range, twin aisle subsonic transport aircraft, powered by two turbo-fan engines. The fuselage has a circular cross section and is entirely pressurized with the exception of the nose cone, tail cone and the landing gear compartments. The flight deck is equipped for a two-crew operation and accommodates two observers. The passenger cabin-seating layout may vary to suit operator requirements. Any combination of Cabin Attendant seats may be provided with a minimum of 8 primary seats. The landing gear consists of
1. Two inboard retracting main gears
2. One forward retracting nose gear

chunks.heading: 5.1.2 Specific Details
chunks.text: The fuel is stowed in, inner and outer tanks in the wings, the centre section and Trimmable Horizontal Stabilizer.

2. AFT cargo compartment
3. Bulk cargo compartment (temperature controlled to carry live or loose cargo)

chunks.heading: 5.2.1 Cabin Windows
chunks.text: Passenger cabin windows are located at eye level mounted at intervals of 530 mm (20.9”). Each window has an outer, middle and inner pane. The inner and outer panes are stressed to maintain cabin pressure. A small vent hole is found at the bottom of the middle pane to equalize the pressure between the inner and outer pane. The inner pane is equipped with a sun shade (Blind).

chunks.text: A White slide armed warning light will illuminate steady to indicate that the door is being opened in the armed mode. A Red cabin pressure warning light flashes if the cabin remains pressurized, when the engines are shut down and the slides are disarmed. chunks.text: The bright coloured self-reeling canvas strap is used to prevent accidents Whenever the aircraft is not being serviced from a particular door and remains opened, it must always be guarded with the door restraint strap WARNING - DO NOT LEAVE AN OPEN DOOR UNATTENDED AS THE SAFETY STRAP ACROSS THE DOOR WILL NOT PREVENT PASSENGERS/CREW MEMBERS FROM FALLING OUT. Note: Door Restraint Strap rolls up automatically during removal procedure. The cabin crew must ensure that the safety strap is fully retracted into its recess before closing the door.

chunks.heading: 5.5.1 CCM Responsibilities
chunks.text:
The Purser shall inform all door primaries to arm slides and cross check prior to every take off. Once the aircraft is parked the Purser should instruct the door primaries to disarm the slides, The PIC shall in- struct to open doors when reqired. The door primaries shall follow the commands and cross check when the slides are armed or dis- armed. Arming
1. Open the transparent cover
2. Remove the safety pin
3. Move the Arming / Disarming lever to the “ARMED” position
4. Stow the safety pin
5. Close the transparent cover
6. Cross check

chunks.heading: 5.5.1.1 Disarming
chunks.text: Once the aircraft is parked/chocks on and the seat belt sign is switched off, the Purser shall initiate a PA announcement for the door primaries to disarm slides, The slides on the right shall be disarmed first.

chunks.heading: 5.5.1.1 Disarming
chunks.text:
Prior to disarming the slides on the right, door primaries on the left shall cross over to the right. The following disarming procedure shall be carried out. (“PIN/LEVER/PIN” verbally stated by the CCM whilst disarming the slide) Primaries shall,
1. Open the transparent cover
2. Remove safety pin from the slot
3. Move the arming / disarming lever to the “DISARMED” position
4. Install the safety pin with the RED STREAMER exposed
5. Close the transparent cover
6. Cross check The slides on the left shall be disarmed next, Once the right side slides are disarmed, both door primaries shall cross over to the left and the left side door primary shall disarm the slide observed by the opposite door primary.

chunks.heading: 5.5.1.2 Cross Checking after arming the door
chunks.text: On command from the Purser the door primaries shall arm the slides and cross check with the opposite door primaries.

chunks.heading: 5.5.1.3 Cross Checking after disarming the door
5.5.2 Precautions
chunks.text:
If the status of the slide is not indicated in the flight deck,
1. The PIC would inform the Purser
2. The Purser shall re check with the relevant door primary
3. The door primary should recycle the procedure and confirm as per the instructions given by the Purser

chunks.text: The proximity of fire or wreckage could render a slide unusable Strong wind conditions could cause movement of the slide At airports, congestion of vehicles/aircraft /movable/immovable structures could block the full extent of the slide

chunks.text: A CCM should be mindful when assessing the use of slides for unusual attitude of the aircraft which may restrict the use of escape slides If sliding angle is reduced due to lower doorsill height, it is recommended that passengers be directed to run down the slides

5. Check for correct slide inflation
6. If the slide does not inflate, pull manual inflation handle located on the right side at floor level

chunks.text: as a raft in a ditching Type “1” door is equipped with a single lane slide and cannot be used as a raft but as a flotation device in a ditching They are stowed in a container hinged on the lower part of the door. When the door is opened in the “ARMED” mode, automatic slide/raft deployment and inflation will occur. The disconnection procedure is clearly marked on the slide. Doors L2/R 2 - the slide-rafts will deploy at an angle away from the engines. Slide/ Raft Deployment

chunks.heading: 5.6.6.2 Side
chunks.text: Deployment

chunks.text: If the slide/raft fails to inflate automatically, pull the manual inflation handle located on the right-side floor level, for manual inflation of slide/raft.

chunks.heading: 5.6.6.5 Slide/Raft Deployment (type “A” door)
chunks.text:
1. Doorsill End
• The Doorsill end of the slide raft is attached to the girt bar.
2. Side and Center Tubes
• The inflated tubes stabilize the slide raft structure. The center tube additionally sepa- rates the sliding lanes
3. Sliding Surface
4. Deceleration Strips
• There are deceleration strips at the end of the slid raft. These strips decrease the speed of evacuees, before ground contact.
5. Far End
• The Far end of the slideraft touches the ground during on-ground evacuation.
6. LED Lights
• The LED lights provide lighting to the sliding surface and at the far end of the slide raft.
• They shall illuminate for approximately 12 min after slide raft deployment.

chunks.heading: 5.6.6.6 Lighting Strips on Escape Slides
chunks.text: Emergency path lighting strips are installed on all slides in the inner corners and at the end of the slide. It will activate when the slides are deployed and will last for approximately 12 minutes provided the power cable remains connected to the aircraft. Locator lights which are installed on the canopy support tubes shall last for 8 hrs powered by water activated batteries.

chunks.heading: 5.6.6.7 Raft deployed in abnormal Conditions
chunks.text: If the raft is not in a conducive angle or attitude for passengers to board (due to water level lower than the doorsill, rough waters), it should be detached and pulled towards the doorsill by the Mooring line. The passengers should be advised to inflate the life vest and board the raft or alternatively Inflate life vest, jump into the water and hold on to the life line and board raft.

chunks.heading: 5.6.7 Detaching Slide/Raft
chunks.text:
The slide raft is held on to the doorsill girt bar, by a lacing referred to as a daisy chain. The daisy chain is covered by a Velcro flap.
1. Lift the Velcro flap to expose the daisy chain and the white pull handle.
2. Pull the white ‘PULL’ disconnect handle, attached to the lacing holding the raft to the girt bar.
3. If the pull handle fails, undo the lacing manually.
4. Once detached, the slide raft would still be connected to the aircraft by the Mooring line

chunks.heading: 5.6.8 Detaching the Slide (L3/R3) - Type ‘1’ Doors
chunks.text:
The slides at L/R 3 type “I” doors (on selected aircraft) are only floatation devices. It should be detached from the aircraft and pulled towards the door using the Mooring line prior to evacuating passengers.
1. Undo the studs holding the Velcro flap at each end of the girt and lift flap up
2. Pull the white “PULL” handle to undo the lacing
3. If the pull handle fails, undo the lacing manually Note: Once detached, the slide raft would still be connected to the aircraft by the Mooring line

chunks.heading: 5.6.9 Disconnecting the Raft Type ‘A’ Doors
chunks.text:
1. Cut the Mooring line with the hook knife, The hook knife is located in a pouch 1/3rd away from the door-sill on top of the buoyancy chamber Or
2. Pull the manual release handle on the top buoyancy chamber at the door-sill end, The manual release handle is located in a pouch covered by a Velcro strip on the top buoyancy chamber

chunks.heading: 5.6.9 Disconnecting the Raft Type ‘A’ Doors
chunks.text:
Or
3. The Mooring line would release at its automatic release point of 375 Kg.

chunks.heading: 5.6.10 Disconnecting the Slide (L3/R3) – Type ‘1’ Doors
chunks.text: When the slide is used as a floatation device it should be disconnected from the aircraft after the passengers have evacuated. In the event the aircraft sinks prior to the disconnection, The Mooring line would release at its automatic release point of 375 Kg. Or pull the manual release handle on the top buoyancy chamber at the door-sill end, The manual release handle is located in a pouch covered by a Velcro strip on the top buoyancy chamber No hook knife / heaving ring/survival kit or sea anchor is installed on the slides.

chunks.heading: 5.6.11 Survival kit attached to the Raft
chunks.text: The survival kit is attached to the raft along with a bellows hand pump to a retrieve line and has to be retrieved from the water once the raft is fully deployed. The canopy & centre masts are located inside the survival Kit. It is bright orange/red in colour to attract attention, is water proof / wind resistant. Not available on Type ‘1’ doors (slides).

chunks.heading: 5.6.12 Erecting the Canopy
chunks.text: Side Masts The side masts are mounted on the top buoyancy chamber of the raft and inflate along with the raft. At the doorsill end both side masts are taped down to prevent damage from the door. The centre masts The centre masts are manually inflated and secured at the Velcro attachment points located at the cen- tre of the raft. Included in the survival pack. When erected, will keep the canopy raised. Masts are not available at Type “I” doors (slides).

chunks.heading: 5.6.12.1 Canopy Erection Instructions
chunks.text:
Canopy erection instructions are printed on the pouch in which the canopy is stowed.
1. Remove canopy from the bag

chunks.heading: 5.6.12.1 Canopy Erection Instructions
chunks.text:
2. Keep the canopy low to prevent it being blown away
3. Prevent occupants standing up in the raft to avoid capsizing
4. Open the canopy
5. Unfold the canopy keeping it low
6. The marking on the canopy ‘BOARD END’ should be next to the girt bar end
7. The marking ‘THIS SIDE UP’ should be on the outer part of the canopy
8. Release the two support tubes held down at the doorsill end
9. Spread canopy lengthwise on the slide raft
10. Canopy support tubes and canopy tie downs are numbered. Odd numbers for the left (when facing the door sill end) and even numbers for the right side and match the numbers accordingly
11. Align the canopy tie down string patches with the canopy support tubes
12. Raise the canopy, downwind first, over the canopy support tubes
13. Two attachment points are located for the canopy to be tied down One on the support tubes, and the other on the top buoyancy chamber For ventilation it should be attached on to the sup-

chunks.heading: 5.6.12.1 Canopy Erection Instructions
chunks.text:
port tubes For maximum weather protection, attach the canopy on to the buoyancy chambers
14. Attach canopy tie down strings to the attachment points on the slide raft. Care should be taken to use easy release knots to tie canopy down, for quick release, to use the signalling devices
15. Manually inflate the centre mast and place them on the Velcro patches located along the centre of the slide
16. Certain canopies are equipped with an opening in the centre to collect rainwater. It is advisable to discard the first amount of rainwater collected as it will be salty. After collecting the required quantity of water, tie up the tube to prevent the interior of the slide raft from becoming wet. Note: Canopy erection instructions are in the slide raft management guide, in the survival kit.

chunks.heading: 5.6.12.2 Raft
chunks.text: The hook knife is located in a pouch on the top buoyancy chamber, on type “A” slide rafts. The manual release handle is located in a pouch covered by a Velcro strip on the top buoyancy chamber on the door sill end Wrap the canopy string around the rubber button on the canopy support tube. Care should be taken to use easy release knots to tie canopy down. The canopy may be rolled up at the sides for ventilation if desired.

chunks.heading: 5.6.12.2 Raft
chunks.text: Raft Inflation Bellows hand pump shall be used to top-up the buoyancy chambers. Attachment points for the pump are located on the raft. Screw the hand pump on to the attachment point and inflate the relevant cham- ber

chunks.heading: 5.7.1 Escape Routes
chunks.text: Escape routes from the flight deck are sliding windows and the secure flight deck door.

chunks.heading: 5.7.1.1 Sliding Windows
chunks.text: Two sliding windows are located in the flight deck, one on each side, and both could only be opened from inside. It’s locked in position and a control handle is located to release it. An escape rope is posi- tioned above the window in a cavity to lower one’s self to ground level. To Open Press down the knob on the operating handle/rotate handle inwards and rearwards, for the window to slide back and lock itself in the open position. To Close Release the locking lever by pulling it towards the aft, slide the window forward and once in position rotate the control handle back to the locking position.

chunks.heading: 5.7.1.2 Escape Rope
chunks.text: Two knotted descent escape ropes are installed in the flight deck one over each sliding window which can withstand a weight of 180 kg. The Flight Crew may use the descent ropes to leave the flight deck through the opened sliding windows, descending facing the fuselage.

chunks.heading: 5.7.2 Secure Flight Deck Door
chunks.text: All SriLankan Airlines aircrafts are equipped with a secure flight deck door. It is a bullet proof door that separates the flight deck from the cabin. It is designed to resist penetration by small arms fire, grenade shrapnel and resist forcible intrusion by unauthorised persons. It is fully compliant with rapid decom- pression requirements. It has a digital keypad located on the door frame. It has an electrical control system, located in the flight deck. A evacuation and decompression panel is located on the lower part of the door. The secure flight deck door shall be closed before the last cabin door is closed, and remain closed until completion of flight leg. As the flight deck door is heavy care should be taken, to close the door gently.

chunks.heading: 5.7.2.1 The Evacuation and Decompression Panel
chunks.text:
The evacuation and decompression panel enables the flight crew to evacuate the flight deck in case of emergency when the secure flight deck door is jammed or stuck, The evacuation and decompression panel could be removed only from the flight deck To remove the evacuation and decompression panel (A330-300,ALS)
• Rotating the handle cover in order to access the panel release handle.
• Pushing the panel release handle and turning it in any direction in order to unlock the panel and kicking the panel open.
• If the escape panel is unlocked, the locked indicator is red. ALH - Kick the panel open

chunks.heading: 5.7.2.2 Digital Key Pad
chunks.text: .The keypad is located on the doorframe and equipped with two indicator lights (green and red) / numerical display. The keys are used to, request entry to the flight deck and the numbers are used to unlock the door. In case the key pad is unserviceable, the Purser shall discuss with the PIC an alternate flight deck entry procedure before departure.

chunks.heading: 5.7.2.2 Digital Key Pad
chunks.text: Key Pad Indicators Green light – steady- Indicates the Flight Crew has unlocked the door and it remains unlocked for 5 seconds. Red light - Steady - Indicates the Flight Crew has denied access, the door remains locked and the emer- gency access keypad is inhibited for a pre-selected time.

chunks.heading: 5.7.2.3 Controls on the Secure Flight Deck Door
chunks.text: The toggle switch located in the flight deck has three positions and an indicator light comes on when the door is opened.

chunks.heading: 5.7.3 Opening the Secure Flight Deck Door from the cabin
chunks.text:
The door could be opened in,
1. Normal operation
2. Secondary operation
3. Emergency operation

chunks.heading: 5.7.3.1 Normal Operation
chunks.text:
1. Press “CALL CAPT” on the handset
2. Establish contact with the Flight Crew and request access to the flight deck If entry is authorized by the Flight Crew:
1. The Flight Crew unlocks the door
2. A green light illuminates steady on the keypad, and kept unlocked for 5 seconds CCM may gain entry by pushing open the door If entry is not authorized:
1. The door will be locked and red light comes on steady on the keypad

chunks.heading: 5.7.3.1 Normal Operation
chunks.text: 2. The keypad is locked for a pre-selected time

chunks.heading: 5.7.3.2 Secondary Operation
chunks.text:
1. Press 01 # on the key pad to request entry If entry is authorized
1. The Flight Crew unlocks the door
2. A green light illuminates steady, and door will be unlocked for 5 seconds
3. CCM may gain entry by pushing open the door

chunks.heading: 5.7.3.3 Emergency Operation
chunks.text:
PIC shall brief the Purser regarding the 2 to7 digit secret code at the pre-flight safety briefing to be used in the event of an emergency. The code shall be referred to as Code Red. CCM shall adopt the following emergency procedure in the event of the Flight Crew does not respond to a call from the Cabin. Press “PRIO CAPT” on the handset to establish contact with the Flight Crew. If there is no response from the Flight Crew;
1. Enter code red
2. The green light on the key pad would start flashing
3. After a pre-selected time of (15 /120 seconds)
4. The door would unlock for 5 seconds/green light would illuminate steady
5. CCM shall gain entry by pushing open the door
6. Precautions Note 1 : In the event of a power supply failure, the flight deck door automatically unlocks, but re- mains closed, Note 2 : In case of a rapid cabin decompression the evacuation and decompression panel automati-

chunks.heading: 5.7.3.3 Emergency Operation
chunks.text: cally opens towards the cabin. In case of rapid decompression in the flight deck, the flight deck door automatically opens

chunks.heading: 5.7.4 Avionics Compartment
chunks.text: The compartment is located behind the captain’s seat directly under the fight deck and houses the elec- tronic equipment of the aircraft, the internal entry door to the avionics compartment is located on the floor level. A ladder is installed under the floor to provide access to the avionics compartment. Another door is installed at the bottom of the avionics compartment that can be opened from inside and outside to exit the aircraft WARNING: THIS AREA IS NOT ACCESSED BY CABIN CREW.

chunks.heading: 5.8.1 PIC‘s Seat
chunks.text:
The seat has the following features,
1. Column mounted
2. Electrically operated, vertical and horizontal positions with a manual back up
3. Manually operated recline control
4. A shoulder harness/lap strap/ crotch strap with a locking lever for restraining and an adjustable lumbar support
5. The life vest is stowed at the back of the seat

chunks.heading: 5.8.2 First Officer’s Seat
chunks.text: Is identical to the PIC’s seat, except, that the electrical and manual controls, are located on the left side.

chunks.heading: 5.8.3 The First Observer Seat
chunks.text:
The seat has the following features,
1. Column mounted
2. A manually operated recline lever
3. A shoulder harness, lap strap/crotch strap with a locking lever for restraining
4. Seat rotation lever
5. The life vest is located behind the seat in a transparent compartment at floor level

chunks.heading: 5.8.4 The Second Observer Seat
chunks.text: The seat has the following features, A fixed seat with a shoulder harness/lap strap and a crotch strap with a single point release buckle The life vest is located in a compartment under the seat Overview of the flight deck seating

chunks.heading: 5.9 Cabin Crewmember Seats/Stations
chunks.text:
The crew seats are categorized as Primary seats/Assist seats/High comfort seats/ Seats without seat belts The Cabin Crewmember seats are equipped with the following features,
1. Service Unit with two oxygen masks each
2. Interphone adjacent to each CCM seat
3. Torch
4. Life vests located under each CCM seat
5. Reading light
6. Attendant Indicator Panel (AIP) adjacent to each crew seat
7. Area Call Panel (ACP)
8. Seat belt with a single point release device (adjustable pelvic restrain)
9. Shoulder harness (on auto locking reel)
10. Auto folding seat pan Operation of Crew Seats
1. Place seat pan down
2. Retrieve lap straps which are stowed at the back of the seat pan and open
3. Sit, lock lap straps around the waist and tighten
4. Pull the harnesses over the shoulders, and insert the metal plate in to the buckle
5. The self-adjusting shoulder harness would reel back the extra slack
6. To extend the shoulder harness it has to be a smooth movement forwards

chunks.heading: 5.9 Cabin Crewmember Seats/Stations
chunks.text:
7. The shoulder harness would lock itself on a whip action
8. To release ,rotate the buckle 90° When not in use the lap strap should be stowed in the cavity at the end of the seat pan

chunks.heading: 5.9 Cabin Crewmember Seats/Stations
chunks.text: Hi comfort seat

chunks.heading: 5.10.1 BC - Seat Features
chunks.text:
1. Seat row indicator
2. Seat belts
3. Electrically operated with manual back up seat adjustments
4. Lumbar support/Recline/ Adjustable leg rest
5. Manually adjustable head rest
6. Air vent
7. Individual reading light
8. Snake head adjustable reading light
9. A rotating tray table for easy exit
10. Hand set, hand held controls
11. Touch system screen
12. Movie screen with touch system and hand controls
13. Life vest for each seat

chunks.heading: 5.10.2 E/Y - Seat Features
chunks.text:
1. Seat row indicator
2. Seat is 17.99” wide and reclines 14.9°
3. Seat belts
4. Manually operated Recline/ Lumbar support
5. Personal air vent
6. Individual reading light
7. Tray table stowed in front or on the side at bulkhead seats
8. Hand set, hand held controls 9.6’ inch Movie screen with touch system and hand controls
10. Life vest located under each seat

chunks.heading: 5.11.1 Over Head Bins
chunks.text: Overhead compartments are provided throughout the entire cabin. It’s designed to hold a specified weight. The stowage compartment doors needs to be locked when not in use.

chunks.heading: 5.11.2 Doghouses/Coat closets
chunks.text: The doghouses and coat closets are located throughout the cabin. It is installed with a locking device. A doghouse is a smaller stowage compartment with a drawer, fixed on the aircraft floor

chunks.heading: 5.11.2 Doghouses/Coat closets
chunks.text: Revision No 02 Revision Date 15 August 2024

chunks.heading: 5.12 Galleys
chunks.text: A-330 Aircraft

chunks.heading: 5.12.1 Galley Power
chunks.text: When the aircraft is on ground, galley power is supplied from the APU. During flight power is generat- ed from the aircraft engines. The galley power master switch is located and controlled from the flight deck and the individual power switches with circuit breakers are located in each galley. Malfunctions observed on any electrical equipment not limited to shall be brought to attention of the PIC and the power source switched off.

chunks.heading: 5.12.1.1 Circuit Breaker Panels (CB)
chunks.text: All electrically operated units such as Ovens/Coffee makers/Refrigerators are connected to the power source through individual CBs with a fuse to guard against any malfunction. The CBs are located on the appliance itself or on a CB panel in each galley. A CB once popped shall nev- er be reset. The defect shall be entered in the cabin defects log book. In the event a CB shall be pulled out for resetting purposes, it shall be carried out only with the consent of the PIC. CCMs shall be aware of the corresponding CB panel in their respective working areas.

chunks.heading: 5.12.2 Galley Sink
chunks.text: Sinks are located in each galley of the A-330 aircraft. A spigot (Tap) is located above all sinks. A vacu- um release knob located in the vicinity of every sink is pulled to drain water; it helps to releasing any trapped air from the sink drain pipes.

chunks.heading: 5.12.2.1 Water Shut Off/Supply Valves
chunks.text: The water shut off valves cuts off water to the spigots and the coffee makers in the respective galleys. In the event water supply is shutoff to a heater the power supply to the element shall be switched off as well.

chunks.heading: 5.12.3.1 Galley Equipment Pre-flight checks
chunks.text:
Shall consist of but not limited to ensure
1. Locking and latching devices are functioning
2. Circuit breakers are not popped out
3. Drain sinks are not blocked
4. Heaters and chillers functioning
5. If concerns are observed it shall be communicated to Purser and an entry made in the cabin defects log book.

chunks.heading: 5.13 Lavatories
chunks.text: Each Lavatory is equipped with the following, Wash basin with hot & cold water Lavatory bowl with a vacuum flush system Air outlet/waste bin/water heater/water shut off valve Bi-foldable or single door with occupied / vacant sign visible Lavatory Service Unit with 110V Razor outlet, Attendant Call Push Button / Return to Seat Pictogram Oxygen Mask Container Diaper changing board, Assist handle for PWD use in selected lavatories. On selected lavatories an unlocking mechanism is installed

chunks.heading: 5.13.1 Door Locking/ Unlocking Mechanism
chunks.text: (Internal) To lock the door move the locking lever to the left and to unlock move the locking lever to the right.

chunks.heading: 5.13.2 Emergency unlocking of the Lavatory Door
chunks.text: From outside (External) The door could be locked/unlocked from outside by lifting the “LAVATORY” sign cover plate and sliding the locking lever to occupied/vacant positions. If the Lavatory is vacant it shall indicate in green.

chunks.heading: 5.13.2.1 Single Blade door A 330-300
chunks.text:
1. Lift up the spring loaded LAVATORY cover.
2. Slide the knob to the side until the indicator shows VACANT
3. Turn the lock-pin (located next to the door locking mechanism) a quarter turn from left to right to release the locking catch and open the lavatory door
4. To reset the locking mechanism , close the door turn the lock-pin push the locking catch back in to position and turn the locking pin to the left or right.

chunks.heading: 5.13.2.2 Bi-folding doors
chunks.text:
1. Lift up the spring loaded LAVATORY cover.
2. Slide the knob to the side until indicator shows VACANT.
3. Push the lavatory door open and /or release the door latches and pull the lavatory door fully open outwards. or
4. Lower the two spring loaded door hinges located on the upper and lower part of the door frame and pull the door outwards.

chunks.heading: 5.13.3.1 Electrical Outlet
chunks.text: Each lavatory is equipped with a power socket for electrical shavers (Voltage 110-115 Volts, 400 Hz)

chunks.heading: 5.13.3.2 Water Heater Units
chunks.text: The water heater has the capacity of 1.5 litres. A thermal switch regulates the water temperature between 40°- 48°c. If the temperature reaches 90°c due to a malfunction the power supply is automatically cut off. The ON/OFF toggle switch is used for manual control. Amber light illuminates when the heater is switched ON. In the event the water supply to the heater has to be turned off, ensure the heater is switched off prior to do so.

chunks.heading: 5.13.3.3 Lavatory Lighting
chunks.text: The lavatory lights are installed above the door of each lavatory and are controlled by a switch installed in the locking device. The fluorescent lamps are on 50% intensity, when the lavatory door is closed/opened and unlocked. When the lavatory is locked the light brightens to 100% intensity and during a total power failure the emergency light in the lavatory illuminates along with other emergency lighting.

chunks.heading: 5.13.3.6 Water Shut-Off Valve
chunks.text: Each lavatory is equipped with a water shut off valve to shut off the water supply to the faucet and lav- atory. The location may vary depending on the aircraft type. In the event the water supply to the heater has to be switched-off ensure water heater is switched –off prior to doing so.

chunks.heading: 5.13.3.7 Vacuum Release Valve
chunks.text: (Float Valve)- In the lavatories. Under each wash basin a float valve is installed. It prevents leakage of the cabin air pressure through the drain lines. The wash basin water could be drained by pulling the ring located at the top of the valve

chunks.heading: 5.13.4 Waste Bin Fire Extinguisher
chunks.text: The automatic fire extinguisher containing 120 grams of Halon and Freon gas is installed in the compartment below the sink of each lavatory. When exposed to heat in excess of 77° C, the Halon Freon gas is discharged within 60 seconds through a single nozzle into the waste bin. Pre-flight Check The needle of the pressure gauge should be in the green zone.

chunks.heading: 5.13.5 Lavatory Smoke Detector
chunks.text: Pre Flight Check The Purser shall carry out the serviceability check of the smoke detector by pressing the ‘system check’ key on FAP.Select systems check hard key to confirm that the smoke detector “<” symbol on the system check page is not flashing. Touchscreen FAP, on the smoke page check the serviceablity of toilet, It is mandatory that CCMs inspect the lavatory smoke detectors for tampering prior to every departure and during flight.

chunks.heading: 5.13.5.1 Indication of Smoke/Fire in a Lavatory
chunks.text:
1. A repetitive triple low chime will sound every 30 seconds over the cabin loudspeakers
2. SMOKE PAGE on the FAP automatically comes on indicating the affected lavatory together with the location on aircrafts with touch screen FAPs
3. Red attention getter on all AIPs flashes, and text displaying the affected lavatory
4. The amber light will flash at the respective ACPs
5. The amber light mounted on the exterior of the affected lavatory would flash
6. A steady red SMOKE LAV button on the Forward Attendant Panel (FAP) and the Additional Atten- dant Panels (AAP) will illuminate

chunks.heading: 5.13.5.1 Indication of Smoke/Fire in a Lavatory
chunks.text: To reset the audio and visual alerts press “SMOKE LAV” on the FAP or AAP of the smoke alert zone.

chunks.heading: 5.13.5.2 Re-Setting the System
chunks.text:
Once the smoke clears the system will reset automatically. By pressing the LAV SMOKE Indicator on the FAP or AAP’s audio and the visual signs on the AIP and ACP will be cancelled, but the following indica- tions will remain on until the smoke clears
1. Amber flashing light on LAV exterior wall
2. SMOKE RESET (FAP) and SMOKE LAV (AAP) buttons illuminated red
3. On the touch screen FAP the smoke page indication CAUTION: SPRAYING AEROSOL CANS IN THE VICINITY OF THE SMOKE DETECTOR MAY TRIG- GER A SMOKE DETECTION EVENT. Programming and Indicator Module (PIM) Systems check in sequence (If Available)

chunks.heading: 5.13.6 Inoperative Lavatory Smoke Detection Systems
chunks.text:
An aircraft may be dispatched with an inoperative smoke detection system. Lavatories may be used provided
1. The associated lavatory/s fire extinguishing system is operative
2. The lavatory/s is checked periodically every 15 minutes, for the absence of smoke/fire

chunks.heading: 5.13.7 Inoperative Lavatory Fire Extinguisher
chunks.text:
Lavatories shall not to be used The aircraft may be dispatched with inoperative lavatory fire extinguishing system/s provided,
1. The associated lavatory waste bin is empty
2. The associated lavatory door is closed /locked
3. The associated lavatory is placarded inoperative
4. The lavatory is checked periodically every 15 minutes for the absence of smoke/fire

chunks.heading: 5.13.8 Inoperative lavatory waste bin cover flap/waste bin access door
chunks.text:
1. The associated lavatory shall not be used
2. The associated waste bin shall be empty
3. The waste bin door / cover flap shall be sealed
4. The lavatory door is closed / locked and placarded inoperative
5. The lavatory is checked periodically every 15 minutes for the absence of smoke/ fire

chunks.heading: 5.13.9 Communication System AIP/ACP
chunks.text: When faced with an emergency, which requires immediate attention the inter-phone system should be the preferred means of communication. The inter communication system is linked to audio and visual signs.

chunks.heading: 5.13.10 Attendant Indicator Panel - AIP
chunks.text: The AIPSs are located in the galley areas to attract the attention of CCMs in the galleys. All visual signs on the AIPs are initiated with a low chime with the following attention getters.

chunks.heading: 5.13.10 Attendant Indicator Panel - AIP
chunks.text: GREEN (steady) General communication RED (steady) Warning alert RED (flashing) Emergency Communication indication would appear in alpha numerical display on the AIP. The caller locations appear on the top part of the screen and systems information is displayed on the bottom half of the screen. The green and red attention getter lights are placed at the two ends of the AIP. Systems warning on the AIP The red attention getter light illuminates as steady or flashing. If smoke is detected in a lavatory, the warning appears on all AIP’s and the red attention getter flashes.

chunks.heading: 5.13.11 Area Call Panel - ACP
chunks.text: The area call panels are located in the main cabin areas to attract the attention of the CCMs in the cab- in. All indications illuminate with a low chime. The lights on the ACP could illuminate steady or flashing.

chunks.heading: A 330
chunks.text: AMBER (Steady) Lavatory Call AMBER (Flashing) Lavatory Smoke BLUE (Steady) Passenger call RED (Flashing) Crew call (From Flight deck) RED (Flashing) Emergency crew call (From Flight Deck) RED (Steady) Crew Call

chunks.heading: 5.13.12 Communication System PA/Interphone
chunks.text:
An interphone handset with integral push buttons for passenger address and crew calls are provided at all crew seat locations. The handset is easily accessible to CCMs when secured onto a primary CCM seat The serviceability of the PA and the Inter phone system shall be checked prior to every departure.
1. The PA system provides adequate sound levels to each row of passenger seats through loud speakers
2. In addition, one loud speaker is installed in each lavatory and each galley Usage
1. Remove the handset from the cradle
2. Press PA button
3. Press the “Push to Talk” (PTT) tabs on the handset and speak into the mouth piece

chunks.heading: 5.13.13 PA Priority
chunks.text:
1. Flight deck
2. L1 station
3. Other cabin attendant stations
4. Pre-recorded announcements
5. Audio / video entertainment
6. Boarding music

chunks.heading: 5.13.14 Function Keys on the hand set
chunks.text: PTT - Pressed (Direct PA/Emergency PA) The announcement could be heard in the flight deck, all cabins, galleys and lavatories. Direct PA func- tion must not be used in a normal situation as it overrides normal PAs. The message DIRECT PA IN USE is displayed in all AIPs.

chunks.heading: PA ALL and PTT
chunks.text: The announcement could be heard in all the cabins, galleys and lavatories.

chunks.heading: PA 1 and PTT
chunks.text: The announcement could be heard in the B/C cabin only.

chunks.heading: PA 2 and PTT
chunks.text: The Announcement could be heard in the E/Y cabin only. The message on the AIP will show that the PA is in use, with the green light illuminated.

chunks.heading: 5.13.14.1 Crew To Crew Call
chunks.text:
1. Remove the handset from the cradle
2. Press INT + desired station

chunks.heading: 5.13.14.1 Crew To Crew Call
chunks.text:
3. A Hi-low chime will be transmitted at the station called
4. Calling station - The called station will be displayed E.g.; L4 ATTND
5. Called station- The green attention getter on the AIP will illuminate and the calling station will be displayed- E.g.; CALL L1 ATTND
6. Once answered the green attention getter and the word CALL will disappear
7. The red segment on the ACP will illuminate at the station called.

chunks.heading: 5.13.14.2 Purser Call
chunks.text:
1. Remove the handset from the cradle
2. Press INT + Purser
3. A HI/HI/Lo chime will be transmitted
4. Calling Station– PURSER text shall appear on the AIP
5. All other stations – AIP text ‘Purser Call’
6. All ACP’s shall display a steady red indicator
7. L1 Station - AIP Steady Green & Text Calling Station’
8. To answer at L1 station – Pick hand set and answer Other stations – Press PUR and answer
9. Purser call cannot be made from L1 station.

chunks.heading: 5.13.14.3 All Attendant Call
chunks.text:
1. Remove the handset from the cradle
2. Press inter phone
3. Press All
4. A Hi-low chime will transmitted throughout the cabin
5. Calling station - The called station will be displayed E.g.; ALL ATTND
6. All other stations- The green attention getter on the AIP will illuminate and display- E.g.; CALL

chunks.heading: ALL ATTND
chunks.text: 7. The red light will illuminate on all ACPs

chunks.heading: 5.13.14.4 Normal Call - Cabin to Flight Deck
chunks.text:
1. Remove hand set from cradle
2. Press CAPT key
3. Press rest stow hand set

chunks.heading: 5.13.15 Emergency calls
chunks.text:
Emergency calls can be initiated from F /deck to cabin and cabin to F/deck Flight Deck to Cabin
1. Triple Hi/Lo chimes
2. All ACPs - Flashing Red
3. All AIPs - Steady red - text “CALL PRIO CAPT” / Flashing red on A 330-300 aircraft
4. CCMs shall answer and identify the station
5. Responding handsets would go into a conference call mode
6. Reset from each hand set after answering Cabin to Flight Deck
1. Remove handset from the cradle

chunks.heading: 5.15 Auxiliary Power Unit (APU)
chunks.text: The Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) is a self-contained unit which makes the aircraft independent of external pneumatic and electrical power supply. Located at the rear of the aircraft. The basic element of the APU is a single shaft gas turbine which delivers mechanical shaft power. On ground It supplies bleed air for starting the engines/ for the air conditioning system. It supplies electrical power to the electrical system. During take off It supplies bleed air for the air conditioning, thus avoiding a reduction in engine thrust caused by the use of engine bleed air for this purpose, when optimum aircraft performance is required. In flight It backs up the electrical system and the air conditioning and restarting the engines The APU may obtain power for starting from the batteries specifically assigned to the APU or in combi- nation with the external power, or from normal aircraft supply. The Flight Crew uses the controls on the APU panel for routine shut down and for emergency shut-

chunks.heading: 5.15 Auxiliary Power Unit (APU)

chunks.heading: 5.21.15.2 Business class seat belt with Air Bag System
chunks.text: The Air Bag is stored in the seat belt itself. The airbag would activate on impact provided the cycle is completed by fastening (buckling) seat belt appropriately. It is so designed, if the seat belt is not fastened appropriately, airbag would not deploy. In the event an extension seat belt is used, the air bag system is deactivated automatically. The air bag is activated over 16G impact triggered by a sensor. The metal part of the seat belt has to be engaged correctly in to the buckle to activate the airbag sys- tem. Defects to the seat have to be logged in the Cabin Defects log book. Any changes to the seat shall be carried out only by an approved maintenance team. Fixing a kangaroo belt on to the BC seat – A standard kangaroo belt could be fixed to the BC seat, the loop on the kangaroo belt should be inserted on the belt that does not contain the air bag. WARNING: SEAT BELTS ON UNOCCUPIED SEATS SHALL NOT BE FASTENED.

chunks.heading: 6.1.1 Description
chunks.text:
The A-320 is a short to medium range, single aisle subsonic transport aircraft, powered by two turbofan engines. The fuselage has a circular cross section and is entirely pressurized with the exception of the nose and tail cone, the landing gear bays, the air conditioning compartments and the cargo compart- ments. The flight deck is designed to accommodate two operating crewmembers and two observers. Any combination for Cabin Attendant Seats (CAS) may be provided with a minimum of 4 primary seats. This Chapter 6 describes the - A 320 and 6A Annex describes the A 321 aircraft
• Doors/Exits
• Landing Gear
• Cargo Compartments
• Flight Deck
• Cabin Crewmember Seats and Stations
• Passenger Seating
• Lavatories
• Communication System
• Control Panels
• Entertainment System
• Water and Waste system
• Oxygen System
• Emergency procedures

chunks.heading: 6.2 Doors/Emergency Exits
chunks.text: The aircraft is equipped with four Type “I” doors and four Type “III” emergency exits. The Type “III” Emergency exits are located over the wings and used only during an emergency evacua- tion. During a ditching the Type “III” exits are used as a last resort. All Type “I” doors become emergency exits in case of an emergency evacuation.

The cabin crew must install the Restraint strap whenev- er a cabin door is open with no stairs or aerobridge is in position. Before closing the door, ensure that the restraint strap is fully retracted into its recess WARNING : DO NOT LEAVE AN OPEN CABIN DOOR UNATTENDED A SAFETY STRAP WILL NOT

chunks.heading: 6.5.1.6 Door Locked / Unlocked Indication System

chunks.heading: 6.5.2.1 External
chunks.text:
Opening Only authorized and trained ground personal may carry out the following procedure. Shall try to establish contact with the PIC, knock on the viewing window to draw attention of a CCM and failing they shall follow the below procedure,
1. Check for the Cabin Pressure warning light through the viewing window
2. Insert hand up to the palm on the external opening handle
3. Lift the handle up to the horizontal position in line with the green mark
4. The door should be moved outwards and forward till locked in position In the event, the slide arming lever (located inside the aircraft) is in the armed position and the door is opened from outside, the lever will automatically move to the disarmed position. Closing
1. Ensure the retention strap is removed and stowed
2. Release the door by pressing the gust lock
3. Rotate the door towards the AFT until the door is aligned

chunks.heading: 6.5.2.1 External
chunks.text:
4. Lower the door operating handle down
5. The door is locked when the handle is fully flushed Internal Prior to opening a door, CCMs shall receive conformation from the ground staff-Two knocks on the door and thumbs up indication. Exception would be at airports where the door has to be opened to position steps. The Purser shall obtain permission from the PIC prior to opening the door at such stations. When the seat belt sign is switched off, the Purser shall advice CCMs to disarm the slides by initiating the following PA announcement,

chunks.heading: ‘CREW DISARM SLIDES AND CROSS CHECK’
chunks.text: The doors on the right shall be disarmed first. Door primaries on the left to cross over to the opposite door. Right side door primary shall then disarm the door observed by the left side door primary. Once the Right side doors are disarmed, door prima- ries to cross over to the left. The door primary shall disarm the door observed by the Right-side door primary. Only the detailed door primaries are permitted to disarm the designated slides during routine operations. Opening Doors Prior to opening the doors, Purser shall confirm with PIC that all slides are disarmed, PIC shall make the following PA announcement,

chunks.heading: ‘CABIN CREW YOU MAY OPEN DOORS WHEN REQUIRED’
chunks.text:
1. Grasp frame assist handle
2. Lift the door control handle fully upwards
3. Push the door outwards and forwards until it locks in its fully opened position
4. Secure the exit using retentions strap Assist Handle Control Handle

chunks.heading: 6.5.3 Closing
chunks.text:
1. The Purser shall obtain PIC approval
2. Ensure the retention strap is removed and stowed
3. Release the door by pressing the gust lock
4. Grasp the assist handle
5. Using the assist handle, move the door rearwards
6. When the door is placed on the frame, pull inwards and lower the door control handle Check Door Lock Ensure the door is locked by checking on the door locking indicators, located on the upper part of the door. Display locked and in green.

chunks.heading: 6.5.4 Slide Arming/Disarming Procedure
chunks.text: The movement of the lever to the armed position connects the girt bar to the door sill which the escape slide is attached. When the slide is disarmed the girt bar is released and the escape slide is released from the attachment preventing the slide from deploying. For normal operation of the door, the slide arming lever shall be in the disarmed position. For emergency operation of door, the slide arming lever shall be in the armed position

chunks.heading: 6.5.4.1 When to Arm / Disarm
chunks.text: A CCM shall arm/disarm a slide only on the Pursers command.

chunks.heading: 6.5.4.2 To Arm the Slide
chunks.text: Remove safety pin and stow in the slot on the support arm of the door and move the arming/disarming lever down.

chunks.heading: 6.5.4.3 To Disarm the Slide
chunks.text: Move the arming/disarming lever up to the disarmed position and install the safety pin.

chunks.heading: 6.5.4.4 Cross-Checking
chunks.text:
Prior to disarming the slides on the right, door primaries on the left shall cross over to the right and ensure the following disarming procedure shall be carried out. (PIN/LEVER/PIN verbally stated by the CCM whilst disarming the slide)
1. Remove safety Pin
2. Move door arming lever to disarm position
3. Insert safety pin The slides on the left shall be disarmed next, Once the right side slides are disarmed, both door primaries shall cross over to the left and the left side door primary shall disarm the slide observed by the opposite door primary. The following disarming procedure shall be carried out. (PIN/LEVER/PIN verbally stated by the CCM whilst disarming the slide)
1. Remove safety Pin
2. Move door arming lever to disarm position
3. Insert safety pin

chunks.heading: 6.5.4.5 Calling Relevant Stations
chunks.text: On A320/A321 aircraft, the Purser shall contact each station individually to confirm that slides are cor- rectly ARMED/DISARMED and cross-checked, and shall also verify with the door/slide page on the FAP when available

chunks.heading: 6.5.5 Emergency Door Opening Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Check the outside conditions
2. Check the lever is in the armed position
3. Hold on to the assist handle on the door frame
4. Lift door control handle up and release
5. The door opens automatically and locks in the open position
6. Should the pneumatic assistance of the door fail, push open door manually.
7. If the slide does not inflate pull the manual inflation handle located on the right hand side at floor level
