• Normal security measures implemented.
• Protects an airline when no known threat exits.
2. Category - AMBER
• Action against airlines interest is suspected
• specific target not ascertained
• enhanced measures implemented
• to restrict access to and increase surveillance of potential targets
3. Category - RED
• Action against airlines interest is certain
• Information is credible to justify full alert measures
• Measures may be implemented for specific flights

chunks.heading: 8.3.4 Security Measures
chunks.text: The security measures shall be implemented by crew at all stations unless written dispensation is given by General Manager Group Security.

chunks.heading: AIRCRAFT
chunks.text:
1. During pre-flight/transit, CCMs shall monitors and those au- thorized to enter the aircraft to ensure that they leave nothing behind that could endanger the aircraft. (Improvised explosive/incendiary devices could be con- cealed or disguised in cleaning and servicing equipment).
2. CCMs shall search toilets/galleys/lockers/ storage areas and containers for unidentified or suspect objects explosives/ in- cendiary devices/ firearms/offensive weapons and stowaways prior to departure.
3. Flight Crew shall search the flight deck for unidentified ob- jects/explosives/incendiary devices/ firearms/offensive weapons and stowaways before departure.
4. During transit stops, CCMs shall man the main exit/entry doors to prevent unauthorized entry into the aircraft.
5. Visits to the flight deck by passengers shall be prohibited.
6. During layovers, aircraft shall be guarded to prevent unau- thorized access. Before flight the aircraft shall be searched

chunks.heading: AIRCRAFT
chunks.text: and guarded.

chunks.heading: BOARDING
chunks.text:
1. Only bona fide passengers shall be permitted to board the flight.
2. CCMs shall ensure such passengers are in possession of boarding passes.
3. Discrepancy in passenger count shall be investigated and resolved prior to departure.

chunks.heading: BOARDING
chunks.text:
4. Guards shall be available at aircraft steps or aerobridge to ensure that boarding passes are checked.
5. Authorized staff shall be subjected to search physically or by metal detector prior to being allowed to board the aircraft.
6. During transit or terminating flights, CCMs shall inspect the cabin to ensure disembarking passengers do not leave behind any article. They shall ensure that only the baggage of the crew remains in the cabin prior to boarding of passengers on an originating flight.

chunks.heading: CABIN BAGGAGE
chunks.text:
1. Prior to entry to sterile area/holding room/ aircraft/cabin bag- gage shall be X-rayed/ physically searched. All passengers/ crew/staff shall be body searched either physically or with metal detector.
2. Require all transit passengers to disembark at each intermedi- ate stop with all of their cabin bags. x

chunks.heading: CATERING
chunks.text:
1. CCMs shall check all catering equipment/meal/ dry stores and bonded items uplifted prior acceptance. Any item which cannot be identified as part of the normal cabin or catering complement shall be offloaded and the PIC advised.
2. All catering equipment/meals/dry stores and bonded items shall be security screened. Security stickers shall be affixed sealing inspected catering containers. Escort shall be provid- ed during transport from the flight kitchen to the aircraft.

chunks.heading: CHECK-IN BAGGAGE HANDLING
chunks.text: 1. The baggage of any person who is offloaded for any reason or fails to board following check-in or transit shall not be uplift- ed at airports where local laws require mandatory offloading, unless such baggage is subjected to a security search subse- quent to determining that the passenger is not onboard.

chunks.heading: CHECK-IN BAGGAGE HANDLING
chunks.text:
2. stations where it is not mandatory to offload baggage of failed to board passengers, the commander may exercise his discretion to proceed with such baggage under the following circumstances:- *In the event of the passenger’s death. *Passenger denied transportation by the airline due to space or weight restrictions. *If the passenger elects to offload himself at an alternate airport as a result of diversion. *If the airline re-routes the bag of the passenger(s).
3. Each passenger shall be asked questions confirming the integ- rity of personal baggage.
4. All check-in and interline baggage must be subjected to secu- rity screening namely X-ray, sniffing with approved explosive detector or physical search.
5. After screening, security at screening/check-in areas shall ensure that passengers do not place unscreened articles into bags that have been screened.

chunks.heading: 8.4 Hijack Management
chunks.text: General Any person, while on board any aircraft, unlawfully by force, or by threat of force, or by any form of intimidation, seizes, or exercises control of that aircraft, or attempts to do so, commits hijack of that aircraft. The Commander must be advised of any threat made to interfere with the normal operations of the flight irrespective of the actions to fulfill the threat. In the event of a hijacking, the primary consideration is the safety of passengers and crew.

chunks.heading: 8.4.1 Motivation, Objectives and Type of Hijackers
chunks.text:
Fall into 5 basic categories
1. Criminals
2. Refugees
3. Mentally Disturbed persons
4. Terrorists
5. Others Understanding the motivation and objectives of hijackers is important because it indicates how they may behave.
1. Criminals - hijack for personal gain. Professional and normally well armed.
2. Refugees - Objective is Political asylum. Amateurs; unlikely to be violent but may be des-

chunks.heading: 8.4.1 Motivation, Objectives and Type of Hijackers
chunks.text:
perate and frightened
3. Mentally
4. Disturbed - motivation varies with form of mental derangement alternatively calm/excita- ble/sometimes suicidal/susceptible to reasoning
5. Terrorists - motivation is always Political. Highly professional; fanatical; prepared to kill and die for their cause
6. Others - motivation varied e.g. Protest purpose; publicity for cause or release of jailed terrorists, etc

chunks.heading: 8.4.2 Aircraft Hijack
chunks.text:
SriLankan Airlines contingency plans for dealing with an aircraft hijack considers the following factors:-
1. The safest place for an aircraft under an act of unlawful interference is on the ground
2. The paramount objective is the safe release of passengers and crew, which overrides all other important considerations such as capture and punishment of the perpetrators and the protec- tion of property
3. There is a need to ensure that the perpetrators of acts of unlawful interference will be confront- ed with a well-organized and effective response, so that damage or injury may be prevented or minimized
4. Negotiations shall always prevail before the use of force until it becomes evident to decision makers that all other possibilities have been exhausted and the consultative process has reached a deadlock
5. Negotiation with the offenders shall be conducted by persons trained and skilled in such mat-

chunks.heading: 8.4.2 Aircraft Hijack
chunks.text:
ters, since this is far more likely to result in the successful termination of the occurrence with the least loss of life, injury to persons and damage or loss of property
6. The key weapon for a hijack cannot be determined but the level of disaster may vary depending on the components used but the human factor and demands shall remain as required as an E.G.; it could be a weapon/invention/an aerosol/biological, chemical threat

chunks.heading: 8.4.2.1 Stages of a Hijack
chunks.text:
There are three distinctive stages. Intimidation Stage
1. The intimidation stage signals the beginning of a hijack. This stage may be violent and abusive language is used, and the hijackers are emotional, vindictive and could also be nervous if the hi- jack has not been thoroughly planned. They would try to establish the control as fast as possible by instilling fear and preventing countermeasures from crew and/or passengers. The hijackers may commit random acts of violence, blind-fold or bind certain passengers, abuse certain crew members in full view
2. The hijackers would also limit the comfort of the cabin population by asking for lights to be dimmed and shutters closed, reserving toilets only for their use, moving all passengers to main economy class making sure males are sitting near the windows. They also may try to create con- fusion by moving passengers around periodically, separating children from parents, and switch-

chunks.heading: 8.4.2.1 Stages of a Hijack
chunks.text: ing clothes with the crew.

chunks.heading: 8.4.2.1 Stages of a Hijack
chunks.text: Custodial Stage The custodial stage is the period when passengers and crew are held captive. A prolonged custodial phase can be very hard on crew and passenger moral. Boredom and despair usually set-in. Hijackers would try to turn their hostages to a symbol of their cause and dehumanize them in order to validate their killing, if it comes to that. It is also a period during which the hijackers would be communicating with crew and authorities. Crew members need to take advantage of this moment to make sure the hijackers continue to pursue them and passengers as individuals. The Resolution Stage A hijacking can be resolved either by negotiation or armed intervention. Resolving a hijack by negotia- tion is often a long and arduous process where there can be a few instances of false hope, followed by what seems to be steps that move the situation backward rather than forward. It is important that crew

chunks.heading: 8.4.2.1 Stages of a Hijack
chunks.text: members do not lose hope or begin to distrust the authorities, if there are few setbacks in the negoti- ation process. Crew members need to understand that the hostage negotiators always have the hos- tage-welfare in mind and that a slow negotiation process is often safer than a quick armed intervention.

chunks.heading: 8.4.3 Hijacker on board – recommended action by cabin/flight crew
chunks.text: Details are outlined in SriLankan Airlines recommended procedures for air crew, for handling a hijack situation. Comply with the initial demand of the hijacker to avoid conflict in the aircraft provided, safety of crew and passengers is not jeopardized.

chunks.heading: 8.4.3.1 Communication to the crew (Cabin to Flight Deck)
chunks.text:
1. Alarm buttons may be installed in the passenger-cabin, to alert the Flight Crew discreetly, of potential threats.
2. Passengers shall not be allowed to visit the flight crew compartment. Only the Cabin Manager/ Purser or a nominated Cabin Crew Member shall use the handset to speak to the Pilot-in-Com- mand (PIC).
3. At the Preflight Briefing, a Secret-Code shall be agreed upon between the Cabin Manager (Purs- er) / Nominated Cabin Crew Member and the Flight Crew, for the purpose of alerting the latter, if open communication is not possible, due to a threat-situation that has arisen in the cabin.
4. If and when the above Secret-Code is heard in the air, if the circumstances permit to do so, the PIC shall take steps to check the authenticity of the communique.
5. If the PIC is satisfied that the communique is authentic, he shall take action forthwith for an emergency landing.

chunks.heading: 8.4.4 Action and Responsibilities of the Flight Deck Crew
chunks.text:
1. Upon confirmation that the aircraft is being subjected to a hijack, the Flight Deck crew shall adhere to the following course of actions:-
2. Ensure the FD door is closed and remains locked.
3. Shall activate transponder 7500 or include “Seven Five Zero Zero” in radio telecom- munication transmission to notify ATC if massage is passed in plain language. If situation appears desperate, transponder code 7500 shall be followed by 7700;
4. PIC, having selected code 7500 and subsequently requested to confirm this code by ATC, according to circumstances, either confirm this or not reply at all.

chunks.heading: 8.4.4 Action and Responsibilities of the Flight Deck Crew
chunks.text:
5. The absence of a reply from the PIC will be taken by ATC as an indication that the use of code 7500 is not due to an unintentional, negligent false code selection.
6. Advice ATC for ground arrangements to counter the situation;
7. Plan to land as soon as possible, at a suitable airport of choice;
8. Unless considerations aboard the aircraft dictate otherwise, the PIC shall attempt to continue flying on the assigned track and at the assigned cruising level at least until able to notify an ATS unit or within radar coverage.
9. If PIC is compelled to depart from its assigned track or its assigned cruising level without being able to make radiotelephony contact with ATS, the PIC shall, whenever possible, adhere to laid down ATS procedures.
10. Place the PIC’s speaker “off”. Minimise volume of First Officer’s speaker - wear headsets.
11. The hijacker/s may try to prohibit the use of radio communication. Crew shall insist that the ATC

chunks.heading: 8.4.4 Action and Responsibilities of the Flight Deck Crew
chunks.text:
must know the aircraft position so as to avoid the possibility of a mid-air collision.
12. If the hijacker/s demand/s a change of radio call sign, crew shall alert ATC.
13. Hide the crash axe and any other item that a hijacker may use as a weapon.
14. When the aircraft is on ground persuade the hijacker/s to release the passengers on board in the following order of priority:
a. Sick and injured;
b. Women and children;
c. Old and feeble;
d. Other passengers and the crew.
5. Convince the hijacker/s that the control of passengers would be easier with a lesser number and the aircraft will need extra fuel.
6. The flight crew shall not leave the passengers and cabin crew behind in order to immobilize the aircraft. However there may be situations where the PIC decides that the escape of the flight crew will improve the resolution of conflict and save lives.
7. Information about the situation shall not be revealed to the media or any other unauthorized

chunks.heading: 8.4.4 Action and Responsibilities of the Flight Deck Crew
chunks.text:
persons
8. Submit a report to GMGS & HCS.

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
• Number of hostages - how they are held;
• Number of injured crew and / or passengers;
• Any damage to the structure of the aircraft which may affect operation.
5. If there are any authorized armed personnel on-board as passengers such as Company security, military or bodyguards of VIPs etc, ensure they are restrained from using weapons or force on the hijacker unless such action is authorized by the PIC. Warn them of the possibility of accom- plices of hijackers who may be disguised as passengers.
6. A personal approach is important especially in the case of a single hijacker. If possible, an experi- enced flight attendant (opposite gender) shall deal with the hijacker/s, with the view to establish appropriate rapport with the hijacker/s.
7. Hijack situations are prone to prolonged delays. Ration the food and water to cope-up with worst situations.
8. The hijacker/s demands can be operationally impossible or too dangerous to comply with. In

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
such situations crew will have to talk to the hijacker/s out of their intention, explain the flight safety hazards. In general, persons authorized to make decisions on the demands made by the hijackers, shall not enter into direct negotiations with them, and shall preferably not be immedi- ately available at the Emergency Operation Centre (EOC) or other command post
9. Under any circumstances, the demands of the hijacker/s to gain access to the FD shall not be ac- ceded to. If the hijacker/s so demand, they may be permitted to talk to the FD crew by using the intercom. Always remember that there may be others in the hijack team who do not disclose themselves initially and may remain seated amongst the passengers.
10. Communication at every level is vital and cabin crew shall establish a line of communication with the hijacker as soon as possible. Cabin crew need to communicate with the passengers as well,

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
to build their confidence.
11. Gain time to form a plan of action in mind; do not antagonize or argue with the hijacker/s. Do not “talk down” to them or appear to be superior. Never make any move unless the hijacker/s understand/s the reasons. Do not make them feel cornered and only one crew member shall approach them at a time.
12. Any relationship built-up between the crew and the hijacker/s may be vital in resolving the situ- ation and in bringing the incident to a successful termination. Shall not be mentally aligned with the hijacker/s or be over friendly.
13. Cabin crew shall tactically prevent the possibilities of hijacker/s are getting direct contact / deal with the flight crew.
14. Crew shall not suggest any cause of action to the hijacker/s. If they do and things go wrong they will almost certainly be held to blame.
15. Terminate the serving of alcoholic beverages to passengers. Try to prevent passengers from con-

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
suming their own liquor; unless it is specifically demanded, alcohol shall not be offered to the hijacker/s.
16. Serve the hijacker/s with plenty of non-alcoholic fluids in order to make him/them use the toi- lets. Use this time to pass important messages to the FD.
17. Explain any sudden noises or changes in crew operating procedures. Most hijackers are “trigger happy” and when excited they may resort to violence.
18. When apparent signs of unrest are noticed in the state of mind of a hijacker, the crew member shall deal with him with self-confidence, and make every effort to persuade him to abandon his attempt, without hurting his self-respect.

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
19. The advice to the crew is to respond with passive resistant and delay tactics in complying with the demands of hijacker/s.
20. Keep the service interphone in an audible condition, if possible.
21. If necessary, negotiate with the hijacker/s to obtain agreement for the passengers to move to and from the toilets special attention has to be given to the elderly, sick and passengers with small children.
22. Crew shall identify if possible, any medically qualified persons / physicians are among passen- gers on board, in order to assist in case of a need.
23. Crew shall keep aircraft cabin clean, neat and maintain hygienic conditions, since incident may be prolonged.
24. Passengers shall be advised not to take any individual initiative/s.
25. Avoid unnecessary conversation or action which may irritate the hijacker or induce panic.
26. Do not attempt heroic actions by underestimating strength of the hijacker, by his appearance or

chunks.heading: 8.4.5 Action and Responsibilities by Cabin Crew
chunks.text:
looks that could be deceptive.
27. If the hijacker/s are threatening to harm a passenger or a crew member in order to demand access to the FD, the cabin crew may seek the assistance of passengers to overpower the hijack- er/s. In order to subdue hijacker/s, sufficient force and restrains and other on-board resources may be used.

chunks.heading: 8.4.6 Guidelines For Handling A Hijack Situation
chunks.text:
Following are the guidelines for dealing with a hijack. However the situation in hand may require ad- justment and adaptation:-
1. Comply with demands/provided that it does not jeopardize safety of passengers/ crew
2. Establish a satisfactory working rapport based on mutual trust. Personal contact with the hijack- ers is essential to gain the trust and co- operation especially in the case of a lone hijacker
3. Efforts shall be made to keep the hijacker/s off the flight deck where possible.
4. Establish a rapport by showing an interest in the hijacker’s problems. However, do not become mentally aligned or sympathize with the hijackers or their ideas. (Stockholm syndrome)
5. Do not antagonize or argue especially on political matters
6. Do not “talk down” to the hijacker
7. At any stage do not make him angry
8. As a general rule do not try to overcome the hijackers
9. Do not make them feel threatened. Ensure that only one crewmember approaches the hijacker

chunks.heading: 8.4.6 Guidelines For Handling A Hijack Situation
chunks.text:
at any one time
10. If the hijackers are mentally disturbed, do not make reference to insanity or mental disorders
11. Do not make any sudden physical movements eg; reaching for a switch, unless the hijackers understand the reason
12. Do not make decisions, offer solutions or give opinions to the hijackers. Let them do the thinking
13. Do not serve liquor unless demanded, as alcohol can only complicate the tense situation
14. If possible, the crew shall attempt to obtain release of as many passengers and crew, giving pri- ority to the sick, old and infants
15. If possible, set aside and save eating and drinking utensils used by the Hijackers.
16. Once on the ground crew shall endeavour to detach themselves from the main negotiating pro- cess and leave the hijackers in direct contact with the official negotiating team. If forced to act

chunks.heading: 8.4.6 Guidelines For Handling A Hijack Situation
chunks.text:
as a communication link, avoid answering questions on behalf of the hijackers and avoid giving opinions
17. Be prepared for the incident to be protracted
18. London syndrome refers to hostages’ argumentative and/or disobedient behaviour, which typically leads to their own demise. It is named after an incident in London in 1981 where the Iranian Embassy was seized by armed intruders; one of the hostages, Abbas Lavasani, was quite uncooperative and constantly argued with the gunmen. Lavasani’ s aggressive behaviour made the other captives more fearful as it increased the tension in the room.After six days of nego- tiation, the perpetrators became frustrated and they seemed to have taken it out on Lavasani. They killed him and threw his body out of the embassy.
19. John Wayne Syndrome -The feeling of helplessness often felt by predominantly male hostages in a crisis situation when they wish they could be the hero but are actually impotent to respond

chunks.heading: 8.4.6 Guidelines For Handling A Hijack Situation
chunks.text: and depression results.” For crew members, either male or female, they are likely to feel as if they have failed in some way shall a hijack occur: Many will have had dreams of how they would save the day, yet when faced with the reality of a hijacking, they feel worthless.

chunks.heading: 8.4.7 The Aftermath Of A Hijacking
chunks.text: After the termination of a hijacking incident, Crew must expect to have to face official inquiries and press conferences; guidance shall always be sought from Management prior to speaking to the media. The general guideline is to allow the Public Relations Department to handle the media.

chunks.heading: 8.5.1 Carriage
chunks.text: The relevant procedure approved by the DGCA of Sri Lanka for Carriage of Arms / Ammunitions by pas- sengers as stipulated in SriLankan Airlines Security Manual Chapter 5 Annexure A.

chunks.heading: 8.5.2 Legal provisions and regulations
chunks.text:
The carriage of fire arms/weapons and ammunition on board an aircraft shall be accepted with the pri- or approval of DGCA/CAASL and storage will be made on following locations,
1. As hold baggage
2. As cargo Fire arms, weapons shall not be accepted for carriage in cabin of Srilankan airlines aircraft as of the airlines security policy. On special circumstances with the concurrence of DGCA/CAASL/ appropriate authority of the host state Srilankan airlines shall accept carriage within the cabin and in pre identified locations. The PIC shall be provided with the names and passport numbers of persons authorized to carry arms and their seating positions. The Purser shall ensure that all authorised individuals aboard the aircraft are known to each other.

chunks.heading: 8.6 Vandalism, Sabotage
chunks.text: Vandalism - is wilful or malicious destruction or damage to property. This is a safety related area. Sabotage - In Aviation Security, Sabotage has been defined as an act of omission, intended to cause

chunks.heading: 8.6 Vandalism, Sabotage
chunks.text:
malicious or wanton destruction of property, endangering or resulting in unlawful interference with International Civil Aviation and its facilities. Security Standards, Security Measures To achieve the Company’s Security Standards certain security measures must be adopted and practiced by all crew. These security measures in certain countries are law, and if not carried out properly, SriLan- kan Airlines will be liable to prosecution. Access To Aircraft - Cabin Crew Cabin crewmembers shall,
1. Control and observe anybody boarding the aircraft at all stations
2. Question anybody who is unfamiliar to the crew or not involved in the aircraft operation
3. Question anybody who is not wearing a photographic I.D. card
4. In all cases of difficulty, the PIC must be informed and reference made to local/UL ground staff Pre-Departure Security Check Search everywhere that does not need a key or tool to open i.e. cupboards, overhead lockers, places to

chunks.heading: 8.6 Vandalism, Sabotage
chunks.text: which passengers have access such as toilets. Pay particular attention to seat pockets and spaces be- tween the fuselage linings and outboard seats. Assistance of an engineer may be required.

chunks.heading: 8.7 Chemical Biological Weapons (CBW) Threat Against Aircraft
chunks.text:
1. Recent terrorist activities have demonstrated their capability, willingness and intent to use CBW. it is therefore necessary to be equipped with knowledge and information on such weaponry and that of the threat posed by its presence on-board an aircraft and some means for responding to this in-flight threat.
2. A primary method of introducing Chemical or Biological Agents (CBAs) inside an aircraft, is aero- sol dispersion. The action of leaking, exploding or manually pouring the substance into the cabin interior will move the agent through simple airborne transmission onto the skin or into the eyes, lungs and nasal passages.
3. CBWs because of their nature, must be dealt with in a separate unique manner that is different from handling explosives. Depend on the location of the suspected device, identifying it and choosing an appropriate action to the threat, require calm thinking, clear communication and a

chunks.heading: 8.7 Chemical Biological Weapons (CBW) Threat Against Aircraft
chunks.text:
considered timely response.
4. It is important to define responsibilities between the Flight Crew and Cabin Crew to deal with a CBW on board an aircraft. a The Flight Crew must focus on flying the aircraft managing the cabin temperature, pressuriza- tion and other systems while coordinating with appropriate agencies.
b. Cabin Crew shall prepare to deal with any suspected CBW located within the cabin while exe- cuting appropriate emergency pre-landing activities. c With an understanding of the CBW’s likely dispersal characteristics, it will be the goal of the Cabin Crew to contain the weapons, aerosol potential, before it spreads though the cabin or if this is not possible, to minimise its effects on passengers and crew.

chunks.heading: 8.7.1 Cabin - Threat without Activation
chunks.text:
If a CBW is reported to be on an aircraft without activation due to the lack of physical symptoms of ex- posure, it shall be noted that exposure to CBA will not likely result in an immediate presence of symp- toms nor will the dispersal of a CBA necessarily be immediately detectable.
1. Flight Crew must take immediate steps to deal with the situation and attempt to minimize aero- sol dispersion.
2. They shall put on masks, goggles, select 100% oxygen and maximise skin coverage. Some CBAs are odourless and will not be sensed until affected.
3. An immediate change in cabin pressure shall not be initiated until the inactivated device is se- cured to the maximum extent possible.
4. Immediately reducing cabin temperature to the lowest practical settings and turning off recircu- lation fans will decrease most aerosol dispersal characteristics.
5. Once the suspected chemical biological container is covered and sealed from the cabin atmos-

chunks.heading: 8.7.1 Cabin - Threat without Activation
chunks.text: phere a gradual descend of the aircraft can be initiated using a descent that minimizes the rate of cabin pressure. Slower the descent and increase in the cabin pressure, lower the risk of agent dispersal during the final phase of the flight. Upon landing and taxing to the airport’s minimum risk location, the aircraft shall be parked diagonal to the surface winds and passengers and crew shall deplane through upwind aircraft exits to minimise the risk of contamination. Even if there appears to be no manifestation of possible chemical/ biological contamination, passengers and crew shall remain together and be quarantined / checked by trained personnel

chunks.heading: 8.7.2 Cabin - Threat with Activation
chunks.text:
1. With the exception of slow acting CBAs, airborne exposure to toxic agents may rapidly generate sudden passenger sickness in an epidemic outbreak.
2. If time permits, consultation with knowledgeable specialists on the difference between biologi- cal agents and chemical agents with regard to dispersion and the speed with which they would generate symptoms, shall be accomplished. Generally, many biological agents will generate symptoms less rapidly than with chemical agents, many of which cause immediate symptoms. Depending on the agent, passengers and Cabin Crew may exhibit chocking, discoloration and fainting, blistering or convulsions that are beyond the means of crew members to effectively deal with while airborne. It is important to remember that symptoms may manifest quickly or slowly, and the chemical weapons itself may be deceptively odourless or of a mild scent.
3. If this situation is reported to the Flight Crew, immediate actions must be taken. They must put

chunks.heading: 8.7.2 Cabin - Threat with Activation
chunks.text:
on masks and goggles, secure the cabin door and deny any entry from the cabin. Next, they must decrease cabin pressures (by raising the cabin altitude) as quickly as possible - and as much possible - to evacuate and dilute the aerosol chemical agent. Additionally, recirculation fans shall be turned off and the coldest possible temperature selected to aid in minimizing agent aerosol dispersion. Passengers and Cabin Crew shall go on oxygen. Doing so will protect them from the effects of increasing the cabin altitude to over 10,000 feet and will help prevent them from ingesting the toxic agent into lungs and/or nasal passages.
4. Rapid descent and diversion to a suitable airport is of critical importance. An immediate landing is paramount to ensure Flight Crew are physically able to land the aircraft and receive time-crit-

chunks.heading: 8.7.2 Cabin - Threat with Activation
chunks.text: ical medical treatment for exposed individuals. If chemical agents are suspected, contamination of large populated areas shall not be a concern whilst landing at a major airport, since these agents are short-lived and dissipate rapidly.

chunks.heading: 8.8 Responses to Acts of Unlawful Interference
chunks.text:
Unruly/Disruptive Passengers
1. In most cases, crewmembers will only experience disruptive passengers very sporadically. In fact the more extreme the incident, the less likely in-flight crew will have to face them. However, sound preparedness for an extreme event is very important and will permit staff to intervene properly when effective action and sound judgment will be most crucial
2. Also, all procedures in this section are to be applied only when the aircraft is in flight. In cases where an act of unlawful interference occurs while the aircraft is on the ground, the aircraft shall remain on the ground and, to the greatest extent possible, be brought to an isolated area of the airport and control of the intervention process given to the appropriate authorities

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
1. Threat assessment is based on a general analysis of the likelihood and consequences of danger- ous events occurring within air carriers’ operations. While threat cannot be reduced, appropri- ate measures can reduce the risk. Factors such as political climate, historical occurrences, poten- tial or real threat all influence the threat level of a particular flight. The determination of threat level is done the national intelligence agencies with collection of risk assessment on a regular basis and disseminate information about the threat to civil aviation which affects Sri lanka.
2. All relevant threat information shall be communicated to the DGCA and who will evaluate the information and advice airport operators, aircraft operators and other entities involved in civil aviation on additional security measures required to counter the perceived threat as and when necessary.
3. Srilankan security management shall conduct risk assessment ongoing basis relate to Srilankan

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
airlines operations in Sri Lanka and overseas destinations.
4. An important part of preventing acts of unlawful interference is for the Security Department to make sure crewmembers are aware of the threat level. Crews have to be able to trust the intelligence provided by the Security Department. A strong relationship based on trust and cred- ibility must be achieved. By being aware that the flight they are working on is operating under a higher than normal threat level, crewmembers can make the necessary adjustment to make sure that the increased threat does not result in an increased risk for the flight.
5. Obviously, threat assessment can only inform the crew of pre-flight threat assessment. Once airborne, if an incident occurs, the crew needs to be able to assess what kind of threat it repre- sents. This is necessary to intervene accordingly and to be able to communicate the appropriate

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
information to flight deck and subsequently to the ground in order to provide the necessary sup- port
6. A four-tiered scheme of threat levels has been devised. This classification scheme shall be pro- moted throughout the air carrier in order to facilitate the communication shall an unruly pas- senger incident situation arise on board an aircraft. The levels are as follows:

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
Level 1 — Disruptive behaviour – suspicious or threatening; Level 2 — Physically abusive behaviour; Level 3 — Life-threatening behaviour; Level 4 — Attempted breach or actual breach of the cockpit;
7. If a disruptive passenger begins acting up while the aircraft is still on the ground, unless the situation can quickly be resolved, he/she shall be removed along with his/her baggage. Again, it shall be stressed that pre-flight observation of the cabin is very important to identify suspect behaviour. Cabin crew need to learn to trust their judgment and understand that every situation is unique and there is no constant recipe to deal with a passenger disturbance. They shall note passengers who are extremely nervous or distant and numb, i.e. suspicious. The first step shall be for cabin crew to attempt to find out why the passenger seems nervous. It could simply be that he/she is sick or afraid to fly

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
8. Whatever the approach, suspicious behaviour shall not go unnoticed; it is both a sound security practice and a good customer service approach to show that you care about the comfort of each passenger. Conversely, cabin crews shall also identify those that might be Able Bodied Personnel (ABPs), such as off duty crewmembers and military personnel
9. Communication is key. Clear and simple communication between cabin crew is very important to co- ordinate teamwork. The flight crew needs to be updated regularly on the progress of the situation by cabin crew. The flight crew shall relay this information to the ground immediately. Lines of command shall be kept very simple when there is a disruptive situation. All staff mem- bers, including sky marshals, shall answer to the Captain whenever possible if there is a disrup- tive situation
10. The general idea is to presume the worst outcome of a situation yet act according to the current

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text:
disruption. Crewmembers need to attempt to diffuse the situation up to the very last moment when it is clear that there is no way to resolve the situation verbally. It is usually instructed that the moment you touch the passenger, you have lost. Therefore, physically confronting a passen- ger or applying restraints shall only be used when all diplomatic approaches have been exhaust- ed. Once restraints have been used, they shall remain on the passenger for the duration of the flight even if he/she promises good behaviour
11. Crew need to be aware that a situation can escalate at any moment, sometimes without warn- ing. Cabin crew and flight crew need to quickly assess if the cabin crew can control the distur- bance. If the answer is negative, the flight crew needs to relay this information on the ground and land as quickly as possible. Any verbal or written threat of a weapon means the situation

chunks.heading: 8.8.1 Threat Assessment
chunks.text: has escalated to threat level 3 and appropriate measures shall be taken

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
The crew response shall be appropriate to the threat level. However, if there is an escalation in threat level, crew need to escalate their response accordingly. Here is a list of integrated crew response meas- ures according to the threat level:
• Level 1 Threat— Disruptive behaviour (Suspicious or verbally threatening)
1. Communicate with flight crew and other cabin crew
2. Be attentive to other activity within the cabin, sometimes a Level 1 disruption can be a diversion

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
to cover a hijacking
3. Lock down the cockpit
4. Suspend passenger traffic in the “clear zone”, the galley area immediately behind the cockpit door
5. Alert able-bodied passengers
6. Attempt to diffuse the situation verbally. If one cabin crewmember fails, consider sending anoth- er one who might have more success
7. Notify passenger of their unacceptable behaviour (Final Warning Document).
8. Flight crew shall be aware that an interception by military aircraft is possible;
9. Document all the events and report them to the air carrier and as necessary the authorities
• Level 2 Threat— Physically abusive behaviour
1. Use separation techniques
2. Communicate with flight crew and other cabin crew
3. Lock down the cockpit
4. Be attentive to other activity within the cabin; sometimes a Level 2 disruption can be a diversion to cover a hijacking
5. Suspend service of alcoholic beverages
6. Suspend passenger traffic in the “clear zone”, the galley area immediately behind the cockpit

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
door
7. Captain shall advise air traffic control and air carrier and request that the appropriate law en- forcement agency meet the aircraft
8. Captain shall consider diversion and landing plan
9. Solicit help from cabin crew and passengers. If passengers get involved, it is important to in- struct them on what kind of action is warranted. Since the 11 September attacks, there have been instances where passengers have used excessive, and sometime abusive, force to neutral- ize disruptive passengers
10. Flight crew shall be aware that an interception by military aircraft is possible
• Level 3 Threat— Life threatening behaviour
1. Communicate with flight crew and other cabin crew
2. Suspend passenger traffic in the “clear zone”, the galley area immediately behind the cockpit door, and block with ABPs and service carts
3. Suspend service of alcoholic beverages
4. Solicit all help from cabin crew and passengers. If passengers get involved, it is important to

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
instruct them on what kind of action is warranted. Since the 11 September attacks, there have been instances where passengers have used excessive, and sometimes abusive, force to neutral- ize disruptive passengers
5. Cabin crew to provide information regarding perpetrators to pilot-in-command
6. Use force to subdue assailants
7. Use restraints and other on board resources
8. If necessary, implement Least-Risk Bomb Location (LRBL) or Chemical/Biological Weapons (CBW) procedures

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
9. Captain will declare an emergency and activate landing plan
10. Squawk Transponder code 7500
11. Prepare for rapid descent
12. Monitor Radio on 121.5MHz and prepare for interception by military aircraft
13. After landing, if possible, pull fire switches and disconnect generators
14. If appropriate, escape from the aircraft (mostly relevant to flight crew)
• Level 4 Threat— Attempted or actual breach of the Flight deck
1. Maintain aircraft command and control at all cost
2. Communicate with flight crew and other cabin crew
3. Solicit all help from cabin crew and passengers via the public address system
4. Defend cockpit using whatever force is necessary to eliminate the threat
5. Use commands and all available resources and necessary forces to subdue the assailant and eliminate the threat
6. Use restraints and other on board resources
7. Cockpit will declare an emergency and activate landing plan for nearest suitable airport

chunks.heading: 8.8.2 Crew Response according to Threat Level
chunks.text:
8. Squawk Transponder code 7500
9. Monitor Radio on 121.5MHz and prepare for interception by military aircraft
10. As soon as operationally feasible, initiate possible rapid descent
11. After landing, if possible, pull fire switches and disconnect generators
12. If appropriate, escape from the aircraft (mostly relevant to flight crew)

chunks.heading: 8.9 Policy for unruly passengers
chunks.text:
1. Passengers who behave in an unruly and disruptive manner in-flight, is an ongoing concern to the airline industry. Disruption of the good order of a flight, will have an impact on other pas- sengers, interferes with crew performance and can threaten the safety of a flight
2. The classification of ‘Unruly / Disruptive behaviour’ in-flight covers a range of conduct and includes
• Acts amounts to violation of the criminal laws of a State
• Acts, not amounting to violations of the criminal law, but leads to jeopardize the safety and security of an aircraft, crew, passengers or property therein
• Acts which jeopardize good order and discipline on board
3. These acts shall be viewed under the same light, as if they have occurred in the public street and public places of cities of the world. Behaviour of this type in those public places would either result in a severe caution from a Law Enforcement Officer or the arrest of the

chunks.heading: 8.9 Policy for unruly passengers
chunks.text: offender

chunks.heading: 8.10 Reporting procedures
chunks.text: All staff of SriLankan Airlines must ensure, that incidents are reported and documented in an effective manner, not only to gain an understanding of the incidents themselves but also to ensure that, suf- ficient and appropriate information is available for legal and judicial purposes in case prosecution of the case is required. Whenever possible, civil and / or penal prosecutions must be pursued along with adequate media coverage of the convictions.

chunks.heading: 8.10 Reporting procedures
chunks.text: Cabin Crewmembers must inform every incident to Pilot in Command through the Purser in Charge. If the passenger continues with unruly or disruptive behaviour, Pilot-in command of the flight, may or- der use of in-flight restraining equipment. The Pilot-in-command may hand over such passengers to the appropriate authority of a contracting state on arrival at destinations.
