chunks.heading: 9.0 FIRST AID
chunks.text: First aid is the provision of initial care for an illness or injury. It is usually performed by a non-expert but by trained personnel until definitive medical treatment can be accessed. All Inflight medical situations shall be reported to the CMO through the VR/Incident, accident form and Illness form or MOR.

chunks.heading: 9.1 The Role of Cabin Crew as a First Aider
chunks.text:
The principle of First Aid is to preserve life/prevent the condition from worsening and promote recov- ery. Passengers look to CCMs for help and assistance and CCMs should make every effort to provide lifesav- ing assistance at all times and are trained to administer First Aid and handle/respond to any situation in a calm/professional manner to the best of their ability when performing duties on board. CCM also shall:
1. Assess the situation without endangering one’s own life
2. Be able to identify a medical need and provide immediate/appropriate treatment
3. Arrange for the casualty to get medical help without delay
4. Maintain extreme hygienic conditions before and after administering First Aid by the usage of latex gloves/ face masks
5. Improvise and be innovative, depending on the situation and condition
6. Never panic when dealing with a situation
7. Be aware (through reference) the contents in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10)

chunks.heading: 9.1 The Role of Cabin Crew as a First Aider
chunks.text:
8. Be aware of all the contents and its use in the First Aid Kit
9. Do not administer drugs or use any item from the Emergency Medical Kit (A10)
10. Be cautious when assisting in handling syringes and needless
11. Stow used needles and syringes safely in the sharps bin located in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10) and hand over to ground staff
12. CCM shall follow procedure as per Ref. 9.14 for usage of First Aid Kits
13. Prohibited from injecting a passenger for any reason (even when requested by a passenger)
14. Keep the PIC briefed of any medical emergency
15. Remain with the patient until handed over to medical personnel
16. Be seated during critical phases of flight even if a medical emergency is in progress
17. Be cautious (to avoid injury) when the seat belt sign is switched on during cruise, when adminis- tering First Aid
18. Complete all relevant documentation

chunks.heading: 9.1.1 Notifying the PIC
chunks.text:
The PIC shall be notified immediately in case of any type of life threatening Medical Emergency to pas- sengers or Crew during flight, but not limited to,
1. Injuries or Serious illness
2. Administering Oxygen
3. Administering CPR/Use of the AED
4. Requirement to use the Emergency Medical Kit (A10)
5. Childbirth
6. Unconsciousness
7. Apparent death

chunks.heading: 9.1.1 Notifying the PIC
chunks.text:
8. Carriage of medical alert passengers
9. Public health emergency of international concerns e.g. Covid, SARS

chunks.heading: 9.1.1.1 Vital information to the PIC
chunks.text: The information communicated to the PIC shall be but not limited to; Type of Emergency Condition of the patient Medical Assistance provided Medication provided

chunks.heading: 9.1.2 Medical Assistance
chunks.text: If required, CCMs should page for medical assistance using the PA. “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, MAY WE HAVE YOUR ATTENTION PLEASE, IF THERE IS A MEDICAL PRACTITIONER, A QUALIFIED NURSE OR PARAMEDIC ON BOARD, PLEASE IDENTIFY YOURSELF TO A MEMBER OF THE CABIN CREW. THANK YOU”. Purser shall ensure the credentials of the medical practitioner are verified. In the event medical assistance is requested on landing for a critically ill (life threatening) passenger. The Purser shall carry out an announcement requesting all passengers to remain seated until the medi- cal assistance reaches the patient. “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, MAY WE HAVE YOUR ATTENTION PLEASE, WE REQUEST ALL PASSENGERS TO REMAIN SEATED UNTIL

chunks.heading: THE MEDICAL TEAM REACHES A CRITICALLY ILL PASSENGER ON BOARD
chunks.text: THANK YOU FOR YOUR PATIENCE AND UNDERSTANDING”.

chunks.heading: 9.1.3.1 Signs and symptoms
chunks.text:
CCMs should determine the nature of the illness/injury by paying special attention to:
1. Dangers/Hazards
2. Level of Response
3. Airway
4. Breathing
5. Circulation
6. Bleeding
7. Fractures
8. Levels of consciousness (please refer levels of consciousness table on page 36) If the passenger is unconscious, look for Medic-Alert Emblem or any other identification in the form of necklace or bracelet and check the back of the emblem to identify his/her condition (E.g. – epileptic/ diabetic/allergies).

chunks.heading: 9.1.3.1 Signs and symptoms
chunks.text:
In All Cases
1. Reassure the passenger
2. Inform the PIC/Purser
3. Allow the passenger to assume the most comfortable posture If required
1. Loosen tight clothing
2. Open air vents in the area
3. Cover the passenger with a blanket
4. Administer Oxygen
5. Obtain medical history from passenger
6. Request presence of medical aid on arrival at destination Documentation In the event of an in-flight medical emergency the following documents should be completed as re- quired: Refer 2.36

chunks.heading: 9.1.4 Care/Management In-Flight
chunks.text:
Falling ill during flight can often be a very frightening experience. When offering care, trust and building confidence is vital. Although the CCM’s responsibilities as First-Aiders are clearly outlined, the caring manner shown during assessing the casualty is important. The following principles shall be applied to all situations:
1. Talk to the person/ask relevant questions that produces a yes or no answer
2. Act calmly and reassure the person constantly, even after treatment
3. Give a clear explanation of what you intend to do. E.g. inform the reason you are loosening his clothing/what to expect when receiving oxygen
4. Do not leave the passenger until he has fully recovered, even if a medical professional has of- fered to assist. The responsibility of a medical professional is only to offer help with areas that CCMs have not been trained on E.g. injecting.
5. Never leave a passenger who is unconscious or in a life threatening situation. Hold the passen-

chunks.heading: 9.1.4 Care/Management In-Flight
chunks.text:
ger’s hand, physical touch can be very reassuring
6. Use reassuring words like “don’t worry”, “you will be fine”, “everything is going to be fine” etc.
7. Avoid words that could cause emotional distress, E.g. ‘Don’t worry; you are not going to die’
8. If the victim is accompanied, allow them to stay with him unless it interferes with the treatment Be cautious of a semi-conscious person hearing you. Avoid discussing the victim’s condition in his presence or in the vicinity of other passengers.

chunks.heading: 9.1.5 Limitations
chunks.text:
CCMs are trained in first aid but they are not considered as medically qualified/nurses or paramedics and are not expected to have detailed knowledge or experience of all medical procedures. CCMs are not expected to:
1. Give complicated medical assistance/Inject any person
2. Undertake any procedures they have not received official training in, or any procedures outside the training manual

chunks.heading: 9.1.6 Precautions
chunks.text: CCMs should take extreme care when administering First Aid or assisting a medical practitioner. Any equipment suspected of contamination should not be touched with bare hands. A marked air sickness bags should be used for proper disposal.

chunks.heading: 9.1.7 Legal Requirement
chunks.text: CCMs are considered competent First Aiders only. A CCM shall act in accordance with what he has been trained to do and will not be found fault with for trying to help a person in need of assistance. A trained First Aider shall not stand back and not use his skills and training to save a life.

chunks.heading: 9.2.1 Resuscitation Procedures
chunks.text: Oxygen is essential to life. The brain, which controls all bodily functions, must have a supply of oxygen. If the brain is deprived of oxygen for more than three minutes it will suffer brain damage. It is therefore vital to establish that the airway is clear; breathing is present and circulation is functioning in an uncon- scious patient. Check the patient’s eyes, dilated pupils could be an indication of lack of oxygen and the blood supply to the brain.

chunks.heading: 9.2.2 Pulse Rate/Breathing Rate
chunks.text: Normal Pulse Rate (Per minute) Normal Breathing Rate (Per minute) Adults - 60 - 80 beats 10 breaths Child - 80 -100 beats 15 breaths Infant - 100 -120 beats 20 breaths

chunks.heading: 9.2.3 Assessment of a Collapsed Passenger (Adults)
chunks.text:
If a passenger has collapsed, immediately check on (DRSABC) D Danger or Hazards For you or the patient, look up/down and around the area R Response Check response by giving verbal commands or if unrespon- sive check the pain response. If the patient is responsive, keep him in recovery position and ask
1. S - signs and symptoms
2. A - Allergies
3. M - Medication taking
4. P - Past medical history
5. L - Last meals taken/
6. E - Extra anything S Shout for help Shout for help, to get help from others A Airway Check/clear the airway for foreign objects. Open the airway using either, head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust method to keep airway open B Breathing Look/listen for signs of breathing for 10 seconds C Circulation Check the carotid pulse (in the neck) for 10 seconds Note: If foreign object present use PPE and remove obstruction using finger if possible, remove den- tures if applicable.
1. If breathing and pulse is present, place in recovery position and treat as an unconscious person

chunks.heading: 9.2.3 Assessment of a Collapsed Passenger (Adults)
chunks.text: 2. If there is no breathing start CPR immediately check vital signs every 5 minutes.

chunks.heading: 9.2.4 Assessment of a collapsed passenger chart
chunks.text:
Note: If there is catastrophic bleeding priority shall be to take necessary first aid precautions to arrest the bleeding. Ref 9.7.35.1
• Check For Danger
• Check For Response
• Shout For Help
• Check Airway(Head Tilt/Chin Lit) (Suspected neck injury jaw thrust)
• Check For Breathing(Look/Listen/Feel)
• Pulse (Carotid)/ Circulation
• Get AED And Emergency Equipment (eg. AMBU Bag/A10/RVAK etc). Start CPR (30 Compression and 2 Breaths)
• Give 01 Shock Resume CPR Immediatly For

chunks.heading: 2 Mins Until Prompted By AED To Allow
chunks.text:
Rhythm Check
• Continue Until Suppport Arrive AED will Check the RHYTHM
• Resume CPR Immediatly For 2 Mins Until Prompted By AED To Allow Rhythm Check
• Continue Until Support Arrive
• Recovery Position
• Monitor No Breathing Or Only Gasping Connect the AED. Stop CPR until AED is connected and follow the instructions given by AED YES - Shockable No - Non Shockable Normal Breathing Pulse Felt

chunks.heading: 9.2.5 Adult – CPR
chunks.text: Chest Compressions Lay passenger on hard/flat surface/kneel beside the passenger. Locate mid of the breastbone or on the breast bone in between nipple line Place the heel of your other hand beside (lower) the fingers/place other hand on top, interlock hands. Keeping shoulders directly over hands /depress chest downward approx. 1.½ - 2 Inches (Keep elbows locked and straight down) Release the pressure on the chest – do not remove hands off the chest. Continue to give compressions at the rate of 100 compressions per minute

chunks.heading: 9.2.5.1 Administering Rescue Breaths to an Adults
chunks.text: If no breathing start CPR immediately. The steps as per the below table Lay the passenger on a hard flat surface. Use chin lift/head tilt method to open the airway.

chunks.heading: Use AMBU Bag or RVAK
chunks.text: Observe for any rise of the chest. Remove AMBU Bag/RVAK and allow the chest to fall. Deliver another breath using the same method (Ambu bag/RVAK) Continue ventilation at the rate of 10 to 12 breaths per minute. Check for pulse every 10 seconds up to a minute. If a neck/spinal injury is suspected, use ‘Jaw thrust’ method to open airway (pull the lower jaw for- ward without moving the head/neck) Continue 30 compressions alternating with 2 breaths of CPR until help arrives. It is not necessary to stop and check the pulse, this shall only be done if the person takes a sudden gasp, a cough or moves suddenly.

chunks.heading: 9.2.6 Administer CPR to Children below 7 yrs/Infants
chunks.text:
Administer CPR to Children below 7 yrs. (depending on body structure)/Infants. Failure to breathe is the main cause of cardiac arrest in children and infants. If breathing can be re-es- tablished the heart will start spontaneously. CPR & chest compressions can be performed on older chil- dren (8 yrs. And above) as same for an adult. For Children below 7 yrs and infants the technique varies.
1. Immediately check on DRSABC
2. If breathing is not present, give 2 rescue breaths up-to 5 until 2 good chest expansion are seen and check circulation
3. Check carotid pulse if child is above 1 year
4. Check brachial pulse (in the arm) if child is below 1 year

chunks.heading: 9.2.6.1 Administer CPR to Children/Infants
chunks.text:
Failure to breathe is the main cause of cardiac arrest in children and infants. If breathing can be re-es- tablished the heart will start spontaneously. CPR & chest compressions can be performed on older chil- dren (8 yrs. and above) as same for an adult. For Children below 7 yrs and infants the technique varies. Immediately check on DRSABC
1. If breathing is not present, give 5 rescue breaths until chest expansion are seen and check circu- lation
2. Check carotid pulse if child is above 1 year
3. Check brachial pulse (in the arm) if child is below 1 year Chest Compressions Chest Compressions for a child is performed with two or one hand depending on the built of the child Depress ⅓ to ½ the depth of the chest Continue to give chest compressions at a speed of 100 compressions per minute. Continue 30 compressions alternating with 2 breath of CPR until help arrives. It is not necessary to stop and check the pulse; this shall only be done if there is a sudden movement,

chunks.heading: 9.2.6.1 Administer CPR to Children/Infants
chunks.text: cough, or gasp.

chunks.heading: 9.2.6.2 Infant (0-1 years) – CPR
chunks.text: Chest Compressions 01 Rescuer - Locate and place two fingers just below the nipple line.

chunks.heading: 02 Rescuer - 2 Thumbs - Encircling Hand Technique
chunks.text: Depress ⅓ to ½ the depth of the chest Continue to give chest compressions at a speed of 100 compressions per minute. Continue 30 compressions alternating with 2 breath of CPR until help arrives. It is not necessary to stop and check the pulse, it should only be done if the infant takes a sudden gasp/coughs or moves suddenly.

chunks.heading: 02 Rescuer - 2 Thumbs - Encircling Hand Technique
chunks.text: No breathing start CPR Below 1 year Administer mouth-to-mouth using RVAK or nose resuscitation at 12-20 breaths per minute. Above 1 year Administer mouth-to-mouth using RVAK resuscitation at 12-20 breaths per minute. Check pulse every minute and if pulse is absent start chest compressions combined with resuscitation. Use Jaw thrust to open the airway in suspected neck injuries.

chunks.heading: 9.2.7 Adult, Child and infant CPR
chunks.text: Adult Child (1 Year to Puberty) Infant 1-Rescuer Compression: Ventilation Ratio 30:2 30:2 30:2 2-Rescuer Compression: Ventilation Ratio 30:2 5 rescue breaths fol- lowed by 30:2 30:2 Compression Rate 100 100 100 Compression Depth 1 ½ - 2 Inches 1/3 to ½ the depth of the chest 1/3 to ½ the depth of the chest Hand Placement Two Hands mid of the breastbone or on the breast bone in between nipple line Two or One Hand mid of the breastbone or on the breast bone in between nipple line 1-Rescuer

chunks.heading: 2 Finger Technique
chunks.text: 1-Rescuer

chunks.heading: 2 Thumbs-Encircling
chunks.text: Hands Technique Just below the nipple line Pulse Check Carotid Carotid Brachial

chunks.heading: 9.2.8 Measuring the Pulse
chunks.text:
1. Carotid
2. Radial
3. Brachial

chunks.heading: 9.2.9 Tracheotomy (Neck Breather)
chunks.text: Is an airway from the throat directly into the windpipe through a hole in the neck (stoma) that could create a total or partial neck breather. Total Neck Breather Breathe only through a neck opening. Seal your mouth around the tube of the Tracheotomy and blow slowly. Partial Neck Breather They breath through an opening in the neck, nose and mouth. Seal the victim’s nose and mouth/ place your mouth around the tube in the Tracheotomy and blow slowly. Artificial Ventilation through a Tracheotomy If the patient stops breathing through the neck breather, artificial ventilation should be given through the Tracheotomy.

chunks.heading: 9.2.9.1 Administering Oxygen through A Tracheotomy
chunks.text: Place the mask over the Tracheotomy and monitor the pressure gauge regularly. Procedure on administering Oxygen (Ref 9.3)

chunks.heading: 9.2.10 CPR without Medical Help
chunks.text:
If medical help is not available, the PIC may decide to divert the aircraft, hence it is vital the PIC is in- formed of any medical emergency. CPR should be carried out until the patient revives. In the event the patient fails to revive CPR may be discontinued after discussion with the PIC and accompanying passengers (if any). If the PIC decide to divert the Aircraft, CPR shall be continued regardless of the time factor and until medical assistance is available. Pronouncing death could be difficult (CCMs are prohibited from pronouncing death). However the fol- lowing signs may be apparent:
1. Check neck/arms/wrists and groins for absence of pulse
2. Look, Listen and feel over the chest for absence of heartbeat and breath
3. Feel chest for respiration or absence of breathing. If there is no movement of chest, place your ear close to the mouth and listen and feel for breath. If in doubt, use a shiny metal surface and

chunks.heading: 9.2.10 CPR without Medical Help
chunks.text:
place it close to the lips (any breath moisture will condense on the surface of the piece of metal)
4. Body colour remains pale and gradually becomes more blue and mottled
5. Pupils remain dilated and fixed with no change and the eyes lose its shine becoming dull and glazed
6. If movement or response is completely absent, place a plastic sheet under the person to con- tain any leakage of bodily fluids. Accompanying passengers (if any) may be allowed to be in the vicinity unless it compromises any safety regulation. Only a medical practitioner could certify death If death is certified by a medical practitioner, CCMs shall not move the body (for autopsy reasons) and it should remain on board until all other passengers have de-planed and formalities (pertaining to that country) are completed.

chunks.heading: 9.3.1 Administering Oxygen to an Adult
chunks.text:
When MEDA bottles of oxygen are requested, the CMO shall inform the Engineering department to stow it on the aircraft. Procedure and Precautions
1. Page for medical practitioner/qualified nurse or a paramedic.
2. Inform the PIC.
3. Ensure no smoking regulation is adhered to
4. Ensure bottle and mask is free of grease and oil
5. Secure the bottle, with the gauge visible
6. Have an extra bottle of oxygen as stand by
7. Two CCMs shall be involved in fixing the oxygen mask to the passenger Operation

chunks.heading: 9.3.1 Administering Oxygen to an Adult
chunks.text:
1. Remove the face mask from plastic bag
2. Ensure the tubing is fixed to the high outlet
3. Wipe/ clean the face of the recipient with a wet towel
4. Open valve by turning ON/OFF knob anti- clockwise
5. Check for the flow of oxygen by pinching mask end of the re-breather bag
6. Place mask over the nose and mouth, adjust elastic band to hold mask in place
7. Place bottle with the gauge visible
8. Purser shall nominate a CCM to monitor the passenger and the flow of oxygen/elapsed time
9. Monitor the bag inflating and deflating as the person breaths
10. Position another bottle of oxygen to be used when required
11. When the gauge reaches 500/250 PSI remove mask. (Continue administering oxygen from an- other bottle if required) After Use
1. Remove the face mask from the passenger
2. Close the valve by turning ON/OFF knob clockwise
3. Disconnect the tube from the bottle
4. Restore bottle of oxygen

chunks.heading: 9.3.1 Administering Oxygen to an Adult
chunks.text:
5. Inform Purser of the location and the final reading
6. Enter in cabin defects log book

chunks.heading: 9.3.2 Administering Oxygen to an Infant/Child
chunks.text:
1. The child face mask should be placed and held gently to the face of the infant/child or kept in place by using the elastic band
2. It is safe to administer oxygen at 4 LPM to an infant under 2 years of age and for children over 2 years

chunks.heading: 9.3.3 MEDA Oxygen
chunks.text:
When a MEDA passenger is airlifted the following regulations shall be adhered to,
1. Ex base - MEDA oxygen could be used to a minimum of 250 PSI
2. Ex Base - If the requirement for Oxygen exceeds the MEDA bottles, additional bottles shall be supplied by the Engineering Department for ex-base and en-route dispatch.
3. Ex En-Route - If an aircraft is dispatched with the minimum requirement of bottles, they could be used to 500 PSI
4. Administering oxygen over the above regulation is at the discretion of the PIC
5. During post decompression, Oxygen from all bottles may be used until the gauge reads zero
6. The Purser shall nominate a CCM to regularly monitor the MEDA passenger throughout the flight. The nominated CCMs shall position an additional bottle of oxygen and change the bottles prior to the elapse time.

chunks.heading: 9.3.3 MEDA Oxygen
chunks.text: Additional bottles of Oxygen shall be secured in the following locations A320 – over head stowage compartment above row 27 D/E/F A321 – over head stowage compartment above row 32 DEF A330-200 - over head stowage compartment above row 31 D/E/F/G A330-300 - over head stowage compartment above row 37 D/E/F/G Announcement Prior To Administering Oxygen “LADIES AND GENTLEMAN, MAY WE HAVE YOUR ATTENTION PLEASE, IF THERE IS A MEDICAL PRACTI- TIONER, QUALIFIED NURSE OR PARAMEDIC ON BOARD; PLEASE IDENTIFY YOUR SELF TO A MEMBER

chunks.heading: 9.4 Resuscitator Vent Aid Kit (RVAK)
chunks.text: Atach One-way Valve to mask port.

chunks.heading: 9.4 Resuscitator Vent Aid Kit (RVAK)
chunks.text:
Precaution
1. Page for a medical practitioner prior to use to initiating CPR using RVAK
2. Don protective gloves
3. Blow through valve to verify operation
4. If the patient vomits, remove mask and clear airway. Clear the mask by sweeping out foreign material
5. Re-apply mask to the patient and continue ventilation Operation Adults/Children
1. Push out dome and attach one-way valve to the mask
2. Direct exhalation port from the nose end of the mask
3. Apply the rim of the mask between the patient’s lower lip and chin keeping the mouth open under the mask
4. Use the thumb to seal and hold the mask in place
5. Open airway and blow gently until the chest rises
6. Remove your mouth and allow the patient to exhale
7. An oxygen tube can be connected to the inlet of the mask
8. If patient vomits remove the mask and clear the airway Infants Follow same procedure as above except,
1. Reverse the mask to ensure the nose part is towards the chin

chunks.heading: 9.4 Resuscitator Vent Aid Kit (RVAK)
chunks.text: 2. An oxygen tube can be connected to the inlet of the mask

chunks.heading: 9.5 AMBU Resuscitator
chunks.text:
Air-Shields Manual Breathing Unit/Resuscitator (Ambu Bag) Precaution (Prior to initiating CPR using AMBU bag)
1. Page for a medical practitioner prior to use
2. Don protective gloves
3. Ensure the face mask is connected to the bag and the bag is connected to the oxygen tube
4. If patient vomits, remove mask and clear patient’s airway. Clear the mask by sweeping out any foreign material
5. Re-apply mask to the patient and continue ventilation Assembling AMBU bag and usage Operation Adults/Children
1. Be guided by Resuscitation Procedures Ref 9.2
2. Connect the tube from the AMBU bag to the high outlet of the oxygen Cylinder
3. Place the mask over the nose and mouth of the patient Ref 9.2.5.1
4. Squeeze the bag to ensuring it produces an elevation in the patient’s chest as it would when breathing normally
5. Squeeze the AMBU bag once, Ref 9.2.3
• Every 2-3 seconds if the patient is a child

chunks.heading: 9.5 AMBU Resuscitator
chunks.text: • Every 5-6 seconds if patient is an adult

chunks.heading: 9.5 AMBU Resuscitator
chunks.text: 6. Continue squeezing the bag until patient starts to breathe normally, or until the medical practi- tioner arrives Infants For Infants follow same procedure as above except, Reverse the mask to ensure the nose part is towards the chin.

chunks.heading: 9.6 Contagious Diseases
chunks.text: During boarding, if you see an indication that a passenger may have a contagious disease, (e.g. measles, chicken pox, etc.) tactfully discuss the observation with the passenger and inform the Purser/PIC who will communicate with the ground/ airport officers prior to taking action. The PIC shall be kept informed and the decision to carry such passengers is at his discretion.

chunks.heading: 9.7 In-Flight First Aid Handling
chunks.text: General CCMs are required to inform the Purser who shall inform the PIC. Purser shall be responsible for handling any of the following but not limited to situations/illnesses on board the aircraft.

chunks.heading: 9.7.1 Cold
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Runny nose
2. Chills
3. Headache/fever Treatment
1. Keep passenger warm
2. Offer 2 Panadol tablets to adults/Calpol syrup to children (Check for allergy)
3. Offer plenty of fluids to drink
4. Use nasal spray

chunks.heading: 9.7.2 Headache
chunks.text:
Treatment
• Offer 2 Paracetamol tablets (Check for allergy), Offer children Paracetamol Syrup accord- ing to body weight (check for allergy prior to administering).
• Encourage intake of fluids

chunks.heading: 9.7.3 Air Sickness
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Sickness caused by motion
2. Dizziness
3. Discomfort Treatment
1. Recline seat

chunks.heading: 9.7.3 Air Sickness
chunks.text:
2. Loosen clothing at the neck and waist
3. Open air vent for fresh air
4. Advise passenger to breathe deeply and slowly and to look at a fixed object Position an airsick- ness bag
5. Administer Promethazine Theoclate 25mg (Avomine) ) if the history is compatible with motion sickness and CCM to inform passenger that it takes approximately 01 hour to get the effect after administration.

chunks.heading: 9.7.4 Toothache
chunks.text:
Treatment
• Offer 2 Paracetamol tablets (check for allergy)

chunks.heading: 9.7.5 Hiccups
chunks.text:
Treatment
• Ask passenger to hold breath and drink a glass of water slowly

chunks.heading: 9.7.6 Diarrhoea
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Abdominal pain
2. Runny bowels Treatment
1. Offer constipating food e.g. rice/toast bread/black coffee
2. Offer fluids (oral re-hydration solution)

chunks.heading: 9.7.7 Alcoholic Intoxication
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Odour of alcohol/face flushed
2. Breathing slow and deep
3. Possible vomiting
4. Slurred speech
5. Bloodshot eyes
6. Partial or complete unconsciousness Treatment Deny any more alcoholic beverages.
1. Offer non-alcoholic drinks i.e. water, soft drinks etc.
2. If the passenger becomes unconscious, maintain an open airway and place the patient in the recovery position – check Airway/Breathing/Circulation (ABC)

chunks.heading: 9.7.8 Using the Digital Thermometer
chunks.text:
1. Wipe the thermometer probe using alcohol or disinfectant swab before using.
2. Press the on/off button next to LCD display.
3. A tone will sound with the screen showing 1888 followed by the last recorded temperature/Lo/ Hi.

chunks.heading: 9.7.8 Using the Digital Thermometer
chunks.text:
4. Position thermometer as desired (Mouth or armpit)
• Mouth -Place the thermometer under the tongue close the mouth.
• Armpit - Wipe armpit dry. Place the probe in armpit and keep arm pressed firmly at side.
5. The degree sign flashes throughout the testing process.
6. When flashing stops an alarm will beep for approximately 10seconds. The measured reading will appear on the LCD screen.
• Turn off the unit after obtaining the reading.
• Wipe the probe with alcohol or disinfectant swab and close the probe with the cover.

chunks.heading: 9.7.9 Using the Infra Red Thermometer
chunks.text:
1. Switch on the thermometer
2. Adjust temperature setting between Celsius and Fahrenheit
3. Direct the device of the wrist or forehead
4. Press trigger and measure
5. Make sure that the device does not touch the skin

chunks.heading: 9.7.10.1 Injury -Non-Embedded - for foreign body in the eye
chunks.text:
Treatment
1. Do not rub the eye
2. Do not attempt to remove with a sharp instrument
3. If it is a simple chemical in the eye, wash with water
4. If foreign body is visible, attempt to wash with water
5. If unsuccessful, cover eye with a sterile eye pad

chunks.heading: 9.7.10.2 Eye Injury -Embedded
chunks.text: CCMs shall refrain from removing an embedded sharp foreign body which has pierced the eye. Cover both eyes with sterile eye pads. Use ring bandages if object is protruding.

chunks.heading: 9.7.11 Eye Infection
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Pain in the eye.
2. Foreign body sensation (irritation) and tearing.
3. Discharge from the eye.
4. Redness of the eye or eyelids. Treatment Use the available eye drops and cover with an eye pad.

chunks.heading: 9.7.12 Eye Irritation
chunks.text: Treatment Use eye-drops for simple irritants e.g. cigarette smoke, moist cotton balls may be used to wipe.

chunks.heading: 9.7.13 Ear Distress
chunks.text:
An unequal pressure between outer and middle ear causes severe pain, particularly on descent than ascent. This occurs due to a blockage in the Eustachian tubes, Eustachian tube gets block from cold, allergies or infection. Pain might be more severe during descent than ascent. Treatment
1. Advice to yawn
2. Advice to swallow
3. “Popping”- hold nose, closes lips and force air gently out only during decent.
4. Move the jaw out and from side to side
5. Feeding will help to relieve ear distress of an infant

chunks.heading: 9.7.14 Food Poisoning
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Nausea
2. Vomiting
3. Diarrhoea
4. Abdominal pain Treatment Offer plenty of fluids and position extra airsickness bags with the passenger

chunks.heading: 9.7.15 Hysterical Attacks
chunks.text: Seldom occurs unless in the company of others. Symptoms Laughing/crying/eye lids tremor. Treatment Monitor situation, do not give attention more than necessary.

chunks.heading: 9.7.16 Indigestion
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Pain in the abdomen
2. Discomfort in the stomach and the chest Treatment
1. Offer anti acid tablets and monitor

chunks.heading: 9.7.17 Drug Overdose
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. May vary depending on the type or nature of the drugs taken
2. Agitation/depression and in extreme cases coma
3. Any person unconscious from poisoning by drugs is seriously ill

chunks.heading: 9.7.17 Drug Overdose
chunks.text:
Treatment
1. If agitated, reassure and apply gentle restraint/keep under close observation
2. If in a coma, treat as an unconscious passenger (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.18 Abdominal Pain
chunks.text:
Abdominal pain due to infection Symptoms
1. loose motion
2. Vomiting
3. Nausea
4. High temperature Treatment
1. Hydrate with ORS
2. Anti ematics (domperidone)
3. Sugar free fruit juice Abdominal pain due to other pathological conditions (e.g. Acute appendicitis, bowel obstruction, renal stone etc… Symptoms
1. Blood in Urine
2. Rapid pulse
3. Restless and agitated
4. Stiff abdomen Treatment
1. Warm compress to act as a comfort to passenger
2. Consider pain relief (Diclafenac Suppository)
3. Do not offer anything to eat or drink
4. Let passengers assume most comfortable position
5. Colicky abdominal pain

chunks.heading: 9.7.19 Asthma
chunks.text:
Muscles of small air passages go into spasm. Symptoms
1. Tight wheezy chest
2. Very anxious
3. Difficulty in speaking/breathing (especially breathing out)
4. Blueness of the lips and nose Treatment
1. Advice passenger to take his own prescribed medication
2. Offer the inhaler if own medication is not available
3. Reassure and calm passenger
4. Advise passenger to lean forward/sit upright to assist breathing
5. Open-air vent
6. Give oxygen if required. Ref 9.3

chunks.heading: 9.7.20 Diabetes
chunks.text: Diabetes is a cause when the body does not produce enough or responds normally to insulin, causing blood suger levels to be abnormally high,

chunks.heading: 9.7.20.1 Hypoglycaemia
chunks.text:
Low blood sugar - Is sudden onset and may be due to over medication or in adequate food. Symptoms
1. Weak/faint/dizzy/ light headed/Pale/sweaty skin
2. Possible rapid pulse
3. Intense hunger
4. Confused/disoriented and appears to be drunk/may be aggressive
5. Limbs may tremble
6. Possible unconsciousness If any of the above symptoms are visible check blood sugar level using the glucometer in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10) with the permission of PIC. Treatment
1. Offer sweet drinks/sugar/honey
2. Offer substantial food i.e. cake etc
3. If unconscious, treat for unconsciousness
4. Raise the blood sugar level as quickly as possible

chunks.heading: 9.7.20.2 Hyperglycaemia
chunks.text:
High Blood Sugar - Develops gradually over a period of days or weeks and could be due to inadequate drugs and over eating Symptoms
1. Excessive thirst
2. High urine output
3. Dry/warm skin
4. Acetone breathe (nail varnish smell)
5. Loss of appetite
6. Possible abdominal pain
7. Possible unconsciousness If any of the above symptoms are visible check blood sugar level using the glucometer in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10) with the permission of PIC. Treatment
1. Encourage passenger to take his own Insulin or medication
2. If unconscious, treat for unconsciousness Ref 9.7.33

chunks.heading: 9.7.21 Heat Exhaustion
chunks.text:
This condition occurs due to loss of fluid and salt from excessive sweating, caused by exposure to exces- sive heat and humidity and is gradual in onset. Symptoms
1. Looks exhausted/pale/cold/clammy skin
2. Rapid breathing and pulse
3. May complain of cramps due to salt deficiency
4. Person may suddenly faint Treatment
1. Lay person flat in a cool place/ elevate the legs and replace lost fluids
2. If the casualty is conscious, offer small sips of fluids to re-hydrate
3. If unconscious treat for unconsciousness Ref 9.7.33

chunks.heading: 9.7.22 Heat Stroke
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. May complain of headache/weakness/dizziness/nausea
2. Hot flushed dry skin
3. High body temperature – over 41° C
4. Rapid pulse and breathing rate Treatment
1. Victim requires immediate rapid cooling, use cool compresses i.e. wet towels
2. Keep head cool and offer cold liquid
3. Open air vent/remove excess clothing
4. If the casualty is conscious, place in a half sitting position with head and shoulders supported
5. If unconscious, treat for unconsciousness (Ref 9.7.33)
6. Administer oxygen if required (Ref 9.3)

chunks.heading: 9.7.23 Epilepsy
chunks.text: Symptoms A fit may last a few minutes. Passenger may be very tired and may need to sleep AURA – A sign which is known to be the onset of a fit. (E.g. blurred vision/a smell/a taste) TONIC – May give out a loud, sharp cry, become stiff and rigid. May stop breathing for 30 to 60 seconds; face flushed or pale and staring eyes. CLONIC – Displays jerky/twitching movements. Throwing of arms and legs. Clenched jaw with the risk of biting tongue. Possible foaming around the mouth may lose control of the bladder/bowel func- tions. May injure himself if the area is not cleared.

chunks.heading: 9.7.23 Epilepsy
chunks.text:
COMA – Once the fit is over he may be unconscious for a few minutes. When conscious, may appear to be confused/dazed or sleepy. Treatment
1. Protect passenger from injuring himself or other passengers
2. Remove sharp objects and pad area with pillows and blankets
3. If passenger is seated, fasten seat belt
4. Do not insert anything into passenger’s mouth including Airways as this could cause injury
5. Do not restrain passenger
6. When the fit is over, immediately check ABC and allow passenger to awaken naturally
7. If unconscious, treat for unconscious. (Ref 9.7.33)
8. Be cautious as fits/seizures may be repeated

chunks.heading: 9.7.24 Fainting
chunks.text:
Caused by heat/excessive hunger/pain etc., resulting in a brief state of unconsciousness due to tempo- rary lack of blood supply to the brain. Symptoms
1. Dizziness/weakness
2. Pale face
3. Sweating
4. Possible nausea
5. Passenger may collapse Treatment
1. Increase blood supply to the brain
2. Lay/sit passenger with head between legs
3. Lay elevate the legs
4. Loosen tight clothing
5. Open air vent
6. If unconscious, treat as an unconscious passenger. (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.25 Hyperventilation
chunks.text:
Over breathing due to uncontrolled fear and anxiety. causes low level of carbon dioxide in the blood Symptoms
1. Visible over breathing (deep and heavy)
2. Dizziness and blurred vision
3. Muscle stiffness/tingling/especially in hands and feet
4. Loss of balance and fainting
5. May complain of feeling pins/needles in the hands and feet Treatment
1. Request passenger to breathe slowly in and out to control breathing rate
2. Reassure since the passenger may be very anxious
3. Cover nose and mouth with an air sickness bag, temporarily and request the passenger to breathe in to it

chunks.heading: 9.7.26 Shock
chunks.text:
Reduction in the volume of circulating blood causes a sudden fall in blood pressure/loss of blood and bodily fluids. When the blood supply is reduced, especially to the brain, the person can become uncon- scious. As there is a reduced amount of circulating blood, the body’s own defence mechanism takes adequate action to maintain blood flow to the vital organs. Symptoms
1. Weakness/dizziness
2. Skin very pale/blue/cold clammy
3. Nausea/vomiting/restless/agitated
4. Fast/shallow breathing
5. Fast/weak pulse
6. Severe chill/body shakes
7. Slow/verbal response
8. May complain of thirst
9. Possible unconsciousness Treatment Conscious
1. Do not give anything to eat or drink
2. Aim - to improve blood supply to the brain, heart and lungs
3. Lie down - elevate legs
4. Keep warm
5. Administer oxygen if required. (Ref 9.3) Unconscious Treat as a unconscious passenger. (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.27 Heart Disorders (Angina)
chunks.text:
It is narrowing of coronary arteries due to exertion/stress/flying in a pressurized cabin etc. Symptoms
1. Severe crushing, central chest pain which can radiate down one or both arms
2. Shortness of breath
3. Skin pale or blue/weak pulse
4. Sweaty and anxious
5. Possible shock
6. Possible unconsciousness Treatment
1. Encourage passenger to take own medication
2. If relieved of pain (by medication) after 10 minutes, treat as a heart attack
3. Reassure
4. Administer oxygen (Ref 9.3)
5. Monitor closely
6. Keep passenger at rest with minimal exertion Most angina sufferers respond to their medication and remain well for the rest of the flight

chunks.heading: 9.7.28 Heart Attack
chunks.text:
Obstruction of the coronary arteries Symptoms
1. Severe, central chest pain may radiate down one or both arms
2. Very short of breath
3. Pale skin/blue/sweaty and clammy
4. Pulse weak and rapid
5. Nausea/vomiting
6. Severe shock
7. Possible unconsciousness Treatment
1. Continuously monitor ABC
2. Administer oxygen (Ref 9.3)
3. Spray GTN under the tongue.
4. Reassure
5. No exertion
6. Treat for shock if required Unconscious Treat as an unconscious passenger (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.29 Cardiac Arrest
chunks.text:
Sudden stoppage of the heart beat Symptoms
1. Unconsciousness
2. Not responding
3. No breathing/ pulse
4. Dilated pupils Treatment
1. Start CPR
2. Continuously Monitor ABC
3. Administer oxygen (Ref 9.3)
4. Reassure
5. No exertion
6. Treat for shock if required Unconscious Treat as an unconscious passenger (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.30 Stroke
chunks.text:
Bleeding artery or a blood clot in the brain generally affecting the middle-aged and the elderly. Symptoms
1. Headache/flushed face/strong pulse
2. Weakness/paralysis down one side of the body
3. Disorientated /weak /slurred/absence of speech
4. Possible loss of bowel/bladder control
5. Possible unconsciousness (with noisy breathing) Treatment
1. Reassure
2. Do not give anything through the mouth
3. Raise head slightly if possible
4. Administer oxygen if required (Ref 9.3)
5. Monitor closely Unconscious Treat as an unconscious passenger (Ref 9.7.33)

chunks.heading: 9.7.31 Allergies
chunks.text:
Allergy may be defined as the overreaction of the protective mechanism of the human body against al- lergenic substances. Common allergens include certain foods (Nuts, shellfish red meat, pineapple), drug allergies, Pollen, dust, Insect allergies. Symptoms
1. Redness on the skin
2. Urticarial Skin rash
3. Itching
4. Eye irritation
5. Nasal congestion
6. Shortness of breath Treatment
1. Advice Passenger to take his prescribed medication In line with the symptoms,
2. Offer Antihistamine 01 tablet for adult, half tablet for child above two years and for children below two years seek medical advice,
3. Keep airway open

chunks.heading: 9.7.32 Choking
chunks.text: Symptoms

chunks.heading: TOTAL OBSTRUCTION PARTIAL OBSTRUCTION
chunks.text:
Unable to cough Coughing Unable to speak Panic and distress May grasp throat Difficulty in talking Blueness of lips Difficulty in breathing May stop breathing May become unconscious Treatment Total/Partial blockage of airway caused by a foreign object
1. Encourage the passenger to cough up the obstruction
2. Stand behind the casualty place both hands around and pull his abdomen sharply inwards and upwards ( abdominal thrust)
3. Give 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades If conscious and breathing, despite evidence of obstruction
1. Encourage him to continue coughing, but do nothing else. Total obstruction Shows exhaustion/becomes blue
1. Give back slaps
2. Reassure passenger
3. Bend casualty over so that the mouth lies at a lower level than the chest
4. Slap sharply with the heel of your hand between shoulder blades 5 times
5. If this does not relieve the obstruction, give abdominal thrusts

chunks.heading: TOTAL OBSTRUCTION PARTIAL OBSTRUCTION
chunks.text:
Abdominal thrust adult/Child (Conscious)
1. Stand behind the passenger
2. Put your arms around the passenger’s abdomen
3. Interlock hands and place between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone
4. Pull both hands towards you with a quick inward and upward thrust
5. Repeat 5 times if necessary.
6. If the passenger becomes unconscious follow the next steps
7. Repeat cycle of backslaps followed by Abdominal Thrusts until foreign object is removed Choking-Collapsed Child (1-7 Years-Conscious)
1. Lean child forward or place over your knee for smaller children with head down
2. Give 5 back-slaps between the shoulder blades. Use less force than for an adult
3. Check mouth and remove any obvious obstruction
4. If back-slaps are unsuccessful, give 5 chest thrusts

chunks.heading: TOTAL OBSTRUCTION PARTIAL OBSTRUCTION
chunks.text:
5. Stand or kneel behind the child
6. Place fist against the breast bone and grasp fist with the other hand
7. Pull sharply inward 5 times at a rate of one thrust every 3 seconds
8. If unsuccessful, give 5 more back-slaps (as described above)
9. If unsuccessful, give 5 abdominal thrusts
10. Abdominal thrusts for children are done in the same way as the adult technique using two hands. Modify your force in order to prevent injury
11. Continue the sequence of back-slaps and chest thrusts, back-slaps and abdominal thrusts until the object is cleared or help arrives Choking - Collapsed Babies (0 – 1 Year Conscious)
1. Lay the baby along your forearm
2. Give 5 back-slaps between the shoulder blades using less force than for a child
3. If unsuccessful, give 5 chest thrusts
4. Place two fingers between nipples and push inwards for thrusts
5. Do not use abdominal thrust on babies
6. If the child/baby falls unconscious, check ABC begin CPR

chunks.heading: TOTAL OBSTRUCTION PARTIAL OBSTRUCTION
chunks.text:
Choking-Collapsed Pregnant Ladies/Obese Persons
1. Give 05 back slaps
2. Replace abdominal thrusts with 5 chest thrusts

chunks.heading: 9.7.33 Head Injury/Conscious/Unconscious
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Bump or cut on head
2. Nausea or vomiting
3. Dizziness
4. Confusion/loss of memory
5. Possible head wound with bleeding
6. Passenger may become unconscious Concussion The brain is free to move a little within the skull and therefore can be shaken by a violent blow or injury. This may cause concussion, a condition of widespread, but temporary disturbance of the brain. There will be a period of unconsciousness, but it is always brief and is followed by complete recovery. If the casualty is unconscious after 3 minutes, suspect a more serious injury. Page for a doctor and place in the recovery position and monitor if there is clear fluid or blood draining considerably from the ear/ nose. If it is a more serious injury, do not plug or try to stop the flow. Loosely cover with a sterile dry dressing to prevent infection. Monitor closely. Symptoms
1. Headache
2. Vomiting/nausea
3. Drowsiness

chunks.heading: 9.7.33 Head Injury/Conscious/Unconscious
chunks.text: 4. Visual disturbances

chunks.heading: 9.7.33 Head Injury/Conscious/Unconscious
chunks.text: Unconscious Passenger Unconsciousness is a prolonged state of unawareness due to heart attack/stroke/diabetes/coma/head injury etc.

chunks.heading: LEVELS OF CONSCIOUSNESS APPEARANCE
chunks.text:
Conscious Awake/orientated alert Semi-conscious Drowsy/ confused/ responds to speech/non-painful Stimulation Unconsciousness Deep sleep/responds to painful stimulation/ Only breathing & Pulse present Treatment
1. Check DRSABC (Ref 9.2.4)
2. Keep in recovery position
3. Administer oxygen if required (Ref 9.3) The Recovery Position An unconscious person should be placed in the recovery position. This position prevents the tongue from blocking the airway. It allows fluid to drain from the mouth, reducing the risk of the passenger in- haling stomach contents. The head/neck and back are kept in a straight line, while the bent limbs keep the body propped in a secure and comfortable position. Prior to turning a casualty, remove his or her eyeglasses if worn, and any bulky objects from pockets. Method
1. Kneeling beside the casualty, open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin
2. Straighten the legs. Place the arm nearest to you at right-angles to the body, elbow bent, with

chunks.heading: LEVELS OF CONSCIOUSNESS APPEARANCE
chunks.text:
both palms placed under cheek
3. Bring the arm furthest from you across the chest, and hold the hand, palm outwards, against the casualty’s nearest cheek

chunks.heading: LEVELS OF CONSCIOUSNESS APPEARANCE
chunks.text:
4. With your other hand, grasp the leg furthest from you and pull the knee up, so that the foot is flat on the floor
5. Keeping the hand pressed against the cheek, pull at the knee to roll the casualty towards you and on to the side
6. Tilt the head back to make sure the airway remains open. Adjust the hand under the cheek, if necessary, so that the head stays in a tilted position
7. Adjust the upper leg, if necessary, so that both the hip and the knee are bent at right angles
8. Page for medical assistance
9. Monitor ABC continuously
10. Administer oxygen if necessary
11. Keep warm and cover with a blanket
12. Do not offer food or drinks by mouth Recovery position for passenger suffering from Heart Attack Recovery position for passenger suffering from Shock Recovery position for passenger suffering from Head Injury

chunks.heading: 9.7.34 Bleeding/Controlling blood loss
chunks.text:
Types of wounds
1. Incised wound- Caused by a clean cut from a sharp edged object and the blood vessels are cut straight across
2. Laceration – Crushing or ripping forces result in tears or lacerations and the wound may bleed less profusely than incised wounds but it is likely to have more tissue damage
3. Abrasion (Graze) – This is superficial wound in which the top most layer of skin is scraped off, leaving a raw tender area. This is caused by a sliding fall or a friction burn
4. Contused wound – Caused by a blunt blow or punch can rupture capillaries beneath the skin, causing blood to leak into the tissues
5. Punctured wound – An injury such as standing on a nail or being pricked by a needle will result in a punctured wound and it is a small entry but a deep track of internal damage
6. Stab wound - Caused by a long bladed instrument usually a knife penetrating the body. Seriously endangers/injury to vital organs

chunks.heading: 9.7.34 Bleeding/Controlling blood loss
chunks.text: 7. Gunshot wound - Caused by a bullet or other missile. May drive into or through the body caus- ing serious internal injury, sucking in clothing and contaminants from the air. The entry wound is small and neat any exit may be large and ragged

chunks.heading: 9.7.35.1 External Bleeding
chunks.text:
Apply Direct Pressure Apply direct pressure using sterile gauze pads. Maintain pressure on wound for about 10 minutes. This will allow the blood to clot. Do not remove original dressing if they become saturated with blood apply further dressings over original dressing. Elevate limbs using triangular bandage. Monitor closely. If the passenger develops signs/symptoms of shock, treat for shock. Apply Tourniquet
1. Used only by CCMs as a last resort
2. Apply 2 -3 inches above the wound using bandage from the First Aid Kit and it has to be be- tween the source of bleeding and the heart
3. Record time of applying tourniquet
4. Release for 15 seconds every 15 minutes
5. Never cover a tourniquet
6. Place “T” mark on passengers forehead
7. Never leave passenger unattended
8. Reassure the passenger continuously

chunks.heading: 9.7.35.2 Internal Bleeding
chunks.text:
Causes Stomach ulcers, miscarriage, fractures, etc. Symptoms For signs and symptoms, refer to Shock. Treatment
1. Assess the situation and make a note of history
2. Observe for any bruising
3. Make passenger comfortable and cover with a blanket
4. If he becomes unconscious, then handle as an unconscious passenger
5. Administer oxygen if necessary
6. Do not give anything to eat or drink
7. Treat for shock

chunks.heading: 9.7.36 Nose Bleeding
chunks.text:
1. Seat passenger upright and tilt head slightly forward to prevent swallowing of blood
2. Request passenger to pinch nostrils firmly until bleeding stops (approximately 15 minutes) can place an ice pack on bridge of the nose
3. After the bleeding has stopped, instruct the passenger to breathe through mouth, and not to blow his nose or spit out any blood
4. If severe nose bleed persists, page for a doctor/medical practitioner

chunks.heading: 9.7.37.1 First degree Superficial - Skin red
chunks.text:
Treatment
1. Pour water (room temp) over affected area for approximately 20 minutes
2. Remove jewellery or constricting clothing from injured area before swelling occurs
3. Apply a burns dressing/cream. Cover with loose dressing. Do not apply pressure to the affected area
4. Consider pain relief (2 Paracetamol tablets after obtaining the allergy history)

chunks.heading: 9.7.37.2 Second Degree Intermediate - Skin red/blistered
chunks.text:
Treatment
1. Pour water (room temperature) over affected area for approximately 20 minutes
2. Do not touch or break blisters
3. Remove any watches, rings, belts or constricting clothing from injured area before it starts to swell
4. Apply a burns dressing/cream. Cover with loose dressing. Do not apply pressure to the affected area
5. Consider pain relief

chunks.heading: 9.7.37.3 Third degree Deep – Skin charred
chunks.text:
Treatment
1. Do not remove anything that is sticking to the burn or interfering with the injured area
2. Apply silver sulphadiazine and Vaseline gauze (antibiotic tulle) to prevent contamination and infection
3. Treat for shock
4. Consider pain relief Do Not Use
1. Adhesive dressings or bandages
2. Break blisters
3. Apply lotions, ointments, creams or fats to the affected area
4. Apply any dressing on chemical burns

chunks.heading: 9.7.38 Back and Neck Injuries
chunks.text:
If suspected back or neck fractures – do not move passenger Symptoms
1. Pain on neck or on the back
2. Paralysis, total or partial, on one or both sides
3. Neck fracture may affect all parts of your body
4. Possible loss of bladder or bowel control Treatment
1. Do not move passenger or lift his head in case of neck injury
2. Reassure passenger and keep him/her warm
3. Immobilize neck with Sam Splint as a neck collar

chunks.heading: 9.7.39 Sprains (On the spine)
chunks.text:
Symptoms Injury caused by over-stretching a ligament at a joint.
1. Pain
2. Swelling
3. Bruising
4. Loss of movement

chunks.heading: 9.7.40 Strains
chunks.text: Injury caused by over-stretching/tearing of a muscle or tendon.

chunks.heading: 9.7.40 Strains
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Pain
2. Stiffness and cramp Treatment Use the RICE Procedure R - Rest affected area I - Ice, to reduce swelling C - Compression (Elastic Bandage) E - Elevation Offer two paracetamols for pain relief. Note : If in doubt – always treat injured part as a fracture

chunks.heading: 9.7.41 Dislocation
chunks.text:
Symptoms
1. Severe pain
2. Deformity of joint
3. Loss of movement of affected limb
4. Swelling and possible bruising
5. Possible shock Treatment
1. Immobilize and support using Sam Splint, Padding, Sling and Bandages
2. Apply a cold pack if swelling appears
3. Offer mild painkiller – e.g. Panadol

chunks.heading: 9.7.42 Fractures
chunks.text: Type of Fractures Kind of Fractures (Closed/Open)

chunks.heading: 9.7.42.1 Closed Fractures
chunks.text:
(The bone is broken, but the surrounding skin is intact) Symptoms
1. Passenger will feel or hear bone break
2. Pain, tenderness, deformity
3. Partial or complete loss of movement
4. Swelling and bruising
5. Possible shock Treatment
1. Keep steady and support affected part
2. Immobilize e.g. Sam Splint or other padding
3. If possible, elevate affected part using sling
4. Treat for shock
5. Mild pain killer like Panadol / Disprin

chunks.heading: 9.7.42.2 Open Fractures/Compound fracture
chunks.text:
The bone is broken and protrudes through the skin Symptoms
1. Wound
2. Protruding bone
3. Moderate-severe bleeding
4. Shock Treatment
1. Keep steady and support affected part
2. Do not attempt to straighten fractured limbs
3. Control bleeding
4. Dress wound/protect protruding bone using ring bandage
5. Immobilize
6. Treat for shock

chunks.heading: 9.8 Bandages
chunks.text: They can be used to secure dressings over wounds, to control bleeding, to support and immobilize inju- ries such as fractures and to reduce swelling.

chunks.heading: 9.8.2 Gauze Bandages
chunks.text: WOW (wide open weave) bandages secure dressing in place and can be used with dressings like jelonet, water jel, and melolin to treat burns, control bleeding and cover wounds.

chunks.heading: 9.8.3 Elastic Bandages
chunks.text: Elastic Bandages can also be described as tension or crepe bandages, and are used to offer support and reduce swelling to muscle and soft tissue injuries i.e. sprains and strains. 9.8.4 Triangular Bandages: A Triangular shaped material used to make slings, to offer support and immobilize fractures and disloca- tions.

chunks.heading: 9.8.5 General rules for bandages
chunks.text:
1. Explain to the casualty what you are going to do and reassure him
2. Make sure the casualty is as comfortable as possible either in a sitting or horizontal position
3. Keep the injured part supported
4. Work directly in front of the casualty and on the injured side
5. Apply the bandage firmly enough to control bleeding (if any) and to hold the dressing in place, but not too tight as it could reduce circulation
6. Leave fingers and toes exposed
7. Ensure that knots do not cause discomfort to the casualty
8. Check circulation to the area every 10 minutes Checking Circulation The circulation to any injured part should always be checked to ensure that a dressing or bandage has not been applied too tightly. Swelling can also affect the tightness of the bandage, therefore, checks must be carried out at regular intervals. Observations should include any abnormal colour, movement, sensation and temperature. Press the finger or toe on the affected part firmly, it will become pale.

chunks.heading: 9.8.5 General rules for bandages
chunks.text: Upon releasing the pressure normal colour (pink) should return promptly. If colour does not return or returns slowly, the bandage may be too tight. Movement The passenger must be able to wriggle the toes or fingers of the affected limb (arm or foot). If move- ment is restricted, loosen the bandage. Be mindful of any numbness, tingling (pins and needles) or any unusual sensation which may indicate that the bandage is too tight.

chunks.heading: 9.8.5 General rules for bandages
chunks.text: Temperature Fingers and toes should be warm to the touch, coldness could suggest that circulation has been affect- ed. If any of the above factors are present the bandage should be removed and the dressing reapplied. Dressings are used to cover wounds, burns and can help to control bleeding. They are used to prevent infection and contamination to the injured site.

chunks.heading: 9.9 Carriage of Stretcher Cases
chunks.text: Duties in looking after a stretcher passenger requires beyond those performed for an ordinary passen- gers. Handling of any medical equipment and sanitary support shall be carried out by the accompanying medical personal accompanying the stretcher passenger. CCMs shall ensure that the passenger and the stretcher are secured at all times.

chunks.heading: 9.10 Childbirth
chunks.text: Passengers pregnant for 29th week, requires a doctor’s certificate to fly. From the end of the 35th week of pregnancy to the end of the 36th week, passengers will only be accepted for flights of 4 hours or less. Passengers who suffer from pregnancy related complications are not accepted after the 34th week of pregnancy. Passengers are not accepted for air travel after the end of the 36 Week of pregnancy.

chunks.heading: 9.10.1 First Stage
chunks.text:
The first stage is when the cervix fully dilates. Approximately 4 – 10 hours. Symptoms
1. Low backache
2. Regular contractions (moderate/severe cramp like pains)
3. Blood-stained mucus (cervical plug)
4. Rupture of membrane surrounding the baby will give way to flow of blood-stained fluid Management
1. Page for medical assistance – Midwife or Doctor of medicine
2. Take the lady to the lavatory to evacuate bowels and bladder and ask her to wash thoroughly between the legs
3. Select a place of maximum space and privacy. Preferably the AFT galley
4. Place blankets and plastic bags under mother
5. Position; Bottle of oxygen / medical kit and sterile scissors
6. Two bowls or any available containers of boiled water
7. One swab to clean the mother and the other to clean the baby’s eyes
8. Plastic bags/air sickness bags for soiled dressings and placenta
9. Wash hands and apply sterile gloves and mask, prepare mother with knees parted and drawn

chunks.heading: 9.10.1 First Stage
chunks.text:
back.
10. The person delivering the baby should not have a cold/sore throat/infection.

chunks.heading: 9.10.2 Second Stage
chunks.text:
Approximately 10 minutes to 1 hour for delivery of the baby Symptoms
1. Stronger, frequent contractions (every 2-3 minutes)
2. Skin between rectum and vagina will bulge (birth imminent)
3. Mother will feel the urge to push
4. Cervix fully dilated Management
1. Protect rectum with sterile pads
2. To prevent rapid delivery apply gentle pressure with palm of hand over baby’s head
3. As head appears ask mother to pant
4. Always support baby’s head to prevent it “shooting” out
5. Once head is delivered check for cord around the neck

chunks.heading: 9.10.2 Second Stage
chunks.text:
If cord is around baby’s neck, attempt to remove cord by gently lifting it over the baby’s head. If not possible, place cord clamps 3 inches apart and cut cord in between clamps using sterile scissors. Management continued,
1. The baby will now turn and the front shoulder is born with the next contraction
2. Rest of the baby will slip out
3. Lift baby onto mother’s abdomen by holding under the armpits
4. Clear mucus from the baby’s mouth and nose using a mucus extractor
5. The baby now starts to breathe and may cry
6. Take note of time of delivery Dealing with the Cord
1. Do not stretch the cord
2. As soon as pulsation has ceased, apply one cord clamp firmly on the umbilical cord 6 inches from the baby’s abdomen, and the 2nd cord clamp 9 inches away from the baby’s abdomen
3. Cut the cord, using sterile scissors, between clamps
4. Then it becomes white between the two clamps
5. Cover end of baby’s cord with sterile gauze pad. Check regularly for signs of bleeding.

chunks.heading: 9.10.2 Second Stage
chunks.text:
6. Do not remove cord clamps at any time Care of baby
1. Dry baby with a towel
2. Clean eyes with cooled boiled water
3. Wrap baby in a blanket and give to mother

chunks.heading: 9.10.3 Third stage
chunks.text:
Delivery of the placenta will be approximately 15-30 minutes after birth. Management
1. Mother may experience further contractions
2. Encourage her to push
3. Do not pull the cord
4. Keep placenta for Doctor’s inspection by placing in plastic bag
5. If baby fails to breathe adequately after delivery;
6. Clear mouth and nose with mucus extractor and perform gentle mouth to nose and mouth re- suscitation. Re-assess every 15 seconds Care of mother
1. Clean mother
2. Apply sanitary pad
3. Make her comfortable and offer a warm drink
4. Record and monitor pulse regularly
5. Observe for bleeding advice mother to cross legs at the ankle
6. Encourage mother to breast-feed the baby Always arrange for a Doctor and Ambulance to meet the flight upon arrival. MOR shall be completed by the PIC and the Purser shall complete an Incident/Accident report before mother and baby leaves the aircraft. The exact time of birth shall be stated on the documentation.

chunks.heading: 9.11 Apparent Death
chunks.text: Flight Crew is not competent or legally authorized to pronounce an individual dead. Therefore, if a passenger appears to be dead, treat him as an unconscious person until a Doctor is present. Use your own judgment to determine if any First Aid steps will be of help. If not, proceed as follows; Ensure the seat belt is fastened and the seat is reclined to prevent him from falling. The unconscious pa- tient should be covered with a blanket up to the neck and surrounded with pillows. If the eyes remain opened, they may be closed. Before landing, request a passenger to assist by holding the unconscious person. Primary CCMs shall return to their assigned seats for landing. The Purser may detail an Assist Crew member to sit on the adjacent seat. Important; in the absence of a Doctor on flight and a person appears to have succumbed, the PIC shall notify the nearest scheduled landing point to have a Doctor and an ambulance to meet the flight. CCM

chunks.heading: 9.11 Apparent Death
chunks.text: should remain available for questioning by the Coroner and provide names and addresses. The name and addresses of persons sitting or working in close proximity to the deceased are to be obtained and submitted with the required reports. Any sort of evidence shall be left undisturbed. CCMs should note down observations as well as the physical sequence of events until the arrival of the Doctor. If death is not pronounced it would be the responsibility of the Station Staff to coordinate and remove the passenger to hospital. In the event a Doctor is on the flight, and he has certified the person has succumbed, the PIC should notify the landing point, and request that the Coroner and/or police be called to meet the flight on arrival. Name, address and contact point of the Doctor attending shall be recorded. Whenever possible, ar- rangements to be made for the Doctor to await the arrival of the Coroner. The Aircraft shall be fumigat-

chunks.heading: 9.11 Apparent Death
chunks.text: ed as per the requirements and laid down procedures prior to the next operation of a flight.

chunks.heading: 9.12 Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
chunks.text:
Attachments
1. AED battery / 01
2. AED memory card / 01
3. Heart pad adult/Child / 01
4. ECG leads (03 cables) / 01 set
5. ECG electrodes / 03 / 01 set
6. Red box with / no 01-10 Usage If the patient has been unconscious for more than 5 minutes start CPR immediately. A victim who does not respond may have an abnormal heart rhythm that stops the heart from pumping blood. Use an AED on a victim of 1 year of age and older only when the victim does not respond and is not breathing. For victims of 8 years or older, start CPR and use an AED as soon as possible For victims 1 to 8 years of age, perform about 2 minutes of CPR before using the AED. Steps
1. Turn the AED on Push the button
2. Follow the visual and audible prompts
3. Attach pads Open the AED pad package and peel away the plastic backing. Attach the sticky side of the pads directly to the victim’s bare chest. The picture on the pad will show you where to place the pads.

chunks.heading: 9.12 Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
chunks.text:
1. Allow the AED to check the heart rhythm
2. Clearing the Victim CCM shall stay away from the victim (remove oxygen if administering) prior to delivering the shock, Ensure no one touches the victim when the AED prompts to clear.
1. Push the SHOCK button when the AED commands
2. Start the steps of CPR right after shock delivery
3. Use the AED quickly. For adult victims the time from arrival of the AED to first shock should be less than 90 seconds
4. If the AED does not command to give a shock, follow the AED visual and audible prompts.
5. Be ready to resume CPR if needed Special Situations Special situations will change the way you use an AED Water Do not deliver a shock when a victim is:
1. Lying in water

chunks.heading: 9.12 Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
chunks.text:
2. Covered with water (E.g. the victim is covered with sweat or has just been pulled from a swimming pool)
1. Move the victim away from standing water
2. Wipe the victim’s chest before you attach the pads Note: Water may cause the shock to flow over the skin from one pad to the other and the energy won’t be transmitted to the heart. If a shock is given in water, the AED also might shock the rescuer. Small Amounts of Water If the victim is lying in a small puddle of water or snow but the chest is not wet or covered with water, you may give shocks. Medicine Patch You should not put an AED pad over ointment or any medicinal patch. so that some of the energy does not reach the heart. Also giving a shock over the patch may burn the victim. If a child or adult has a medicine patch in the same place where you would attach the AED pad, take the medicine patch off while wearing gloves. Quickly wipe the chest where the patch was before you put on the pad.

chunks.heading: 9.12 Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
chunks.text: Implanted Pacemaker or Defibrillator Some children or adults may have an implanted pacemaker or defibrillator. These devices make a hard lump under the skin of the chest or in the abdomen. The lump is smaller than a deck of cards. You should not place an AED pad over this lump because the implanted device may block the delivery of the shock to the heart. Look for a lump under the skin of the chest place the pads at least 1 inch away Hairy Chest If a victim has a hairy chest, the AED pads may stick to the hair instead of the skin on the chest. If this happens, the AED will not be able to check the victim’s heart rhythm or deliver a shock. The AED will prompt you to check the pads. Shave body hair if applicable. If the pads stick to the hair instead of the skin, press down firmly on each pad. If the AED still commands you to check the pads, pull off the pads off shave the area place a new set of pads.

chunks.heading: 9.12 Automated External Defibrillator (AED)
chunks.text: Follow the AED visual and audible prompts.

chunks.heading: 9.13.1 Guidelines for CCMs
chunks.text:
As per SLCAIS 045, the following are general guidelines for CCMs when facing a suspected case of com- municable disease on-board. During an outbreak of a specific communicable disease, the World Health Organization (WHO) or Civil Aviation Authority of Sri Lanka may modify or add further procedures to these general guidelines. However these general guidelines provide a basic framework of response to reassure the CCMs and help them manage such an event effectively, in a timely manner. 9.13.2 Identification: A communicable disease is suspected when a passenger or Crewmember has fever (temperature 38⁰C/100⁰F or greater) associated with one or more of the following signs or symptoms:
1. Appearing obviously unwell
2. Persistent coughing
3. Difficulty in breathing
4. Persistent diarrhoea
5. Persistent vomiting
6. Skin rash
7. Bruising or bleeding without previous injury
8. Decreased consciousness or confusion of recent onset

chunks.heading: 9.13.1 Guidelines for CCMs
chunks.text:
9. Headache with stiff neck or
10. Has a fever that has persisted for more than 48 hours or
11. Has symptoms or other indications of communicable disease, as the CAASL may announce through posting of a notice.

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text: (a) Don a mask The passenger suspected, shall be given a mask to wear covering the nose and mouth secured firmly. If the mask becomes damp /humid, it should be replaced by a new one. When the mask is disposed ensure hands are protected by wearing surgical gloves in a secure/ sealed plastic bag. Wash hands thoroughly for 20 Seconds with soap/water. Use alcohol based hand rub (contains at least 60% alcohol) if soap and water is not available. If the suspected passenger cannot tolerate a face mask, the designated Cabin Crewmember/s or passengers seated around two (2) rows in-front, back and either sides of seats shall don masks. CCM/s shall not place themselves at risk by close contact with the passenger. (E.g. by more frequent hand and face contact by mask adjustments). (b) Direct Contact with Body Fluids If there is a risk of direct contact with body fluids, the designated CCM/s shall wear disposable gloves.

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text: The gloves are not intended to replace hand hygiene. These gloves shall be removed and disposed in a Bio-hazard bag (or a plastic bag, sealed and labelled as “Bio-Hazard”, if a Bio-hazard bag is not availa- ble). Wash hands thoroughly and use an alcohol based hand rub. (c) Inform Pilot in Command The PIC shall be informed to report the case/s to the ATC of the Departure and Arrival destinations. PIC shall also inform the next station of the requirement for cleaning and disinfection of the aircraft. Public Health Emergencies Involving Operation Aircraft

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text:
(d) Guidelines for CCMs Disposing of contaminated items – All items which comes in contact with the suspected person shall be disposed into the Bio-hazard bag (or a thick plastic bag and sealed. This bag shall be labelled as “BIO- HAZARD” with a permanent marker).
1. Check with accompanying passengers if they too have similar symptoms.
2. Ensure hand carried cabin luggage of the suspected passenger is/are off loaded along with the passenger and comply with Public Health Authorities request at the destination.
3. Unless stated otherwise by Ground Medical Support or Public Health Officials, request the other passengers who have been occupying seat rows adjacent to the suspected passenger (2 rows in- front, back and either sides) to complete the passenger locator card available in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10) and R1 First Aid Kit.
4. A general way of hand cleansing, performed by means of applying an antiseptic hand rub is to

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text:
wash one’s hands with soap and flowing water for at least 20 Seconds. Touching the face with hands should be avoided. Hands should be washed frequently on board. (e) A questionnaire for Cabin Crewmembers in such a situation;
1. Are the symptoms consistent with Communicable Disease?
2. (Symptoms may include: fever, weakness, muscle pain, headache, sore throat, vomiting, and diarrhea, rash or bleeding)
3. Is the environment of the plane contaminated? (By vomitus, spilled blood, other body fluid)
4. How many passengers and staff were exposed?
5. Is there a doctor or any other medical person on board?
6. Does the operator have access to ground – based medical support?
7. Has the passenger received medical assistance during the flight?
8. Does the passenger require medical assistance during the flight? (Clinical signs and symptoms among passengers and severity)
9. Are any enhanced precautions for the disembarkation of other passengers needed?

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text: senger should be provided with tissues and asked to cover the mouth and nose when coughing

chunks.heading: 9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
9.13.3 Procedure to be adopted by CCM
chunks.text:
after the flight or
9. If a CCM/s suspect that there is a risk of getting a Communicable Disease following the interac- tion between the sick passenger & the CCM/s. (Risk of infection depending on type of disease, flight duration, level of exposure and level of immunity).
10. If CCM(s) develop symptoms of infection during flight, they should discontinue on board duties as soon as it is safe to do so and follow the procedure
11. Do not prepare or serve food or beverages if you have symptoms of illness that could be conta- gious.

chunks.heading: 9.13.5 Public health Passenger Locator Form
chunks.text: The Purser shall fill up the public health passenger locator form located in the Emergency Medical Kit (A10)/BC First Aid Kit.

chunks.heading: 9.13.6 Universal Precaution Kit
chunks.text:
The content of an aircraft universal precaution kit would typically include:
1. Dry powder that can convert small liquid spill into a granulated gel.
2. Germinal disinfectant for surface cleaning.
3. Disinfectant wipes & Dry wipes
4. Face/eye mask (separate or combined), Gloves (disposable)
5. Polythene Apron and Oversleeves.
6. Polypropylene scoop with scrape.
7. Biohazard bag.
8. Instructions.

chunks.heading: 9.13.7 Universal Precaution Kit Usage
chunks.text:
1. Put on protective clothing provided (Gloves, face/eye mask, Apron & Oversleeves)
2. Sprinkle powder liberally over the spill area (The liquid & powder will become a gel)
3. Remove gel using scoop & scrape, dispose of gel scoop & scrap into biohazard bag
4. Spray area with disinfectant, clean with dry wipe
5. Remove protective clothing & place in biohazard bag
6. Wipe hands using disinfectant wipes

chunks.heading: 9.14 First Aid Kit
chunks.text:
Procedure on Usage of First Aid Kits
1. CCMs shall not break the seals during pre-departure safety/security check
• CCMs shall check and tally the seal numbers against the numbers indicated on the sticker pasted on the First Aid Kit along with the expiry date. The sticker shall have the medical cen- tre stamp of approval and signature. In the event seal numbers do not tally, contact support services staff for First Aid Kit replacement prior to departing CMB.
2. Cabin crew shall open the First Aid Kits when required only with the consent of the Purser and the PIC has to be kept informed.
• Cabin Crew to page for a medical practitioner prior to administering medication from the First Aid Kits.
• In the absence of a medical practitioner, inform Purser indicating the symptoms and medication requested by the passenger. The Medication Consent Form (MCF) needs to be completed and signed by the passenger before medication is administered. The form needs

chunks.heading: 9.14 First Aid Kit
chunks.text:
to be submitted along with the VR.
• At all times it is recommended to use the EY First Aid Kit/s, first and the BC First Aid Kit to be used as a last resort if the required medication/item is not available in the EY first aid kits.
• The following Medication Consent Forms (MCF) shall be available in all First Aid kits,
• Adult Medication consent form – For administering medicine to an adult.
• Infant/Children Medication consent form - Shall be signed by both parents/Guardian if travelling before administering medication.
• Please indicate the flight number and date on the top-right corner of each consent form.
• An Illness report shall be completed only if a medical practitioner is available to attend to the casualty, if not only the consent form to be submitted.
3. Once any First Aid Kit is opened, if a Flight Crew change takes place at a transit station the join- ing PIC shall be informed regarding same and at a layover station the disembarking Purser shall

chunks.heading: 9.14 First Aid Kit
chunks.text:
enter the new seal numbers on the transfer of instructions. The taking over crew shall inform the operating PIC regarding the First Aid Kit that has been opened and shall check, the new seal numbers against the transfer of instructions. In the event the seal numbers do not tally, crew to open the First Aid Kit and carry-out a security check and re seal the kit. Purser to indicate details on the VR.
4. On arrival in CMB, CCMs shall enter comment as “First Aid Kit opened” in the Cabin Defects Log- book, The seal numbers of the used First Aid kit shall be entered on the Voyage Report and Seal Form
5. The unopened First aid kits would remain on-board to be used for the next flight. Pre-flight Check – Correct Number, Correct Location, Correctly Secured, Clear of Obstructions, Seal intact.

chunks.heading: DANGEROUS GOODS REGULATIONS
