chunks.heading: 10.0 DANGEROUS GOODS
chunks.text: Dangerous goods are defined as articles and substances, which pose a significant hazard to health, safety, property or environment, when transported by air (They include common items such as battery electrolyte, butane gas, fire-works, ammunition, weed-killer, paint, mercury) and which are shown in the list of dangerous goods in these Regulations or which are classified according to these Regulations.

chunks.heading: 10.1.1 United Nations Subcommittee of experts
chunks.text: Develops recommended procedures for the transport of all types of dangerous goods except radioac- tive materials. These procedures, applicable to all modes of transport are published in the Recommen- dations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods – Model Regulations. International Atomic Energy Authority (IAEA) develops recommended procedures for safe transport of radioactive material

chunks.heading: 10.1.2 Relationship to ICAO
chunks.text: ICAO uses these recommendations as the basis for developing regulations for the safe transport of dangerous goods by air by any aircraft. ICAO regulations are codified in Annex 18 and its technical instructions for safe transport of dangerous goods by air (DOC 9284-AN/905) published once every two years .These regulations are for the transport of dangerous goods by air from to or through the member states of ICAO. The ICAO Technical instructions for safe transport of dangerous goods by air, provides the basis under which dangerous goods can be transported safely by air at a level of safety necessary to ensure that the aircraft or its occupants are not at risk.

chunks.heading: 10.1.3 IATA/DGR
chunks.text: The IATA Dangerous Regulations contains all the requirements of the technical Instructions. IATA has in- cluded additional requirements, which are more restrictive than the Technical Instructions and Reflects industry standard practices or operational considerations.

chunks.heading: 10.2 Dangerous Goods Incident
chunks.text: An occurrence other than a dangerous goods accident associated with and related to the transport of dangerous goods by air, not necessarily occurring on board an aircraft, which results in injury to a per- son, property damage, fire, breakage, spillage, leakage of fluid or radiation or other evidence that the integrity of the packaging has not been maintained Any occurrence relating to the transport of dangerous goods which seriously jeopardizes an aircraft, or its occupants is also deemed to be a dangerous goods incident

chunks.heading: 10.3 Dangerous Goods Accident
chunks.text: An occurrence associated with and related to the transport of dangerous goods by air which results in fatal or serious injury to a person or major property damage

chunks.heading: 10.4 General Philosophy
chunks.text: Dangerous goods can be transported safely by air provided certain principles are strictly followed. These principles and procedures include,

chunks.heading: 10.4.1 Classification
chunks.text: Dangerous Goods are classified according to criteria determined by the United Nations Sub Committee of Experts on the Transporting Dangerous Goods.

chunks.heading: 10.4.2 Prohibition
chunks.text: Some dangerous goods have been identified as being too dangerous to be carried on any aircraft under any circumstances.

chunks.heading: 10.4.3 Packing
chunks.text: Packaging is the essential component in the safe transport of dangerous goods by air. The IATA Danger- ous Goods Regulations provide packing instruction for all dangerous goods acceptable for air transport with a wide range of option for inner, outer and single packaging. Packings are subject to performance tests and are tested by institutes authorized by authorities.

chunks.heading: 10.4.4 Marking and Labelling
chunks.text: The package is marked with required markings and bear the required labels to ensure that the hazards can be recognized without relying on accompanying documentation in an emergency.

chunks.heading: 10.4.5 Documentation
chunks.text: This ensured that they are correctly accepted, handled and loaded and if an incident or accident occurs, either in-flight or on ground, what the correct response should be. Shipper shall fill up the Dangerous goods declaration form with all details

chunks.heading: 10.4.6 Notification to Pilot in Command
chunks.text: The Pilot in Command must know what any emergency that may occur is on board the aircraft in order to properly assess and action. The pilot in command must also convey this information if possible, to air traffic services to aid in the response to any aircraft incident or accident.

chunks.heading: 10.4.7 Avoiding Hidden Hazards
chunks.text: Information regarding “Hidden Dangerous Goods” must also be conveyed to passengers, crew and ship- pers to assist them in the recognizing dangerous goods.

chunks.heading: 10.4.8 Accident/Incident Reporting
chunks.text: Dangerous goods accidents or incidents must be reported.

chunks.heading: 10.4.9 Training
chunks.text: Dangerous Goods training is a mandatory (legal) requirement for all individuals involved in the prepa-

chunks.heading: 10.4.9 Training
chunks.text: ration or transport of dangerous goods by air to ensure that they can carry out their responsibilities. Cabin crew shall be trained in IAAT DGR category 11

chunks.heading: 10.5 State Variations
chunks.text: State may impose additional restrictions to the ICAO regulations known as state variance

chunks.heading: 10.5.1 Sri Lanka (VCG)
chunks.text: VCG 01-No aircraft operator shall transport dangerous goods by air to, from or over Sri Lanka without explicit approval in writing from the Director General of Civil aviation, Sri Lanka VCG 02 -Permission is usually granted for a specified period of time, subject to strict compliance with ICAO technical Instructions and any other conditions which the Director general of Civil Aviation deems necessary VCG 03-Application for permission shall be made to: Director General of Civil Aviation, Civil Aviation Authority of Sri Lanka, No: 152/1, Minuwangoda road, P.O.Box 056, Katunayake, Sri Lanka VCG 04 - Infectious substances, including diagnostic specimens and biological products, are not permit- ted in international mail either to or from Sri Lanka VCG 05 - No transport by air of any weapons, explosives or other dangerous devices, articles or sub- stances which may be used to commit an act of unlawful interference, may take place from to or in

chunks.heading: 10.5.1 Sri Lanka (VCG)
chunks.text: transit through Sri Lanka VCG 06 -English language shall be used for marking packages and over packs. VCG 07 - Radioactive shipments need prior approval from the Sri Lanka Atomic Energy Regulatory Coun- cil when transported by air. VCG 8: On shipment to, from or transiting through Sri Lanka, a 24hr emergency response tele- phone number of a person who has all the information on the contents (Including access, country, and city codes) must be provided on the shipper’s declaration form

chunks.heading: 10.6 Operator variations
chunks.text: Operators may impose additional restrictions to the ICAO and IATA regulations known as operator vari- ance

chunks.heading: 10.6.1 Srilankan Airlines (UL)
chunks.text: UL-01 The shipper must provide a 24-hour emergency telephone number of a person/agency who is knowledgeable of the hazards, characteristics and actions to be taken in the case of an accident or inci- dent concerning each of the dangerous goods being transported. chunks.heading: 10.7 Dangerous Goods Strictly Forbidden for Air Transport
chunks.text: Substances and objects that may combust, react dangerously, inflame, produce a dangerous evolution of heat, release toxic vapor, corrosives or inflammable gas or smoke under transportation conditions are strictly forbidden on aircraft Certain dangerous goods forbidden for transportation without an exception are considered to be highly dangerous for air transportation. It may however be possible for these goods to be carried on board in exceptional conditions and with approval of the relevant country. Carriage of dangerous goods is at the discretion of the carrier

chunks.heading: 10.8.1 Totally Prohibited dangerous goods
chunks.text: Cannot be transported by air under any circumstances.

chunks.heading: 10.8.2 Prohibited unless exempted
chunks.text: Under special exception from the authorities of the state, air transport is permitted

chunks.heading: 10.8.3 Transported as Air cargo
chunks.text: Items permitted on a passenger aircraft shall be permitted on a cargo aircraft. Items permitted on a cargo only aircraft shall not be permitted on a passenger aircraft.

chunks.heading: 10.8.4 Excepted Quantities
chunks.text: Special provisions for transport of very small quantities of dangerous goods as cargo, which exempts them for the usual provisions for Dangerous goods including documentation hazard labels and segrega- tion. Dangerous goods in excepted quantities are not required to be indicated on the NOTOC. Excepted quantities packages are not permitted on carry on or checked luggage and are marked with a special EXCEPTED QUANTITIES label.

chunks.heading: 10.8.5 Limited quantities
chunks.text: Items where the risk in carriage can be reduced to an acceptable level by limiting the quantity per package, and by packing in accordance with the regulations. Maximum gross weight is 30 kgs. Limited quantities packages are not permitted on carry on or checked luggage, are marked with a “Y” label and a UN specified packing is not required.

chunks.heading: 10.8.6 Treated as Non-Dangerous Goods
chunks.text: Articles and substances which do not fall within the definitions of dangerous goods as shown in these Regulations and which in the event of leakage may cause a serious clean-up problem or corrosion to aluminium on a long-term basis must be checked by the shipper to at least ensure that the packaging is adequate to prevent leakage during transportation. These may include brine, powdered or liquid dyes, pickled foodstuffs, etc.

chunks.heading: 10.9 Dangerous Goods In Operators Property
chunks.text:
DG regulations does not apply for the operator’s property carried for operational reasons/air worthi- ness and state requirements under specification such as,
1. Air worthiness Oxygen cylinders, Fire extinguishers
2. Consumer goods Aerosols alcohol, Perfume, Dry ice
3. Specifications Properly packed, stowed and monitored. The provisions have been expanded to allow operators to carry and use on board during flight electron- ic equipment such as personal entertainment devices and credit card readers containing lithium batter- ies and spare batteries for these devices. Replacement devices containing batteries and replacement batteries must be shipped in accordance with the regulations. (Properly packed to ensure the batteries will not short circuit) Ordered by procurement section as replacement or for Operator use must be shipped as Dangerous Goods.

chunks.heading: 10.10 Units of Measure
chunks.text: The units of measurement to be used in the transport of dangerous goods by air are those specified by the International System (SI) as modified for international civil Aviation by Annex 5 to the Chicago Con- vention on International Civil Aviation. SOLIDS Kilo grams

chunks.heading: LIQUIDS Litres
chunks.text: PRESSURE Pasqual’s RADIO ACTIVITY Becquerel’s. (Bq) RADIATION Sieverts (Sv) LENGTH Meters

chunks.heading: 10.11 Classes of Dangerous Goods
chunks.text: The regulations divide dangerous goods into 9 classes reflecting the type of risk involved, Some hazard classes are further subdivided into hazard divisions due to the wide scope of the class. The nine hazard classes and their divisions are listed below. The order in which they are numbered is for convenience and does not imply a relative degree of dan- ger, This means that class 1 is not necessarily more dangerous than class 3 or 4 etc

chunks.heading: 10.12 Subsidiary Risks
chunks.text: Some dangerous goods have properties which meet the definition of more than one hazard class or division. The less serious hazard of such substances is described as a subsidiary risk.

chunks.heading: 10.13 Marking and Labeling
chunks.text: Correct marking and labeling of dangerous goods packagers are important to handle them safely. It will enable to identify the hazard, contents and properly stow them. The hazards can be recognized without relying on accompanying documentation in an emergency

chunks.heading: 10.13.1 Marking
chunks.text: The shipper is responsible for all marking of exact package of dangerous goods

chunks.heading: 10.13.2 Labeling
chunks.text: Each package must be of such a size that there is adequate space to affix all required hazard and han- dling labels

chunks.heading: 10.14 Hazard labels
chunks.text: Hazard labels are used to identify the nine classes of dangerous goods. A typical hazard label has a diamond shape with the hazard identification symbol on the top half and the class or division number in the bottom corner. The hazard label indicates the type of danger the article may pose. A package with a hazard label must not be allowed in the cabin or cockpit. Should you discover a package with a hazard label in the cabin, check with the passenger and notify the PIC immediately. In some instances, the box may have previously been used to pack dangerous goods, but now contains other harmless material. In this case the label must be removed from the box PIC/Ground staff kept informed.

chunks.heading: 10.15 Handling Labels
chunks.text: Handling labels are Rectangle in shape In addition to hazard labels, handling labels are used to provide information on the proper handling and stowage of packages of dangerous goods.

chunks.heading: 10.18 Dangerous Goods Emergency Procedure
chunks.text:
General The first alert to a dangerous goods spillage or leak may be from a passenger who notices an unusual odor or fumes or who simply identifies an item that is leaking from cabin baggage. when a dangerous good is discovered in the cabin, crew must notify the flight crew immediately. The cabin crew should ask the passenger concerned to identify the item. The passenger may be able to provide the cabin crew with some guidance on the hazard involved. The cabin crew should try to collect as much information as possible, e.g. check for:
• A dangerous goods label
• Numbers on the packaging
• Written information on the packaging
• Odours
• Fumes
• Smoke
• An effect on passengers. When assessing an appropriate course of action to be taken in the event of an incident involving dan- gerous goods, the following should be considered, Note: These conditions apply whether the aircraft is involved is carrying passengers, cargo, or both.

chunks.heading: 10.18.1 Dangerous Goods in The Cargo Compartments
chunks.text: The passengers and crew should be evacuated from the aircraft prior to any attempt is made to open the cargo compartment doors. The cargo compartment doors should be opened with the emergency services in attendance.

chunks.heading: 10.18.2 Flight Crew Procedure
chunks.text:
1. The PIC shall land as soon as possible.
2. Use protective breathing equipment (Gas-tight breathing equipment shall be worn when attend- ing to an incident involving fire or fumes)
3. The (NOTOC) is immediately made available to the rescue and firefighting services along with Emergency Response Guidance (ERG)

chunks.heading: 10.18.3 Cabin Crew Procedure
chunks.text: CCM should take prompt action and move passengers away from the area involved, if necessary, pro- vide wet towels or cloth and give instructions to breathe through them.

chunks.heading: 10.18.4 Emergency Response Kit (ERK)
chunks.text: In case of leakage/spillage use the items contained in the Emergency Response Kit.

chunks.heading: 10.18.4.1 Location
chunks.text:
• A 330 aircraft - R2 overhead compartment
• A 320 aircraft - L2 overhead compartment (MRE - R2 overhead comperment)
• A 321 aircraft - R4 overhead compartment

chunks.heading: 10.18.4.2 Improvise Galley Equipment
chunks.text: Many items may be found in galleys that can be used for emergency responses such as, boxes/heat-fire resistant gloves/polyethylene bags/blankets/ towels etc.

chunks.heading: 10.18.4.3 Protection
chunks.text: Hands should be protected before touching suspicious packages or bottles. Fire-resistant gloves or oven gloves covered by polyethylene bags may provide suitable protection.

chunks.heading: 10.18.4.4 Reaction
chunks.text:
Care should be taken when mopping up spillage or leakage to ensure no reaction is created between what is to be used to mop and the DG item. If reaction is suspected, mopping up should be avoided and the spillage should be covered with polyethylene bags. 10.19 A Spillage or Suspected Dangerous Goods in Powder Form.
1. Items affected should be left undisturbed
2. The spill should not be covered with a fire agent or diluted with water
3. Passengers should be moved away from the area
4. The area should be covered using polyethylene/plastic bags or blankets
5. The area should be kept isolated
6. After landing inform ground staff who shall inform the DG coordinator
7. Qualified personnel shall deal with the item
8. Purser to carry out necessary documentation

chunks.heading: WARNING: DO NOT LEAVE HANDS UNPROTECTED WHEN TOUCHING SUSPICIOUS PACKAGES
chunks.text: OR BOTTLES. CAUTION: IN GENERAL, WATER SHOULD NOT BE USED ON A SPILLAGE OR WHEN FUMES ARE PRESENT AS IT MAY HELP SPREAD THE SPILLAGE OR INCREASE THE RATE OF FUMING. CONSID-

chunks.heading: ERATION SHOULD ALSO BE GIVEN TO THE POSSIBLE PRESENCE OF ELECTRICAL COMPONENTS
chunks.text: WHEN USING WATER.

chunks.heading: 10.19.1 Disembark Passengers/Crew
chunks.text: Even if it has not been necessary to complete an emergency evacuation after landing, passengers and crew should disembark before any attempt is made to open the cargo compartment doors or further action is taken to deal with a dangerous goods incident. The cargo compartment doors should be opened with the emergency services in attendance. Ground Personnel/Emergency Services should be informed of nature of the item and the location. Pass on any other relevant information by the quickest available means including a copy of the NOTOC.

chunks.heading: 10.20 Undeclared/Mis-declared DG Items Check List
chunks.text:
Srilankan Airlines has to report any undeclared or mis declared dangerous goods discovered in the cargo or in the passenger baggage to the CAASL within 24 hours after occurrence of the incident. Such reports must also be sent to the appropriate authority of the State in which this occurred. Procedures Retrieval Prior To Flight When a DG item is undeclared or mis-declared by a passenger the ground staff should retrieve the item prior to departure. Carry out necessary documentation and inform the DG coordinator. Retrieval during Flight When a DG item is undeclared or mis-declared by a passenger and identified by the crew,
1. PIC should be informed immediately,
2. Retrieve item from passenger, place in a thick polyethylene bag and stow in a safe location, (Empty cart/container/overhead compartment)
3. After landing, identify the item to the ground staff who shall inform the DG coordinator
4. Carryout the necessary documentation (Incident/Accident Report)

chunks.heading: 10.20 Undeclared/Mis-declared DG Items Check List
chunks.text: DG item may be allowed to be carried in acceptable quantities subject to obtaining prior approval from the operator.

chunks.heading: 10.21 Dangerous Goods Incident/Accident Procedure
chunks.text: Notify PIC Any incident concerning dangerous goods should be notified immediately to the pilot-in-command who should be kept informed of all actions taken and of their effect. It is essential that the cabin crew and

chunks.heading: 10.21 Dangerous Goods Incident/Accident Procedure
chunks.text: the flight crew coordinate their actions and that each is kept fully informed of the other’s actions and intentions. Minimizing the spreading of smoke and fumes into the flight deck is critical for the contin- ued safe operation of the aircraft, therefore it is always essential to keep the flight deck door closed. Crew communication and coordination are of utmost importance. The use of the interphone is the primary means of communication unless the interphone system fails. Identify the Item Ask the passenger concerned to identify the item and indicate its potential hazards. The passenger may be able to give some guidance on the hazard(s) involved and how these could be dealt with. In Case of Fire Use Standard Procedure/Check Use Of Water Standard emergency procedures shall be used to deal with any fire. In general, water should not be used on a spillage or when fumes are present since it may spread the spillage or increase the rate of

chunks.heading: 10.21 Dangerous Goods Incident/Accident Procedure
chunks.text: fuming. Consideration should also be given to the possible presence of electrical components when using water.

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: Collect emergency response kit and other useful items Collect emergency response kit and other useful items for use in dealing with the spillage or leakage: A supply of paper towels or newspapers or other absorbent paper or absorbent fabric (e.g. Seat cushion covers, head rest protectors); Oven gloves or fire-resistant gloves, if available; At least two large polyethylene waste bin bags; and At least three smaller polyethylene bags, such as those used for duty-free or bar sales or, if none available, airsickness bags Don rubber gloves and smoke hood The hands should always be protected before touching suspicious packages or items. Fire-resistant gloves or oven gloves covered by polyethylene bags are likely to give suitable protection. A PBE should always be worn when attending to an incident involving smoke, fumes or fire. Move passengers away from area and distribute wet towels The use of therapeutic oxygen bottles or the passenger drop-out oxygen system to assist passengers

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: in a smoke- or fume-filled passenger cabin should not be considered since considerable quantities of fumes or smoke would be inhaled through the valves or holes in the masks. A more effective aid to passengers in a smoke- or fume-filled environment would be the use of a wet towel or cloth held over the mouth and nose. A wet towel or cloth aids in filtering and is more effective at doing this than a dry towel or cloth. Cabin crew should take prompt action if smoke or fumes develop and move passen- gers away from the area involved and, if possible, provide wet towels and give instructions to breathe through them. Place dangerous goods item in polyethylene bags If it is absolutely certain that the item will not create a problem, the decision may be made not to move

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: it. In most circumstances, however, it will be better to move the item and this should be done as sug- gested below. Place the item in a polyethylene bag as follows: Prepare two bags by rolling up the sides and placing them on the floor; Place the item inside the first bag with the closure of the item, or the point from which it is leaking from its container, at the top; Close the first bag while squeezing out the excess air; Twist the open end of the first bag and use a bag tie to tie it sufficiently tight to be secure but not so tight that pressure equalization cannot take place; Take off the rubber gloves while avoiding skin contact with any contamination on them; Place the rubber gloves in the second bag Place the first bag (containing the item) in the second bag, which already contains the rubber gloves and secure the open end in the same manner as that used for the first bag. Stow polyethylene bags

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: If there is a catering or bar box on board, empty any contents and place the box on the floor, with the door upward. Place the bag(s) containing the item and any soiled towels, etc., in the box and close the door. Take the box or, if there is no box, the bag(s) to a position as far away as possible from the flight deck to a rear inbound toilet. Do not place bag(s) against the pressure bulkhead or fuselage wall. If a rear galley is used, bag(s) can be stowed in an empty waste bin container. The toilet door should be locked from the outside. In a pressurized aircraft, if a toilet is used, any fumes will be vented away from passengers. Receptacle containing the dangerous goods is kept upright or the area of leakage is kept at the top. Ensure that the position of the box or bags will not impede disembarkation from the aircraft Treat affected seat cushions/covers in the same manner as Dangerous goods item

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: Seat cushions, seat backs or other furnishings which have been contaminated by a spillage should be removed from their fixtures and placed in a large bin bag or other polyethylene bag, together with any bags used initially to cover them. They should be stowed away in the same manner as the dangerous goods item causing the incident. Cover spillage on carpet/floor Cover any spillage on the carpet or furnishings with a waste bag or other polyethylene bags, if availa- ble. If not, use airsickness bags opened out so that the plastic side covers the spillage or use the plastic covered emergency information cards. Carpet which has been contaminated by a spillage and which is still causing fumes despite being covered, should be rolled up, if possible, and placed in a large bin bag or other polyethylene bag. It should be placed in a waste bin and stowed, when possible, either in the rear toilet or rear galley. If the carpet cannot be removed it should remain covered by a large bin bag or

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: polyethylene bags, etc., and additional bags should be used to reduce the fumes. Regularly inspect items stowed away/contaminated Furnishings Any dangerous goods, contaminated furnishings or equipment which have been removed and stowed away or covered for safety should be subject to regular inspection. After landing

chunks.heading: 10.21.1 In Case of Spillage or Leakage
chunks.text: Identify the item Identify to the Ground Personnel DG Item and where stowed upon arrival. Pass on any other relevant information. Assist the emergency response team in furnishing specific and accurate details of the DG item and behaviour. Inform the DGR Coordinator Inform the DGR coordinator the location of DGR item type of hazard experienced ect. Entry in Maintenance and Cabin Defects Logbook Make an entry in the aircraft maintenance logbook for maintenance work, and that the emergency response kit or any aircraft equipment used is replenished or replaced.

chunks.heading: 10.22 PED Fires - Cabin Crew Checklist
chunks.text: Description: - The following checklist is based upon guidance issued in the ICAO Emergency Response Guidance for Aircraft Incidents Involving Dangerous Goods. In case of fire involving a portable electronic device: Notify PIC Any occurrence concerning a fire in the cabin should be notified immediately to the pilot-in-command who should be kept informed of all actions taken and of the effect. It is essential that the cabin crew and the flight crew coordinate their actions and that each is kept fully informed of the other’s actions and intentions. Identify the item It may not be possible to identify the item (source of fire) right away, especially if the fire has started in a seat pocket or the device is not readily accessible. In this case, firefighting procedures should be applied as a first step. If the item is contained in baggage, the crew’s actions would be similar to the actions for a device that is visible or readily accessible.

chunks.text: CAUTION: IN ORDER TO AVOID INJURY FROM A FLASH FIRE, IT IS NOT RECOMMENDED TO OPEN THE AFFECTED BAGGAGE WHEN THERE IS ANY INDICATION OF SMOKE OR FLAMES. It is im- portant to wear available protective equipment (e.g. protective breathing equipment, fire gloves) when fighting a fire. Communication and coordination are of utmost importance. The use of the interphone Remove power It is important to instruct the passenger to disconnect the device from the power supply, if it is deemed safe to do so. A battery has a higher likelihood of catching fire due to overheating during or immediately following a charging cycle, although the effects may be delayed for some period of time. By removing the external power supply from the device, it will be assured that additional energy is not being fed to the battery to promote a fire. Visually check that power to the remaining electrical outlets remains off until the aircraft’s system can be determined to be free of faults, if the device was previously plugged in. The removal of power may occur simultaneously to other cabin crew actions (e.g. obtaining water to douse the device). Depending on the aircraft type, in-seat power may have to be turned off by the flight crew members. Caution: Do not attempt to remove the battery from the device. Douse the device with water (or non-flammable liquid) Water (or other non-flammable liquid) must be used to cool a battery that has ignited to prevent the spread of heat to other cells in the battery. If water is not available, any non-flammable liquid may be used to cool the device. Note. — Liquid may turn to steam when applied to the hot battery. Leave the device in its place and monitor for any reignition A battery involved in a fire can reignite and emit flames multiple times as heat is

chunks.heading: NON-FLAMMABLE LIQUID. THIS SHOULD BE DONE WITH EXTREME CAUTION AND ONLY AFTER
chunks.text:
CAUTION:
A) DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PICK UP OR MOVE THE DEVICE; BATTERIES MAY EXPLODE OR BURST INTO FLAMES WITHOUT WARNING. THE DEVICE MUST NOT BE MOVED IF DISPLAYING ANY OF THE FOLLOWING: FLAMES/FLARING, SMOKE, UNUSUAL SOUNDS (SUCH AS CRACKLING), DEBRIS, OR SHARDS OF MATERIAL SEPARATING FROM THE DEVICE.
B) DO NOT COVER OR ENCLOSE THE DEVICE AS IT COULD CAUSE IT TO OVERHEAT.
C) DO NOT USE ICE OR DRY ICE TO COOL THE DEVICE. ICE OR OTHER MATERIALS INSULATE THE

chunks.heading: DEVICE, INCREASING THE LIKELIHOOD THAT ADDITIONAL BATTERY CELLS WILL REACH THER -
chunks.text: MAL RUNAWAY.

chunks.heading: (e.g. APPROXIMATELY 10-15 MINUTES)
chunks.text: The device can be moved with caution following a certain period, once it has cooled down and if there is no evidence of smoke, heat, or if there is a reduction in the crackling or hissing sound usually asso- ciated with a lithium battery fire (e.g. after approximatly10-15 minutes). The waiting period may vary based on the device and its size. A suitable empty container (line it with 2 waste bin liners), such as a pot, jug, galley unit or toilet waste bin, must be filled with enough water or non-flammable liquid to completely submerge the device. It is important to wear available protective equipment (e.g. protective breathing equipment, fire gloves), when moving any device involved in a fire. Once the device is com- pletely submerged, the container used must be stowed and, if possible, secured to prevent spillage. MONITOR THE DEVICE AND THE SURROUNDING AREA FOR THE REMAINDER OF THE FLIGHT

chunks.heading: (e.g. APPROXIMATELY 10-15 MINUTES)
chunks.text: Monitor the device and the surrounding area for the remainder of the flight to verify that the device does not pose further risk. Complete the required documentation, so that the engineering is notified of the event, proper mainte- nance action is undertaken and the emergency response kit or any aircraft equipment used is replen- ished or replaced, if applicable.

chunks.heading: 10.23 Hidden Dangerous Goods
chunks.text:
Articles and Substances under a general description may contain hazardous articles that are not ap- parent. Such articles may also be found in baggage. With the aim of preventing undeclared dangerous goods from being loaded on an aircraft and passengers from taking on board those dangerous goods which are not permitted in their baggage. Check-in staff shall check with passengers if such items have been packed.

chunks.heading: 10.24.4 Dangerous Goods Emergency Response Guidance
chunks.text: Emergency procedures for flight crew in relation to dangerous goods can be found in the current ICAO publication Emergency Response Guidance (ERG) for aircraft incidents involving Dangerous Goods (doc9481-AN/928), generally referred as Red Book. A copy of this document is available in the EFB. Cab- in crew shall use the ERG for reference.

chunks.heading: 10.24.5 Power banks carried by passengers and crew for Personal Use
chunks.text:
1. Limited to a maximum of two (02) power banks per passenger. a Lithium-Ion batteries - Watt hour rating equal to or less than 100 Wh.
b. Lithium metal batteries - equal to or less than 2g of lithium metal
2. A maximum of two (02) power banks with a watt-hour (Wh) rating exceeding 100 Wh but not exceeding 160 Wh may be carried, subject to operator approval
3. Power banks are forbidden for transport in checked baggage and shall be carried only as carry on baggage
4. Shall not be charged using in seat/inflight power during all phases of flight.
5. Shall not be used to recharge or power other portable electronic device during critical phases of flight. (during taxi, take-off and landing)
6. Not be placed in cabin baggage loaded in the overhead storage compartment. They shall be placed in cabin baggage under the seat or the seat pocket in front.
7. Must be individually protected to prevent short circuiting when not in use (by placement in orig-

chunks.heading: 10.24.5 Power banks carried by passengers and crew for Personal Use
chunks.text: inal retail packaging or by otherwise insulating terminals, e.g. by taping over exposed terminals or placing each power bank in a separate plastic bag or protective pouch).

chunks.heading: 10.24.5.1 Portable electronic devices/Power Banks/Spare batteries carried by the Flight
chunks.text: Crew/Cabin Crew in the performance of their operational duties. Portable electronic devices, such as electronic flight bags, personal entertainment devices, and credit card readers, containing lithium metal or Lithium-ion cells or batteries and spare lithium batteries for such devices or power banks carried onboard shall meet the above provisions and conditions for the carriage. Flight and cabin crew shall adhere to all regulations and restrictions as stated when carrying such devices to carry out the functions for which they are responsible. Any portable electronic devices containing lithium metal or lithium-Ion cells or batteries carried on- board for use or Duty-free sale during the flight or series of flights shall meet the provision and condi- tions for carriage. Spare lithium batteries and power banks must be individually protected to prevent short circuiting and protected from unintentional activation when not in use.

chunks.heading: 10.24.5.1 Portable electronic devices/Power Banks/Spare batteries carried by the Flight
chunks.text:
Power Banks/Spare batteries carried by crew for the purpose of carrying out their operational duties a Lithium metal batteries - lithium content shall not exceed 2g
b. Lithium-ion batteries shall not exceed a watt hour rating of 100. Crew members may carry up to two (02) power banks, with each power bank limited to a maximum rating of 100 Wh or 2g and carried in carry-on baggage only Cabin crew shall ensure passengers are made aware of the applicable requirements through the ap- proved onboard announcement (SEPM Ref 2.15.2.23), monitor compliance with these requirements throughout all phases of flight, and address any non-compliance or safety concerns immediately in accordance with standard operating procedures.

chunks.heading: 10.25.1 Suspected dangerous goods in powder form
chunks.text:
1. Inform PIC
2. Leave item undisturbed
3. Do not use an extinguisher or a non-flammable liquid if fumes are visible
4. Move passengers away
5. Cover using a non-absorbent material
6. Isolate area
7. After landing inform ground staff who shall inform the DG coordinator. Qualified personnel shall deal with the item
8. Purser - Carry out necessary documentation

chunks.heading: 10.25.2 Dangerous Goods Incidents/Accident Procedure
chunks.text:
Initial Action
1. Notify PIC
2. Identify the item In Case of Fire
3. Use standard procedures/check use of water In case of spillage or leakage
4. Collect emergency response kit or other useful items
5. Don rubber gloves and smoke hood
6. Move passengers away from area and distribute wet towels or cloth
7. Place dangerous goods item in polyethylene bags and stow
8. Treat affected items in the same manner as dangerous goods item
9. Cover spillage on carpet/floor
10. Regularly inspect items stowed away and contaminated furnishings After Landing
11. Identify to ground personnel dangerous goods item
12. Make appropriate entry in maintenance and Cabin Defects log book
13. Inform the DGR Coordinator

chunks.heading: 10.25.3 PED Fires
chunks.text:
1. Inform PIC
2. Identify the item
3. Use standard firefighting procedure
4. Disconnect from electrical outlet if possible or switch off power
5. Douse adjacent cells with water to prevent ignition
6. Do not move the item
7. If item involves aircraft equipment switch off power and check before switching on power for defective systems (High Voltage, Short Circuits)
8. When the device has cooled (after 10-15 mints) fill a container with enough water (or non-flam-

chunks.heading: 10.25.3 PED Fires
chunks.text:
mable liquid) and using protective equipment, place the device in the container to completely submerge. Stow in toilet (away from flight deck) and secure the container to prevent spillage.
9. Purser – Make necessary documentation

chunks.heading: 10.25.4 Lithium battery fire in the flight Deck
chunks.text:
On identifying a Lithium Battery fire
1. Flight deck crew shall inform the cabin crew
2. CCM shall ensure all flight crew are on oxygen,
3. Don a PBE/ heat resistant gloves
4. Use a HALON extinguisher to contain/ extinguish the fire
5. Disconnect device from the power outlet
6. If no flames are visible or the fire is extinguished, Remove the device from flight deck
7. If smoke becomes a greater threat – Flight deck crew to initiate smoke removal procedure
8. When the device has cooled (after 10-15 mints) fill a container with enough water (or non-flam- mable liquid) and using protective equipment, place the device in the container to completely submerge. Stow in toilet (away from flight deck) and secure the container to prevent spillage.
9. Monitor regularly
10. On landing identify the item to ground staff
11. Inform DGR coordinator and carry out a log entry

chunks.heading: 10.25.5 PED inadvertently crushed or damaged in electrically/Mechanically adjustable seat
chunks.text:
1. Notify PIC / Other CCMs
2. Obtain information from passenger, To identify the item
3. Where he/she suspects that the item may have dropped or slipped into.
4. If the seat was moved since misplacing the item.
5. Don protective equipment and retrieve item.
6. If smoke or flames appear, Apply PED FIRE checklist.
7. After landing inform ground staff
8. Purser to make necessary documentation.
